title: Detroit Lions vs. New Orleans Saints preview, prediction: On Paper
summary: Welcome back to another season of On Paper, my statistical-heavy Detroit Lions preview that attempts to be as objective as possible. For those new to On Paper, a brief explanation. At the heart of On Paper are eight charts that detail each team’s primary units (pass offense, run offense, pass defense, run defense). Those charts […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - DECEMBER 03: Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions throws a pass in the first quarter against the New Orleans Saints at the Caesars Superdome on December 03, 2023 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Chris Graythen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome back to another season of On Paper, my statistical-heavy Detroit Lions preview that attempts to be as objective as possible. For those new to On Paper, a brief explanation. At the heart of On Paper are eight charts that detail each team’s primary units (pass offense, run offense, pass defense, run defense). Those charts are filled with weekly performances that compare it to the opponent’s average. This provides proper context to show that holding the Lions passing offense to 120 yards is much different than holding the Jets to that yardage. Cells that are green indicate a better than average performance, yellow is within 5% of averages, and red means you stunk that week. Then we compare the units that face off. If there’s one thing about NFL previews that enrages me, it’s when analysts compare units (ie: who has the better offense, defense, QB?). That doesn’t matter. The quarterbacks don’t ever share the field. Instead, it matters how the Lions pass offense matches with the opponent’s pass defense. So after throwing a bunch of stats at you, I provide a key matchup and my overall thoughts on who has the advantage in each matchup—which is graded on a 1-5 scale based on how big the advantage is, how important I believe that matchup is to the overall outcome, and just my overall confidence. This is the only part that is a bit subjective. At the end, I add up all the advantages, see who has the edge, and provide a final score prediction. In the comments, be sure to give your score prediction. The closest to the actual score will get a shout out in next week’s On Paper . Now, let’s get to it. Lions pass offense (6th in DVOA in 2025) vs. Saints pass defense (19th) Despite a running game that fell apart, significant issues on the offensive line, and an offensive coordinator that just didn’t fit, Jared Goff and the Lions passing offense remained pretty efficient all season. The 2025 season will always be a great counter-example to those who claim Goff needs everything to be perfect around him to be successful. In 2025, the Lions and Goff finished: 4th in yards per attempt (7.4) 3rd in passer rating (103.6) 7th in dropback EPA (0.167) 9th in dropback success rate (48.5%) By nearly every metric, this was a top-10 passing offense. So what has changed this year? Well, in terms of weapons, nothing is really all that different. Sam LaPorta is healthier, Isaac TeSlaa is a year older, and that’s about it. But the offensive line has been completely revamped. Penei Sewell went from right to left tackle. Rookie Blake Miller takes his spot on the right. Cade Mays Juice Scruggs takes over at center for Graham Glasgow. And Ben Bartch and Christian Mahogany are still battling for the left guard position. Second-year right guard Tate Ratledge? You just stay there and keep being you. Pass protection was an issue last year. Despite Goff being one of the quickest quarterbacks in time-to-throw (fifth), he also faced the 14th-highest pressure rate, and took a career-high 38 sacks (eighth among all NFL quarterbacks). The Lions also ranked 31st in ESPN’s pass block win rate and 24th in PFF pass blocking grade. Are the Lions decidedly better on the offensive line in 2026? It’s impossible to know right now, but I’m not entirely optimistic it will look better to start the year given just how many moving parts there are. So some protection issues should be expected early, but Goff should still be able to orchestrate at a top-10 level of efficiency. The Saints’ pass defense wasn’t good last year, but as you can see from the chart, it got significantly better as the season went on. Part of that is due to playing ONLY terrible passing offenses in their final eight games, but it’s reasonable to think they also improved as a unit down the stretch. If you didn’t pay attention to the quality of their opponents, the difference between the first and second half of the season would be incredibly stark: Weeks 1-9 29th in passer rating allowed (107.2) 26th in dropback EPA 27th in dropback success rate Week 10-18 7th in passer rating allowed (74.7) 5th in dropback EPA 1st in dropback success rate Those are drastic swings and shouldn’t be ignored completely. It’s very normal for a team to start figuring things out in Year 1 of a new coaching staff toward the end of the season. But… also… just look at those offenses. They didn’t face a single team who averaged a passer rating above 90 in their final eight games. That makes trying to predict how 2026 will go difficult. The Saints didn’t make a ton of changes on defense this offseason. They lost linebacker Demario Davis but replaced him with a far younger Kaden Ellis. They also bolstered the interior of their defensive line with second-round pick Christen Miller… but they lost Brian Bresee to a season-ending injury and Cam Jordan won’t play this week. Last year, the Saints were pretty inconsistent as a pass rushing team. They ranked 24th in pressure rate (31.9%), 23rd in PFF pass rushing grade (66.6), and 22nd in ESPN pass rush win rate (35%), but they still produced the 10th-most sacks. Coverage was a different story. Kool-Aid McKinstry had a bit of a breakout year (17 passes defended, 3 INTs), and the Saints sport a trusted safety duo in Justin Reid (66.7 PFF grade last year) and Julian Blackmon (82.4). Player to watch: Chase Young vs. Blake Miller. Right, I forgot about Young. Despite playing just 12 games, he produced 49 pressures and 10.0 sacks. Last year, he almost played exclusively opposite the left tackle (529 snaps there vs. just 13 on the right), but I wouldn’t be surprised to see New Orleans change up strategy when the options are Penei Sewell or a rookie in his first NFL game. Advantage: Lions +1. I’m probably not going to move far from +1s early in the season with very little relevant data to go off of. However, I can feel pretty confident in Detroit here because they’ve been doing it longer and more consistently, and I’m still not sure who the Saints are just because they played a bunch of terrible offenses to finish 2025. Lions run offense (10th) vs. Saints run defense (8th) After some inconsistent—but occasionally great—performances early in the season, Detroit’s run offense absolutely collapsed down the stretch, and it was a big part of their downfall—losing four of their last six games. The season-long stats are not encouraging. Detroit ranked just: 9th in yards per carry (4.6) 23rd in rush EPA (-0.037) 16th in rushing success rate (41.0%) The only thing that kept Detroit’s stats even mildly afloat were the explosive runs from Jahmyr Gibbs. He ranked ninth in 10+ yard rushes (27), third in 20+ yard rushes (10), and t-second in 30+ yard rushes (six). The Lions offensive line ranked 13th in PFF run grade, 20th in run block win rate, and 20th in adjusted line yards. There is hope the offensive line changes and a switch to a more innovative offensive coordinator will help out the run game this year, but that remains a theory, not a fact. The Saints gave up a lot of rushing yardage last year (2050, 14th most), but that was largely a result of always trailing in games and facing the third most rushing attempts in the league. On a per-play, basis, they were actually quite sound. In 2025, they ranked: Eighth in yards per carry allowed (4.0) 2nd in rush EPA (-0.136) 9th in rush success rate (39.0%) That’s the bad news for Detroit. The good news? Two of the Saints best run defenders from last year will not be playing in this game. Demario Davis—their leader and best linebacker who posted an 89.3 run defense grade—left in free agency. And veteran defensive lineman (82.1 grade) Cam Jordan is out with an injury. Kaden Ellis, the linebacker they added this offseason, doesn’t…
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Lions vs. Saints preview: 3 key player matchups
summary: The Detroit Lions and the New Orleans Saints will open their 2026 campaigns at Ford Field, both hungry to put their respective fourth-place division finishes in the rearview mirror. Despite each sharing last-place finishes in 2025, that is about the only thing the Lions and Saints have in common headed into the new season. New […]
full_text: The Detroit Lions and the New Orleans Saints will open their 2026 campaigns at Ford Field, both hungry to put their respective fourth-place division finishes in the rearview mirror. Despite each sharing last-place finishes in 2025, that is about the only thing the Lions and Saints have in common headed into the new season. New Orleans is in year two of Kellen Moore’s tenure as head coach, and after a promising rookie season, Tyler Shough opens the season as the starting quarterback. At the top of the roster, wide receiver Chris Olave is likely the only All-Pro who will be active on gameday while still in a starting role. All-Pro running back Alvin Kamara has been recovering from an MCL sprain through training camp ( but could play ) while the Saints have added running back Travis Etienne to the room this offseason. Further, All-Pro defensive end Cam Jordan has been ruled out for the game with a hamstring injury. In contrast, the Lions will field young, All-Pro talents on both sides of the ball with Jack Campbell, Aidan Hutchinson, Amon-Ra St. Brown, and Penei Sewell. Beyond that, Jared Goff is entering his sixth season as the Lions’ quarterback, while Jahmyr Gibbs is the betting favorite for Offensive Player of the Year and was likely drafted as the first pick in most fantasy football drafts across the country. Why am I so focused on the blue-chip talent on each roster? Well, it is because identifying winning matchups and exploiting them is the center of Dan Campbell’s philosophy: “Here’s my philosophy on offense, and defense for that matter: We’re going to run a system that puts our best on your worst. That’s what we’re going to do because that’s what we did in New Orleans. We’re going to find a way to put our guys in one-one-one matchups, whether it’s run or pass. If you’re telling me that our left tackle is better than their right end, and we can run outside zone all day – we’re going to run outside zone, as long as we cut off the back side. Why not? If we can exploit a weakness, we’re going to do it.” With the apparent advantage the Lions have in elite talent at each level of the field on both sides of the ball, there should be plenty of areas where the coaching staff can dictate winning matchups. Let’s take a look at three of them. Jack Campbell vs. Tyler Shough It’s officially Captain Jack season. Jack Campbell enters his first year as a captain and the green-dot linebacker with complete ownership of the defense, facing a young passer in Shough. Campbell enters the year with this defense being his now. And it’s not just talk. Second-year defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard let him call the defense from the field for a full practice during training camp. Captain Jack Campbell. pic.twitter.com/oGMI1GMb36 — Detroit Lions (@Lions) September 8, 2026 With all due respect to the ascending quarterback, Shough will simply be in a very difficult environment to succeed on Sunday. In his favor, Shough will play behind what appears to be a strong offensive line on paper. From left to right, the line includes 2025 first-round pick Kelvin Banks Jr., newly acquired left guard David Edwards, Erik McCoy at center, right guard Cesar Ruiz, and 2024 first-round pick Taliese Fuaga at right tackle. Conventional wisdom would suggest that head coach Kellen Moore will try to support his young quarterback by leaning heavily on the run game behind this offensive line. But that creates an interesting opportunity for Campbell to show off his command of the defense. As the quarterback of the defense, Campbell will be responsible for communicating and adapting Kelvin Sheppard’s evolving disguise-oriented scheme . The Saints and Shough ranked 30th in the NFL in play action rate at just 18.6% in 2025, per NFL NextGen Stats . If New Orleans wants to establish the run but not put Detroit’s box defenders in conflict through play action, then Campbell’s job on gameday is one layer less complicated. The less Campbell is forced to be reactive, the more he can lead the Lions defense. D.J. Reed vs. Chris Olave While the Lions have plenty of blue-chip talent, the one area of the team that is lacking elite, proven talent is the secondary. Expect the Saints to try to use their best matchup piece, Chris Olave, to their advantage. But it might not be that simple. Just as only four wide receivers made the Lions’ initial 53-man roster, the Saints also kept only four on the active roster: Olave, Devaughn Vele, and rookies Bryce Lance and Barion Brown. Missing from this list is 2026 first-round pick Jordyn Tyson. As a result, the key matchup to watch is Lions cornerback D.J. Reed against Olave. The question of whether Reed can bounce back after his first season in Detroit was hampered by a significant hamstring injury will be critically telling about the team’s ultimate ceiling. Week 1 will be an excellent first test. Olave finished the 2025 season with a 27.9 percent target share for the Saints, which ranked seventh among wide receivers who had at least 100 targets on the year, per NFL NextGen Stats . Kelvin Sheppard will have a few options to slow down the Saints offense. Without a true stable of experienced wide receivers available for New Orleans, Sheppard will have the luxury of devoting more resources to stop the run, put pressure on the passer, or mix double coverage looks toward Olave. But the best-case scenario is if Reed can match up with Olave stride for stride. If Reed can limit the All-Pro receiver to a modest season opener, the options for Sheppard become variable and unpredictable. That makes Reed’s assignment more than just an individual matchup, but an opportunity to give Sheppard more freedom for the rest of the defense. Detroit interior OL vs. New Orleans interior DL One of the biggest questions of training camp in Detroit has been how the interior offensive line would look after the position battle at left guard between Christian Mahogany and Ben Bartch, along with newly acquired center Cade Mays. Well, the injury to Mays means Juice Scruggs is in line to be the starting center likely until the Week 6 bye, and Bartch’s battle through his own injuries has given the edge to the guard spot to Mahogany (for now) . Right guard, however, is a different story. Second-year, second-round pick Tate Ratledge is poised to break out after a strong finish to 2025 that has carried over into a strong 2026 training camp. Across the line, the Lions’ interior three will face a Saints group that is missing its best defensive tackle. Bryan Breese suffered a season-ending ACL injury early in camp , leaving New Orleans vulnerable. To fill the void, the Saints will show a rotation of veterans Davon Godchaux, Nathan Shepherd, John Ridgeway, and rookie second-round pick Christen Miller. This creates an opportunity for Detroit. Will the competition and depth in the Lions offensive line room prove themselves against a favorable matchup? Or will the offensive line start off on a poor note, inviting the same criticisms that followed the 2025 opener at Lambeau Field? The performance of Mahogany ( and/or Bartch ), Scruggs, and Ratledge will be under the magnifying glass of many Lions fans. Three key matchups. Three opportunities. Jack Campbell has an opportunity to make life difficult for a young quarterback. D.J. Reed has a chance to neutralize the Saints’ most prolific threat. And the Lions’ interior offensive line has a runway to establish itself against a New Orleans front missing one of its best players. It’s not a light; it’s a freight train. It’s about to be fun.
author: Anthony Balaj

title: 2026 NFL predictions: Detroit Lions’ record, NFC North winner
summary: As we’ve reached the end of the work week and it’s nearly, truly NFL Week 1, it’s time to really lean into some of our heavier predictions for the Detroit Lions’ 2026 season. If you ask the public, they seem evenly split about the future of the Lions. Some are convinced they’ll bounce right back […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 14: Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions celebrates a touchdown against the Chicago Bears at Ford Field on September 14, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images As we’ve reached the end of the work week and it’s nearly, truly NFL Week 1, it’s time to really lean into some of our heavier predictions for the Detroit Lions’ 2026 season. If you ask the public, they seem evenly split about the future of the Lions. Some are convinced they’ll bounce right back and be in the contender conversation. Others think 2025’s 9-8 disappointment was the beginning of the end. In today’s 2026 NFL prediction, we tackle two topics: What will the Lions’ record be in the regular season and playoffs — and who wins the NFC North? Let’s tackle them one-by-one. As always, you can make your own predictions by voting in the polls below each section. Previous 2026 Detroit Lions predictions: Offensive MVP predictions Defensive MVP predictions Breakout Player of the Year Rookie of the Year Who will win the NFC North? Anthony Balaj: Detroit Lions Ultimately they are the most complete team in the division with the most experienced quarterback. Morgan Cannon: Detroit Lions After a one-year hiatus from the top, the Lions will reclaim their grip on the NFC North crown. However, I do expect it to be a tight race for most of the regular season. Just like it has been the last several years, including in 2023 and 2024 when the Lions went back-to-back as division champions. Jeremy Reisman: Detroit Lions The Packers and Bears have far more questions about their defense than the Lions do, and only Chicago can match Detroit’s offensive performance, in my opinion. The Vikings are the wild card here, as I expect their defense to remain dominant. I’m not a big Kyler Murray believer, so give me the Lions. Ryan Mathews: Detroit Lions The Detroit Lions will win the NFC North. The Green Bay Packers will not win the NFC North. Al Karsten: Detroit Lions The Bears’ defense will prove too vulnerable for their offense to make any real postseason run in a regression season, while the Packers will struggle to keep treading water under Matt LaFleur with one of the worst combined offensive line and cornerback groups in football. The Vikings’ defensive attrition will keep Brian Flores’ unit from remaining quite elite enough. Their offense should improve under Kyler Murray and a refurbished rushing attack, but Minnesota will hover around .500 while flirting with a Wild Card spot. Meanwhile, it will be apparent from the starting gun that the Detroit Lions are the most complete, well-coached, and relentless team in the NFC North race. Dan Campbell’s crew will claim its third black-and-blue division crown in four years, but with its sights set on much bigger achievements. Erik Schlitt: Detroit Lions Look for a refocused Lions team to take advantage of a friendly schedule in 2026 and prove last year’s struggles are behind them. This team has some injury obstacles to overcome early in the season, but they are still loaded with talent and should be the favorites to win the majority of their games. John Whiticar: Detroit Lions I think the Bears are primed for a regression after wildly outperforming their luck last season. The Packers will be competitive as usual, but unless they can find a running game without Josh Jacobs, they will be a one-dimensional offense. The Vikings are a mess on offense, but they still have a great coach leading that defense. It will not be easy for the Lions despite a fourth-place schedule, but I think they have enough talent on both sides of the ball. Brandon Knapp: Detroit Lions Easiest schedule in the NFL, a roster that is going to get players back as the season goes on (Isiah Pacheco, Kerby Joseph, Brian Branch, Cade Mays) to help strengthen the team, and a new offensive coordinator who can fix the offense is a perfect combo for a winning season. The Bears and Packers have a tougher schedule, but also bigger question marks than the Lions do when it comes to their rosters. While the Vikings schedule is easier than the Bears and Packers, the offense needs to get fixed for them to be a true threat again as the defense can only take them so far. What will the Lions’ 2026 record be, and how far will they go in the playoffs? Anthony Balaj: 13-4, Super Bowl A slight gift of the last place schedule, the Lions earn the 1-seed and home-field advantage through the postseason. Ford Field will be electric as the Lions are Super Bowl bound after defeating the Dallas Cowboys in a shootout. Morgan Cannon: 12-5, Super Bowl 12-5 and I have them making it to the Super Bowl in Los Angeles. Can someone say storybook year for the likes of Lions quarterback Jared Goff and wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown.? Jeremy Reisman: 11-6, NFC Championship game I believe I’m a bit more skeptical than most when it comes to the Lions’ offensive line. Detroit did their best to improve from last year, but there’s only so much they could’ve done in one offseason. There are going to be a lot of bumps in the way, and that’s going to limit their efficiency early in the season. Conversely, I’m weirdly optimistic about the defense. And by the time the season ends, I wouldn’t be surprised if Detroit is sporting a top-10 unit on both sides of the ball. They ride that to the NFC Championship game, where the competition in the conference is just too challenging for a Super Bowl run. Ryan Mathews: 11-6, Super Bowl The Lions will go 11-6 this year, a firm step back in the right direction, returning to the playoffs in the process. Al Karsten: 13-4, Super Bowl The Detroit Lions will finish 13-4, securing the No. 2 seed in the NFC and home-field advantage for the first two rounds of the playoffs before winning the NFC Championship on the road. From there, Detroit will show that the NFC remains the superior conference by bringing home the Super Bowl for the third consecutive season—and fifth time in the last seven years. Erik Schlitt: 13-4, NFC Championship game As is tradition, when the schedule came out, I shared my prediction for the Lions’ season , and I see no reason to move off that spot: give me 13-4 with an NFC North title. I expect the Lions to host at least one playoff game at Ford Field and reach the NFC Championship. From there… well, I don’t want to jinx anything. John Whiticar: 11-6, Divisional round I am optimistic about the Lions roster except for one position: cornerback. As good as the rest of the roster could be, they have a glaring weakness at corner, both in terms of starters and depth. The rest of the team should be good enough to carry them through the regular season, but once the playoffs roll around, you need lights-out defensive play. I like the front seven, but the secondary makes me nervous if faced with a deep playoff push. Brandon Knapp: 13-4, NFC Championship game 13-4. NFC Championship game loss. The Lions take advantage of the weak schedule and win the division and claim the No. 2 seed in the NFC. I see them losing to the Bills, Patriots, and to the Packers and Vikings on the road. The loss to the Vikings is a game they shouldn’t lose, but that defense at home is tough to play. As for the playoffs, I think they lose to the Rams in the NFC title game, but this game isn’t as heartbreaking as the 49ers version. The Rams defensive line will be too much for Detroit’s young front and that will be the difference maker. Make your prediction for the Lions’ 2026 record here:

title: Detroit Lions sign Tom Kennedy to 53-man roster, add new defensive back

full_text: Aug 22, 2026; Detroit, Michigan, USA; Detroit Lions wide receiver Tom Kennedy (85) returns a kick against the Washington Commanders at Ford Field. Mandatory Credit: Lon Horwedel-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Detroit Lions finally filled the last spot on their 53-man roster, signing wide receiver Tom Kennedy from the practice squad to the active roster. To backfill Kennedy’s spot on the practice squad, Detroit added defensive back Natrone Brooks. Kennedy’s addition to the 53-man roster was expected, even if the delay was a bit odd. Earlier in the week, coach Dan Campbell leaked that Kennedy would play in Sunday’s game against the New Orleans Saints, and special teams coordinator Dave Fipp confirmed he would be the team’s starting punt returner, while also being in the mix at kick returner. Kennedy has been on and off the Lions’ roster for the past seven years. Detroit raves about his work ethic and his ability to provide depth to all of the wide receiver positions. It’s quite possible he’s the WR4 on the team behind starters Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jameson Williams, and Isaac TeSlaa. Former UFL receiver Tay Martin is also in that competition. As for Brooks, he has spent the last four offseasons with the Atlanta Falcons. He made a total of 26 game appearances and one start over the last two seasons. He initially made Atlanta’s 53-man roster this year, but after they claimed three players, he was cut and cleared waivers last week. While Brooks, 26, has previously spent the last three years in Atlanta working as a cornerback, he made the transition to safety this offseason. It’s unclear what position the Lions view him as, but Detroit could use a little more depth and insurance at safety while Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph are out.

full_text: Aug 2, 2026; Allen Park, MI, USA; Detroit Lions defensive back Christian Izien (27) looks on during Detroit Lions training camp at Meijer Performance Center. Mandatory Credit: Paul Barnick-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Detroit Lions and New Orleans Saints were back on the practice field on Thursday as they prepare for their Sunday afternoon showdown at Ford Field in Detroit. The Lions last practiced on Tuesday and provided an estimated injury report on Wednesday, but Thursday will be a true reflection of where players stand with their injuries. With that in mind, let’s take a look at Thursday’s injury report and get you up to date with what we know. N o practice on Thursday None Once again, every player on the active roster was accounted for and at practice, a terrific sign for those who unexpectedly landed on Wednesday’s injury report. Limited practice EDGE Derrick Moore (hamstring) DL Mekhi Wingo (groin) DB Christian Izien (groin) Moore’s hamstring injury was expected to keep him “down for a little bit,” but coach Dan Campbell was hopeful that, at this point in Week 1, he’d ”be ready to roll,” but back-to-back limited practices will put his availability in question. Wingo impressed with his athleticism and versatility in camp, but a groin injury could limit his impact, so his progress will be worth monitoring as we get closer to game time. Izien’s availability for the opening game was not clear the last time the media spoke with Campbell, but getting some practice work in is a step in the right direction. If available, the Lions would get a huge boost at nickel on defense and on special teams. Full practice LB Jimmy Rolder (hamstring) LB Trevor Nowaske (knee) CB Ennis Rakestraw (ankle) CB Keith Abney (hand) S Thomas Harper (ankle) While Rolder getting in another practice under his belt on Thursday is good news, it wouldn’t be surprising to see the Lions be cautious with him as he returns to game action. With seven linebackers on the roster, they can afford to take it slow with his rehabilitation. Nowaske’s late camp leg injury doesn’t seem like it will impact his availability too much, but we’ll see how the rest of the week plays out. Rakestraw and Abney were unexpected additions to this week’s injury report, so we’re hoping to get an update on their statuses on Friday when Campbell meets with the media again. That being said, full practices are very encouraging. Harper looks to be in a solid spot to return to play this week, and it sounds like coaches are planning on him being available. title: 9 takeaways from Detroit Lions coordinators: Week 1 vs. Saints
summary: The three Detroit Lions coordinators—Drew Petzing, Kelvin Sheppard, and Dave Fipp—all met with the media on Thursday to discuss the upcoming season, and Sunday’s game against the New Orleans Saints. Here are my nine biggest takeaways from each session. Offensive coordinator Drew Petzing What he likes about Ben Bartch, guard rotations We still don’t know […]
full_text: Detroit Lions offensive coordinator Drew Petzing walks onto the field for practice during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Monday, August 10, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The three Detroit Lions coordinators—Drew Petzing, Kelvin Sheppard, and Dave Fipp—all met with the media on Thursday to discuss the upcoming season, and Sunday’s game against the New Orleans Saints. Here are my nine biggest takeaways from each session. Offensive coordinator Drew Petzing What he likes about Ben Bartch, guard rotations We still don’t know who will line up at left guard to start the season: Ben Bartch or Christian Mahogany. Petzing was asked specifically about Bartch, and here’s what he had to offer about the veteran lineman. “We talk about the physicality and the communication, probably the two most important things for an offensive lineman as a starting point outside of just winning your one-on-one. I think he’s done a really nice job of that,” Petzing said. “He’s a really smart player. He’s played in a couple different offenses and communicates well. The physicality is there, the finish is there, the attitude is there.” As for the guard rotation, Petzing downplayed the panic over it. He said he’s been a part of it in Arizona, and while it’s not ideal, he thinks they’ll be fine if that’s the route they go. “It’s an opportunity for those guys to continue to compete and earn their reps and to help this team win games,” Petzing said. Juice Scruggs improving with play, confidence The other key to Detroit’s offensive line is Scruggs, who is expected to step in for the injured Cade Mays at center. Petzing said he challenged Scruggs early on to get louder and have more conviction in his pre-snap calls, and he’s risen to the occasion. “If you don’t say anything or you’re too quiet, that’s where problems arise,” Petzing said. “Hey, at the end of the day, if all 11 people on the field are doing the same thing, we got a chance. Might not be the perfect thing, but as long as we’re on the same page, we got a chance to play good football. And I think he’s really embraced that. I think he’s done a nice job of that here really these last couple of weeks.” Sam LaPorta can do everyting One of the most anticipated developments with Petzing is how he’ll utilized Pro Bowl tight end Sam LaPorta. He helped Cardinals tight end Trey McBride set NFL records, and with LaPorta’s game already so developed, the sky is the limit. Unsurprisingly, Petzing has come away impressed by the vast amount of things LaPorta can already do—well beyond just catching the football. “He’s very dynamic in the passing game, big body, great body control, great hands, really good route runner, uses his body at the top of routes,” Petzing said. “But, I think his ability to do pass pro, to play in the run game, to play off the ball and on the move or outside the core is really impressive. I think there’s very few guys in the league that can do all of those jobs at such a high level. And I think when you have a guy like that, it does put a lot of stress on a defense.” Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard Veteran safeties will give Lions MORE versatility than last year Earlier this week, Lions coach Dan Campbell hyped up the secondary , with a particular emphasis on starting safeties Chuck Clark and Avonte Maddox. Sheppard followed suit, noting that their extensive experience—16 seasons combined—will give Detroit the knowledge base to expand their defensive playlist. “I have all the confidence in the world in these guys because—and, hell—we’re actually going to be able to do things that we weren’t able to do before,” Sheppard said. He was asked to clarify if that meant more than what Detroit could do with Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch, to which he said he meant more generally last season. He can’t wait to see Alim McNeill A common theme of Sheppard’s press conference was to not hype up anyone or anything until the team actually takes the field on Sunday. There are too many unknowns. However, when it came to Lions defensive tackle Alim McNeill, Sheppard couldn’t hold in his enthusiasm. “I’m so excited for that player,” Sheppard said. “When I say it, it’s almost emotional because I know what he wanted to be last year and he just couldn’t. And it had nothing to do with, ‘Why isn’t Mac doing’—no, he just couldn’t. A lot of that tape, he couldn’t even put his foot in the ground and plant, but he was still out there for his brothers. So I’m just telling you right here, Sept. 13th, I cannot wait to see number 54.” Don’t expect a ton of simulated pressure One of the more trendy strategies on defense is what is known as “simulated pressure.” In short, it’s a defense feigning a lot of pressure pre-snap, only to have many players—sometimes unexpected players like defensive linemen—drop into coverage. The purpose is to speed up the opposing quarterback into a mistake while disguising both the coverage and pressure looks. Sheppard said the versatility of DJ Wonnum and Derrick Moore being able to potentially drop into coverage does give them the versatility to utilize this strategy—while making a wise crack about the criticism he’s received for dropping Aidan Hutchinson into coverage. “Yeah, it gives a lot of flex,” Sheppard said. “Hutch dropped two times and you’d have thought he dropped 20 from the word around the street. ‘Why is he in coverage?’ He dropped twice, guys. Let’s relax. But no, it gives you a lot of flexibility. You may see a d-tackle, d-end. These guys are so versatile now.” But he did warn that it’s not his favorite strategy to use. “I’m actually not a huge simulated guy,” Sheppard said. “So, it’s a time and a place for it, but I’m not just hell bent on simulating pressure.” Special teams coordinator Dave Fipp Returners more or less confirmed We already knew that Tom Kennedy was going to be the team’s starting punt returner after coach Dan Campbell spilled the beans earlier in the week. When it comes to the kick returners, it certainly sounds like it’s going to be Kennedy and running back Jacob Saylors. “We feel good about both those guys being back there,” Fipp said. “They both have experience doing it. Obviously, Saylors (did) a bunch a year ago.” Last year, the Lions’ leading kick returners were Saylors (33 for 897 yards), Kennedy (16 for 447), and Kalif Raymond (six for 161). As for why the Lions chose Kennedy over veteran Greg Dortch, who was cut by the team, Fipp passed the buck and said that was not his decision. He offered generic praise for both players. Challenge of starting all over on scheme I thought Fipp made a really good point about how job is much different from the other coordinators. While the offense and defense can start building their scheme in the spring—knowing which players they can rely on—the same can’t be said of Fipp. He often has to wait until after roster cuts to know which players he’ll have on special teams, and so when I asked him if he’s going to do anything different on kickoff this year, he said he needs to figure out what this newly formed unit can do well together. “We don’t spend a lot of time on scheme in the preseason,” Fipp said. “It’s the last thing I’m worried about because you build something for this group of players, all of a sudden that group changes, that cut down day, and now you have a totally different group. So, ultimately for us, it’s putting these guys in as good a spot as we can do it going into the first game and then figuring out as we go the best way to put this thing together.” Not worried about Jake Bates Bates had a very up-and-down training camp and some of that spilled over to the preseason, where he missed two extra points in the finale. Fipp staunchly defended Bates, noting that every kicker goes through a process in the league that sometimes takes until Year 6 to really click. “I feel good about Jake. I think a couple years ago I said there’s going to be a process of some ups and downs. I think historically,…

title: 2026 NFL season predictions: Detroit Lions Rookie of the Year
summary: If the Detroit Lions are to accomplish every goal for the 2026 season, they will undoubtedly need some serious help from their 2026 rookie class. While Detroit only made two picks in the first three rounds, five players made their 53-man roster, and at least three of them are expected to have a significant-to-major role […]
full_text: Aug 22, 2026; Detroit, Michigan, USA; Detroit Lions offensive tackle Blake Miller (76) during pregame warmups before their game against the Washington Commanders at Ford Field. Mandatory Credit: Lon Horwedel-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect If the Detroit Lions are to accomplish every goal for the 2026 season, they will undoubtedly need some serious help from their 2026 rookie class. While Detroit only made two picks in the first three rounds, five players made their 53-man roster, and at least three of them are expected to have a significant-to-major role this season. Which one of them steps up and elevates the team this year? Here are our staff’s 2026 Detroit Lions predictions for Rookie of the Year. Vote for your pick at the bottom of the page. Previously: Offensive MVP predictions Defensive MVP predictions Breakout Player of the Year Who will be the Lions’ 2026 Rookie of the Year? Ryan Mathews: Derrick Moore Derrick Moore will be the Lions’ rookie of the year in 2026. Detroit traded up to nab Moore in the second round of the draft, so it’s clear they view him as being a difference-maker. His preseason play and performance at training camp certainly allude to Moore being exactly what the Lions needed on their defensive line. John Whiticar: Blake Miller I am pleasantly optimistic about this rookie class, and the likes of Derrick Moore, Keith Abney, and Skyler-Gill Howard could make an impact early on. That being said, this is clearly Miller’s award to lose. He is playing a pivotal position on arguably the most important part of this offense, the offensive line. He has both the talent and opportunity to shine as a rookie. Erik Schlitt: Blake Miller A day-one starter from the jump, Miller looks like a ready-made NFL right tackle. He’ll make some rookie mistakes this season; that’s all part of the learning process, but I also expect him to be a steady presence on the field and an important catalyst in the run game. Al Karsten: Blake Miller The Lions’ pro-ready, athletic, problem-solving first-round rookie right tackle Blake Miller will endure some peaks and valleys early on, but by Halloween, he’ll prove the Lions made a sound investment in their future in the trenches. By then, the offensive line will start to look scary, bludgeoning teams up front and allowing Drew Petzing to play mad scientist with his bevy of skill-position weapons. Miller will emerge as one of the most important stabilizing rookie additions of the Dan Campbell-Brad Holmes era. Morgan Cannon: Blake Miller Chalky response here, but the answer to me is rookie right tackle, Blake Miller. He is about as battle-tested as they come after a long and productive career at Clemson, and he has the athletic profile of someone who could really take off once he gets his legs under him as a pro. If he can hold down the right side of the offensive line across from perennial All-Pro Penei Sewell, the Lions will likely feel pretty good about their first-round selection from the 2026 NFL Draft. Brandon Knapp: Derrick Moore The only reason is why he edges out Blake Miller for me is because of who else is on the defensive line. Aidan Hutchinson, Alim McNeill, Tyliek Williams, DJ Wonnum. While that list isn’t elite, you have two solid players in Hutchinson and McNeill. Williams is a young and improving defensive tackle. And Wonnum brings a veteran presence. I think the focus for opposing offensive lines will be focused majorly on the interior and Hutchinson that Wonnum and Moore will get plenty of one on one opportunity that they’ll capitalize on. Jeremy Reisman: Derrick Moore No disrespect to Miller—who I expect to have understandable ups and downs his rookie season—but I think Moore could have a greater overall positive impact. Moore happens to play a position where his successes are more impactful and his mistakes easier to hide, and that’s doing a lot of the heavy lifting here. Regardless, Moore is in a great spot to get on the field early as a pass rushing specialist, and with his supporting cast, I think he could finish his rookie season in the 6-8 sack range. Anthony Balaj: Blake Miller While Skyler Gill-Howard and Derrick Moore may come with more big moments and highlights, Miller already is proving to not be a concern for the Lions through the end of training camp. When a rookie offensive tackle can step right into the starting lineup without much of a hiccup, it’s a huge win for the organization.

title: Dan Campbell makes bold claim about Detroit Lions secondary
summary: Last week, Detroit Lions general manager Brad Holmes faced a barrage of questions regarding Terrion Arnold and the state of the team’s cornerback room. Things got a little heated, as Holmes attempted to defend the team’s process in evaluating Arnold’s legal situation and ultimately deciding to part ways. And when it came to criticism about […]
full_text: Detroit Lions safety Thomas Harper (12), left, and safety Chuck Clark (36) during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Monday, August 10, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Last week, Detroit Lions general manager Brad Holmes faced a barrage of questions regarding Terrion Arnold and the state of the team’s cornerback room. Things got a little heated, as Holmes attempted to defend the team’s process in evaluating Arnold’s legal situation and ultimately deciding to part ways. And when it came to criticism about whether he had done enough to insulate the cornerback position to take on the blow of Arnold’s departure, Holmes repeated time and time again that he liked the players they have. “We like the guys we have, we like what we’ve done, and we feel good about what’s in the room right now,” Holmes concluded, ending the contentious back-and-forth with a reporter. Whether the Lions are in good shape in the secondary is certainly a matter of an opinion, and Holmes has no other option than to defend his guys. Detroit’s starters at cornerback are certainly capable, with D.J. Reed being good enough to warrant a three-year, $48 million deal last offseason and Rock Ya-Sin stepping up in 2025 and allowing just a 77.7 passer rating when targeted (per PFF) over 17 games and six starts. But the depth is where there is palpable concern. Roger McCreary is a former second-round pick, but his inconsistent play has led to just 10 starts over the last two seasons; Detroit will be his third team in two years. Ennis Rakestraw—also a former second-round pick—hasn’t started a single game and had a very rocky training camp and preseason. Keith Abney is a rookie who looks like he still needs time to develop and Khalil Dorsey is primarily a special teams weapon. Things get even more complicated at safety. Their elite talents Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph will miss at least the first four games of the season while on the Physically Unable to Perform list. And while Detroit did a valiant job protecting themselves by signing Chuck Clark and re-signing Avonte Maddox, both players will be 30 by the season’s end. Still, during his weekly radio appearance on 97.1 The Ticket, Lions coach Dan Campbell doubled down on Holmes’ comments. “This is the best position we’ve been in in the secondary without those two guys [Branch, Joseph] in a long time,” Campbell said. Okay, maybe he tripled down on Holmes’ comments. He explains: “Maddox and Chuck are very reliable, dependable, smart football players—highly competitive. Rock and Reed, man, are highly competitive (and) get the job done. They’re gonna compete, they’re gonna battle, nothing’s too big for them,” CAmpbell said. “We’ve got McCreary, we’ve got Abney, we’ve got Rake. I like where we’re at.” To be fair, Maddox, Clark, Ya-Sin, and Reed have all played a lot of football and have earned their keep in this league. But it’s certainly fair to be worried about Detroit’s depth both at safety and cornerback, where mostly inexperienced players reside. Campbell concluded his thoughts by pointing out that the entire defense operates as a whole. He doesn’t need these players to be superstars, but rather do their job on Sundays—something he believes they are more than capable of doing. “It’s about a team, man,” Campbell said. “Does everybody have a role to play and can they be good in that role? And that answer is yes. So, I feel good. I feel really good with where we’re at going into Week 1.”

title: Packers got help from long-time OL coach Harry Hiestand in camp
summary: The Packers’ offensive line got some additional help from a long-time college and pro offensive line coach. According to reporting from the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel’s Tom Silverstein, Harry Hiestand spent training camp with the Packers in what appeared to be a consultant-style role. Hiestand is about as decorated as an offensive line coach can be, […]
full_text: SOUTH BEND, IN - APRIL 23: Notre Dame Fighting Irish offensive line coach Harry Hiestand looks on during the Notre Dame Blue-Gold Spring Football Game on April 23, 2022 at Notre Dame Stadium in South Bend, IN. (Photo by Robin Alam/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Packers’ offensive line got some additional help from a long-time college and pro offensive line coach. According to reporting from the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel’s Tom Silverstein , Harry Hiestand spent training camp with the Packers in what appeared to be a consultant-style role. Hiestand is about as decorated as an offensive line coach can be, boasting success and connections to significant players at just about every stop in his multi-decade career. Dating back to the 1980s, Hiestand coached with eight different college programs and one NFL team, the Chicago Bears, in two different stints. From 2005 through 2009, Hiestand worked with the Bears under head coach Lovie Smith, then returned to Chicago under Matt Nagy in 2018, staying through the 2019 season. In between those two tours with the Bears, Hiestand had stops at Tennessee and Notre Dame, and the latter appointment probably explains how he ended up in Green Bay. His time with the Fighting Irish overlapped with Matt LaFleur’s one-year stint there, so Hiestand’s role with the Packers turns out to be not that much of a surprise. In football, even more so than other businesses, it’s about who you know as much as what you know. So what’s Hiestand up to in Green Bay? That’s not exactly clear, as Silverstein laid out. He characterizes Hiestand as a “consultant,” but it might be more complicated than that: The well-respected Hiestand coached on the field during training camp, taking over some of the duties Butkus, Gordon or a quality control coach would normally handle. It meant, instead of having one offensive line coach in charge, under the supervision of the offensive coordinator and head coach, the Packers had three line coaches, plus an offensive coordinator who used to be a line coach, in the linemen’s ears. Hiestand isn’t listed in any official capacity on the Packers’ website, and Silverstein reports that he may still be offering some kind of insight to the team during the season, but his exact role, if any, is a mystery. Still, with as many questions as the Packers are facing on the offensive line, having another voice in the room hardly seems like a bad thing. Whatever pointers Hiestand can offer are probably worth whatever trade offs arise when you shake things up a bit.

(Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Minnesota Vikings are generally not expected to be a front-runner in the race for an NFC North title this season. They have the worst odds to win the division of any of the four teams, and there are questions up and down their roster. However, for a Green Bay Packers team looking to get a good litmus test of where they stand to start the year, a road game in Minnesota might be just what the doctor ordered. You want to figure out your offensive line? You’re going to have to do it quickly in this game against Brian Flores’ tough, creative defense. You need to figure out who you can count on at defensive tackle and edge? A matchup with an offensive line that looks questionable (especially on the interior) should provide some opportunities. Your new defensive coordinator needs to settle into a groove with his new personnel? Cool, go face the quarterback he just coached for the last two seasons in Arizona and whose tendencies he therefore knows extremely well. At least one Packers defender is eager for the challenge of a road game against a divisional opponent for the opener. As fans, maybe we should take a page from Zaire Franklin and embrace the challenge that awaits the Packers as well. full_text: (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Green Bay Packers defensive lineman Warren Brinson (calf) and linebacker Ty’Ron Hopper (Achilles) remain out of practice for the second straight day, according to the Packers’ injury report , but the good news is that things are trending upward for left tackle Jordan Morgan (knee). Morgan, who was a limited participant on Wednesday, was listed as a full participant on Thursday. That’s a good sign, considering the team usually has a lighter practice, sometimes even a walkthrough, on Fridays for Sunday games. This could have been the last chance for Morgan to give it a full go. As of now, we don’t know what is specifically wrong with Morgan’s knee or when his injury occurred. With that being said, here are the players who were limited during Thursday’s practice: LG Aaron Banks (knee tendinitis) RT Zach Bako-Belwele (recovering from a partially torn patellar tendon) DL Devonte Wyatt (recovering from a 2025 ankle injury) DL Javon Hargrave (knee) EDGE Barryn Sorrell (foot) All five of those players were also limited participants on Wednesday. On the Minnesota Vikings’ end of the injury report, safety Jacob Thomas, safety Jakobe Thomas (yes, they have very similar names) and tackle Caleb Tiernan were all limited on Thursday. Jakobe Thomas was a non-participant on Wednesday and is moving in a positive direction after falling ill. The Vikings managed to pull […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - JANUARY 4: Brian Flores defensive coordinator of the Minnesota Vikings before the game against the Green Bay Packers at U.S. Bank Stadium on January 4, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Minnesota Vikings went 9-8 last season despite the worst regular quarterback play I’ve ever seen. Something called Max Brosmer started a game against the Detroit Lions wherein he completed nine passes for 51 yards while taking seven sacks for 48 yards, and still somehow his team won the game. The Vikings managed to pull off a winning record and finish ahead of the Lions via the head-to-head tiebreaker because their defensive coordinator Brian Flores is basically Tony Stark building the arc reactor in a cave in the desert with a box of scraps . He’s unlike any other defensive coordinator in the league in that he almost never rushes the “normal” amount of people. It’s always too many or too few, and it’s never who you would expect. He’s part necromancer, part general, part abstract painter. He’s not thinking four moves ahead, he’s performing moves in some other game he knows you will end up playing later but haven’t even heard of yet. And for the Green Bay Packers, specifically, Brian Flores is going to be a problem on Sunday. If the Packers were fully healthy, I wouldn’t worry so much. If they had everyone going, I think they’re familiar enough with the Flores attack that they would be able to work around it. I also think if they were playing the Bears, who have a terrible defense, or the Lions, who have a good-but-conventional defense, I would be picking the Packers to win this week. But as of Wednesday, Zack Bako-Bewele and Aaron Banks were limited in practice. I think Bako-Bewele probably plays, but there’s a good chance he will be limited as he was much of last year, and if he can’t go, the disaster that is Anthony Belton is likely to step in. That’s only a part of the problem though, as the interior of the Packers’ line is easily their weakest unit, and their biggest vulnerability is with some combination of Sean Rhyan, Aaron Banks, Jacob Monk, and/or Jager Burton being charged with keeping the Flores blitzes at bay. Do you trust any of those guys to make the right read when Dallas Turner suddenly stunts inside, followed by Andrew Van Ginkel directly behind him while Jalen Redmond drops into coverage? Banks has been terrible in Green Bay, even when healthy, and there is no evidence he is healthy. The rest of them are, at best, “young and promising,” but without experience against what Flores brings, this is very worrisome. They’re even not very good when defenders are running right at them in predictable ways! It’s just a bad matchup, and it’s made worse by the fact that Minnesota will likely be completely and totally unconcerned about the Packers’ running game, with poor line play and no Josh Jacobs around. This will allow them to come after Jordan Love all day without much fear of getting burned. And since they coaxed Harrison Smith out of retirement to play safety, the Vikings will also have the benefit of a coach-on-the-field presence to help clean up any mistakes the younger Minnesota defenders make in the back end. All of that said, the Vikings are not some juggernaut, and they have plenty of exploitable flaws in their own right. Gone are Jonathan Allen and Javon Hargrave (the latter headed to the Packers, where he too is limited in practice). Gone, most importantly, is Jonathan Greenard. The Vikings definitely lost some talent, and they definitely lack the experience necessary to run Flores’ scheme perfectly. But their sack leaders from last season, (Dallas Turner, Andrew Van Ginkel, Eric Wilson, and Jalen Redmond) are all still on the team, and all perfectly capable of blitzing. Their leaders in passes defended (Van Ginkel, Harrison Smith, Byron Murphy, Josh Mettellus, and Isaiah Rodgers) are all still on the team. There wasn’t that much turnover. They’ve all played this system before. Flores also seems to be the rare coordinator that is able to defy the highly variable nature of year-to-year defensive variance. One reason the Vikings are a popular pick to finish last in the division is that it’s almost impossible to maintain defensive excellence for multiple seasons in a row. The Vikings have finished in the top three in FTN’s DVOA metric for two consecutive seasons , and in the FTN Almanac author Dan Pizzuta points out that their projection system has the defense projected as about league average, but that if anyone can defy the odds, it might be Flores. Over the course of the entire season I suspect the Vikings’ defense is closer to tenth than first, as personnel absolutely matters. But for this game specifically? Andrew Van Ginkel is going to be abusing Monk/Belton/Banks over, and over, and over. Minnesota swept the Lions last year largely because Flores is so adept at finding the weak link on the other side of the field and exploiting it until you are forced to take that player off the field. Against the Lions, that was all-world running back Jahmyr Gibbs, who is amazing at everything but pass protection where he held a 50.5 pass blocking grade at PFF . Every time Gibbs was on the field, Flores overloaded the line and managed to get a blitzer singled up on him, resulting in five sacks of Jared Goff in each of their two games. The Vikings had a 51.1% blitz rate last season, with the next-highest defense coming in at 39%. On early downs they blitzed even more at 54.7% of the time. If you can pick up the Vikings’ blitz, you can almost certainly hurt them, and my hope for this game is that running back Chris Brooks, who is good in pass pro, and tight end Mark Redman see plenty of time to help out. But this matchup stinks for Green Bay, on the road, in a noisy indoor stadium, where Flores and Kevin O’Connell have had forever to prepare. Worst of all, the Packers will not be able to fall back on terrible quarterback play with Kyler Murray now running the show. A quick reminder that this team went 13-4 just two seasons ago with a similar offensive unit (finishing 9th in points scored) and Sam Darnold at the helm before anyone thought Sam Darnold could be anything at all. Justin Jefferson finished that season with 1,533 yards and 10 touchdowns. I don’t think Murray is great, but I don’t think he has to be, and before Ben Johnson was the toast of the NFL as an offensive mind, Kevin O’Connell was right there in the conversation. I am optimistic about the Packers overall. I think they are very talented up and down the roster (with a few small exceptions), and I even think they will get the line sorted eventually. Right now, however, other than facing an opponent like Seattle or Houston, this is as bad an opening matchup as they could have gotten given their current weaknesses and level of health.

title: Josh Jacobs pleads no contest to battery and criminal damage charges
summary: Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs recently had his initial hearing in his court case, after being charged with battery and criminal damage, pushed forward by two months. Today, Jacobs showed up in person to plead no contest to both misdemeanor charges. Currently, Jacobs is on the NFL’s commissioner exempt list, where he will […]
full_text: (Photo by John Fisher/Getty Images) | Getty Images Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs recently had his initial hearing in his court case , after being charged with battery and criminal damage, pushed forward by two months. Today, Jacobs showed up in person to plead no contest to both misdemeanor charges . Currently, Jacobs is on the NFL’s commissioner exempt list, where he will remain until the league rules on a potential suspension for the running back. The Packers, up to this point, have stood by Jacobs and have allowed him to participate in activities in the facility — which is allowed while he’s on the exempt list, as long as he doesn’t practice or play in games. Jacobs was initially charged with battery with a domestic abuse enhancer, criminal damage with a domestic abuse enhancer, disorderly conduct with a domestic abuse enhancer, strangulation and suffocation and intimidation of a victim. The State of Wisconsin demands that, to reach the domestic abuse enhancer, the victim in the crimes must have been someone who has (or had) lived with the assailant, has a child with the assailant or has been married to the assailant. Because Jacobs’ girlfriend, as described in the police report, did not fit that mold, the enhancers were dropped from his charges. According to the police report, there was footage retrieved from Jacobs’ complex that shows “the altercation” between him and his unnamed girlfriend via an open garage door. Per the report, Jacobs “grabbed her and threw her to the ground,” resulting in injury. Allegedly, he later damaged her phone, which is where the criminal damage charge stems from. ESPN’s Rob Demovsky , live at court today, stated that the court has accepted Jacobs’ no-contest plea — which means that the accused is willing to accept punishment but not officially admit guilt — on five conditions: He doesn’t commit any further criminal acts. He has no contact with the victim. He accepts supervision. He accepts counseling. He pays restitution to the victim. The Athletic’s Matt Schneidman has reported that Jacobs’ attorney stated in court that Jacobs has already volunteered to attend counseling . — Updates: The District Attorney is asking for a conviction on the battery count and will accept the deferred agreement on the criminal damage of property if he meets the five stipulations. DA David Lasee said he will not seek jail time for Josh Jacobs. — Rob Demovsky (@RobDemovsky) September 10, 2026 Josh Jacobs statement: “I fully understand the seriousness of the situation and I take full responsibility.” — Matt Schneidman (@mattschneidman) September 10, 2026 Jacobs is ordered by the court to pay a $1,000 fine on the misdemeanor battery charge. — Matt Schneidman (@mattschneidman) September 10, 2026 A statement regarding Josh Jacobs and today’s legal developments: pic.twitter.com/q7LBD0oSyk — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) September 10, 2026 With Josh Jacobs pleading no contest to misdemeanor charges of battery and criminal damage to property, the NFL said there is “no timetable” as to when he could be disciplined. A league official said: We have been closely monitoring all developments in the matter which remains… — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) September 10, 2026

full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - NOVEMBER 23: Jordan Love #10 of the Green Bay Packers scrambles with the ball against the Minnesota Vikings during the first quarter at Lambeau Field on November 23, 2025 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images While I think the Packers should win, they come into Week 1 facing an interesting test. If nothing else, the Vikings should represent a sort of ruthless competency. They don’t have any outright stars on defense, but they’ve got a madman running the show in Brian Flores and he’ll do anything at any moment. They’ll have to be on their game to counter a Vikings’ defense that should still be dangerous even if its overall talent level isn’t terribly high. Then, on offense, the Vikings have great talent at receiver, a good tight end, and a quarterback who should at least be an upgrade over what they had last year. If they can at least get to a baseline level of NFL performance at quarterback, that’s enough to be dangerous. In short, Justin Jefferson could break things open at any time — best be on your game. I’d argue this is a good place for the Packers to be. If the first couple of weeks of the regular season are essentially an extended preseason anyway, what better opponent to face than one who really forces you to execute? The Vikings can do that for the Packers, and if the Packers aren’t ready, they’ll lose. I still do expect them to win, but a loss wouldn’t be a surprising outcome at all. Even if the Packers have a legitimate claim as the best team in the NFC North, and I think they do, no divisional game is going to be a cakewalk this year. title: ESPN gives an update on a Tucker Kraft extension
summary: Jeremy Fowler dropped a long Week 1 buzz article for ESPN on Thursday morning, and it included some nuggets on where the Green Bay Packers and tight end Tucker Kraft stand on an extension. In the past, general manager Brian Gutekunst stated that he wanted a Kraft deal done going into the regular season, but […]
full_text: (Photo by Joe Sargent/Getty Images) | Getty Images Jeremy Fowler dropped a long Week 1 buzz article for ESPN on Thursday morning, and it included some nuggets on where the Green Bay Packers and tight end Tucker Kraft stand on an extension. In the past, general manager Brian Gutekunst stated that he wanted a Kraft deal done going into the regular season, but there is no deal in place yet. Here’s what Fowler had to say about the situation: This summer has featured complete market resets at cornerback and defensive tackle, and tight end could be next. It’s the only offensive or defensive position without a player making $20 million or more per season, but the Packers’ Tucker Kraft is hoping to change that. He remains in discussions about a new contract, but it has been a bit of a standoff so far. Green Bay hopes to get something done by the end of Week 1, so perhaps urgency prevails here. If Kraft can get a deal above that $20 million threshold, that sets the stage for Detroit’s Sam LaPorta. The Lions have interest in extending him, but his situation might carry into the season. $20 million per year might sound like a lot for a tight end, but it’s really not that big of a jump from where the position is at right now. As we wrote after the Kyle Pitts extension , here are the four highest-paid tight ends in the league from an average-per-year perspective: George Kittle: $19.1 million per Trey McBride: $19 million per Kyle Pitts: $18 million per Isaiah Likely: $13.3 million per Once Pitts signed for $18 million per year, it was assumed that Kraft would receive more than him. The only question was whether he was going to get paid in line with George Kittle and Trey McBride or truly become the highest-paid tight end in the league, despite him coming off an ACL tear. At least according to Fowler, Kraft’s camp is eyeing to “reset” the tight end market, even if the ceiling at the position rises by only about a million dollars per year. Fowler is also correct in that Sam LaPorta is the other tight end situation to pay attention to, as he’s the only other significant tight end going into a contract year in 2026. With Pitts off the table, it’s the Kraft and LaPorta show, as far as tight end extensions go. A big question is who will be first to sign, and whether or not the second player’s number will rise to try to beat the first’s benchmark.

title: Chris Brooks could decide the Packers’ Week 1 matchup against Minnesota
summary: One of the more underrated matchups going into the Green Bay Packers’ regular-season opener against the Minnesota Vikings, at least to me, is how running back Chris Brooks will do against defensive coordinator Brian Flores’ blitz-heavy front. The Packers have said that they will be trying out a running back-by-committee approach early on in the […]
full_text: (Photo by Timothy Hurst/MediaNews Group/The Denver Post via Getty Images) | Denver Post via Getty Images One of the more underrated matchups going into the Green Bay Packers’ regular-season opener against the Minnesota Vikings, at least to me, is how running back Chris Brooks will do against defensive coordinator Brian Flores’ blitz-heavy front. The Packers have said that they will be trying out a running back-by-committee approach early on in the season, but I want to talk about blocking, not ball-carrying, when it comes to what Brooks can bring to the table. Everyone and their mother knows that Flores wants to blitz. It’s in his DNA. It’s who he has been, who he is and who he will want to be in the future. Arguably, Packers head coach Matt LaFleur’s best trait as a coach has been his team’s pass-rushing plans, as there have been few players up front who have been allowed to take over games, even when the team has matched up against the Aaron Donalds, Myles Garretts and Aidan Hutchinsons of the world. His line gets a lot of chip help from tight ends, funky spacing that puts rushers in bad positions pre-snap and running backs who add on to the protection. That’s where Brooks had thrived in the past. Below is a clip from Week 1 last year, where Brooks, against a mugged-up Detroit Lions front, passes off a linebacker and takes on a defensive tackle on a stunt to allow Jordan Love to make a big throw in the middle of the field. Yes, a defensive tackle. Packers RB Chris Brooks picking up a blitzing linebacker, passing him off and then taking on a defensive tackle pic.twitter.com/CD5olFPx84 — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) September 8, 2025 Last year, PFF graded Brooks as the fourth-best running back league-wide in pass protection . To make this short and simple: He’s a really good blocking back. I’d expect that the Packers will want to lean into Brooks’ blocking ability, especially on obvious passing downs, against Flores’ aggressive scheme. Especially when three of Green Bay’s starting offensive linemen are currently on the injury report and were limited during Wednesday’s practice . So don’t discount Brooks being a difference-maker in the Week 1 matchup, even if he’s not going to receive the bulk of the carries out of the backfield. It also probably helps the Packers that they just signed safety Kahlef Hailassie, who was with the Vikings for all of training camp and was just released two days ago, to their practice squad. Teams usually spend two weeks of game planning for their Week 1 opponent, rather than one, because they receive that extra week between cutdowns and the start of the regular season. Maybe Hailassie knows a little about the pass-rush plan that Flores has for the Packers and had installed over the last week, and he’ll want to share that with Brooks. You’ve got to love a little gamesmanship.

title: The Packers’ defense was the opposite of the Seahawks last season
summary: Here’s an interesting stat that I saw last night during the NFL regular-season opener, when the Seattle Seahawks were able to take down the New England Patriots in the Super Bowl rematch. According to Sümer Sports, the 2025 Seahawks played five defensive backs 81 percent of the time when opposing offenses played two or fewer […]
full_text: (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here’s an interesting stat that I saw last night during the NFL regular-season opener, when the Seattle Seahawks were able to take down the New England Patriots in the Super Bowl rematch. According to Sümer Sports, the 2025 Seahawks played five defensive backs 81 percent of the time when opposing offenses played two or fewer receivers, which led the NFL, while the Green Bay Packers did so on just 14 percent of snaps, the second-lowest rate in the league, only behind the Detroit Lions. 2025 teams that refused to match heavy sets pic.twitter.com/RBCwI9tuMA — Sam Bruchhaus (@sambruchhaus) September 10, 2026 That might be a little wordy, so I want to break this down piece by piece. Generally, NFL defenses tend to match the number of outside cornerbacks and slot defenders on the field to the number of receivers the opposing offense throws out there. Why? So they can have bigger bodies on the grass against heavier personnel sets (like multi-tight end or multi-back looks) when teams are running the ball more frequently, and so they don’t have to play a linebacker in coverage against a slot receiver in three-receiver sets, when opposing offenses pass the ball more. Under defensive coordinator Jeff Hafley, the Packers stuck to their “matching” personnel rules pretty strictly, outside of the red zone and short-yardage plays. To me, it’s not a surprise that they only broke “matching” personnel 14 percent of the time. In fact, I was a little surprised it was that high. If you only measured plays between the 20s, that number probably drops. Meanwhile, the Seahawks, who play a quarters-based scheme that new defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon is expected to run in Green Bay, played their nickel or dime subpackages on more than four-fifths of their plays when they got heavy personnel looks from the offensive side of the ball. For perspective, only five teams in the entire NFL didn’t match heavy personnel with primarily a “base” defense last year, and two of those — the San Francisco 49ers and Buffalo Bills — barely crossed the threshold with a 51 percent rate. The reason that Seattle can do this is that Nick Emmanwori, the Seahawks’ slot defender, essentially can play both as a slot defender and as a Sam linebacker. For the most part, a slot defender in a 4-2 nickel look is basically playing the 4-3 Sam linebacker role anyway, just split out from the formation when the slot receiver is detached from the formation. When that slot receiver motions into the formation, potentially as an insert player to help run block, the slot defender usually travels with him, putting the slot defender in a more traditional Sam linebacker role pre-snap. The Seahawks seem perfectly fine allowing Emmanwori to play both of those spots, no matter what opposing offenses throw out on the field. Meanwhile, the Packers haven’t been as confident in their slot defender, Javon Bullard, right or wrong. Gannon’s Cardinals didn’t match heavy personnel on 23 percent of snaps last year, a good jump up from the Packers’ 14 percent mark in 2025, but still nowhere near the Seahawks’ 81 percent rate. In the NFL of old, a slot defender and a slot receiver were both of the mold of players who were too small to play on the outside. Now, with how run games want to manipulate both positions, those players are much bigger, as slot defenders are also asked to be Sam linebackers and slot receivers are being asked to play some tight end-like roles. It should be no surprise that defenses with Emmanwori (6’2”, 220 pounds) and Kyle Hamilton (6’4”, 218 pounds) are the most comfortable in just letting their nickel personnel stay on the field and having their slot defenders add on as a strong-side linebacker. For what it’s worth, and it’s only the preseason, Gannon’s defense in the preseason typically matched personnel with the opposing offense. Maybe we’ll see his unit play more six-defensive-back looks against multi-tight-end sets in the regular season, though, as the team has shown a three-safety Penny defense , built to stop the run with extra defensive backs on the field, during the summer.
