title: Vikes Views: 2026 Season Preview
summary: I came into last season a little too optimistic about J.J. McCarthy. I bought into the hype and predicted a 12-5 season, which makes me a bit hesitant heading into this year. That said, the NFL schedule makers did the Vikings a few favors. A slate that includes the NFC South should provide some timely […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - AUGUST 28: Justin Jefferson #18 of the Minnesota Vikings walks on the field after a preseason game against the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High on August 28, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. The Broncos won the game 34-6. (Photo by Justin Edmonds/Getty Images) | Getty Images I came into last season a little too optimistic about J.J. McCarthy. I bought into the hype and predicted a 12-5 season, which makes me a bit hesitant heading into this year. That said, the NFL schedule makers did the Vikings a few favors. A slate that includes the NFC South should provide some timely opportunities throughout the season, and the softer stretch in Weeks 3-5 will give the team time to settle in with Kyler Murray at the helm. Hopefully, I won’t be looking back after the 2026 season with the same regret I felt following 2025. 2025 : 12-5 , too optimistic on the young QB 2024 : 9-8 , I didn’t believe in Darnold, couldn’t have been more wrong and they ended 14-3. 2023 : 11-6 prediction , might have been good if Cousins didn’t go down, they eneded 7-10. 2022 : 13-4 , I was called a homer, but I was right. Disappointing ending to the season though. Week 1: Packers @ Vikings The Vikings will get off to a good start with Kyler Murray. The Packers defense without Micah Parsons will be different than later in the season. The Vikings defense will be able to handle a team with no WR1 and Jacobs out of the lineup. Vikings 20 – Packers 13 Week 2: Vikings @ Bears Week 2 won’t be as easy on the Vikings. Chicago won the NFC North last season and might have even improved from there. The Vikings defense will keep it close, but the offense won’t be able to take advantage. Bears 23 – Vikings 20 Week 3: Vikings @ Buccaneers Road game after a couple of early divisional games can be tough. I have a feeling Murray might find his zone a little bit in the warm Florida weather. Vikings 24 – Bucs 17 Week 4: Dolphins @ Vikings I think the Fins are going to be one of the worst teams in the league this season. I can’t see them giving the Vikings defense any trouble. The Vikings will cruise to a victory at home. Vikings 27 – Dolphins 13 Week 5: Vikings @ New Orleans Another team with a questionable starting QB. Going into New Orleans is never fun. However, the bounties won’t be enough this time though. Vikings 20 – Saints 10 Week 6: Bye Early bye might be a good thing. 5-1 is a very optimistic start, but it’s the easier portion of the schedule. Week 7: Colts @ Vikings I hate playing Daniel Jones. Jonathan Taylor is elite. The Colts will have a strong run game and a veteran QB with decent weapons. The Vikings stumble out of the bye. Colts 27 – Vikings 16 Week 8: Vikings @ Lions The Vikings continue with another tough game on the road in Detroit. I don’t know if I have confidence in Murray’s ability to go into this environment and pull through. They Vikings won’t be able to completely stop the Lions’ offense. Lions 24 – Vikings 17 Week 9: Bills @ Vikings – MNF Josh Allen rolling in on Monday Night Football will be fun. The Vikings will be reeling after back-to-back losses. I think Vikings will be able to move the ball well. The Bills won’t have the weapons to keep up. Vikings 27 – Bills 16 Week 10: Vikings @ Packers The Vikings will struggle a little more against the Packers defense if Micah Parsons is back healthy. Parsons along with not being inside US Bank, will slow them down a little too much. Packers 20 – Vikings 17 Week 11: 49ers @ Vikings – SNF The 49ers offense might be scary if they can figure out Mike Evans, Deebo, and McCaffrey all on the field. The 49ers have a lot of weapons and I’m not counting on enough injuries for them to not handle their business against the Vikings. 49ers 31 – Vikings 17 Week 12: Falcons @ Vikings The schedule gives the Vikings a little bit of a break with the Falcons coming into town. They’re hoping to recapture the magic of Tua’s 2023 breakout season, if they don’t, Michael Penix Jr is likely going to see the field by Week 12. I don’t think either QB will have enough. Bijan is always going to be tough to stop, but a one dimensional offense won’t be enough. Vikings 27 – Falcons 16 Week 13: Panthers @ Vikings Matching up against the worst division in the NFL is going to do the Vikings a lot of favors this season. I can’t see the Panthers coming into Minnesota and walking away with a victory. The Vikings move to 4-0 against the NFC South. Vikings 31 – Panthers 13 Week 14: Vikings @ Patriots – TNF The Patriots offense has a few new weapons they’ll need to figure out, but by the time Week 14 rolls around, I have a feeling they’ll be looking good. Their defense will once again be one of the best in the league. A short week on the road is usually not good. Late in the season in New England won’t be any different. Patriots 24 – Vikings 10 Week 15: Lions @ Vikings – SNF This is where the season gets interesting. Two divisional games with two winnable non-divisional games in between. If the Vikings can pull off a victory here, it will likely launch them into a playoff run. If they can’t, the season will sputter to a finish. Call me a homer, but I think they can do it. Vikings 27 – Lions 24 Week 16: Commanders @ Vikings The Commanders are a hard team to read. Jayden Daniels amazing rookie year was followed up with an injury filled year 2. Stephon Diggs and Terry McLaurin will give him weapons to do so. However, I think the Vikings will ride the momentum of the victory against Detroit. The crowd will be ready to go. Vikings 24 – Commanders 20 Week 17: Vikings @ Jets The Jets stink. They’re be vying for the #1 pick by now. Vikings 30 – Jets 6 Week 18: Bears @ Vikings The Bears will have wrapped up the NFC North by the time we get here. The Vikings will be in the Wild Card and need a win. The Vikings will ride a four game win streak into the playoffs. Vikings 24 – Bears 13 11-6 would be a great first season for Kyler Murray with the Vikings. The team will head into the playoffs with a good head of steam. I don’t think they’re serious contenders, but it’s truly anyone’s game in the playoffs. I was late to come around to the idea of Kyler leading this team, but I think Kevin O’Connell can make it work. Maybe I’m getting soft in my old age, but I keep looking at this roster and thinking it’s better than a lot of people want to admit. The defense should be one of the best in the league. Justin Jefferson is still Justin Jefferson. The offensive line looks improved on paper, and if the running game takes a step forward, Murray won’t need to be Superman every week. That’s really the key to the entire season. The Vikings don’t need Murray to play like an MVP candidate. They need him to avoid the mistakes that have followed him throughout his career and make the plays that are there when they present themselves. If he can do that, 11-6 feels very realistic. If he plays better than that, the Vikings could surprise some people.

summary: The Minnesota Vikings and Green Bay Packers released the first update of their injury reports this week after Thursday’s practice in advance of their Sunday afternoon matchup at US Bank Stadium. Here they are. Minnesota Vikings Green Bay Packers Injury Report Terms and Glossary Injury designation definitions: Probable = the league defines a Probable injury […]
full_text: The Minnesota Vikings and Green Bay Packers released the first update of their injury reports this week after Thursday’s practice in advance of their Sunday afternoon matchup at US Bank Stadium. Here they are. Minnesota Vikings Player Name Position Injury Wednesday Thursday Friday Injury Designation Jakobe Thomas S Illness DNP LP Jacob Thomas S Ankle LP LP Caleb Tiernan T Ankle LP LP Green Bay Packers Player Name Position Injury Wednesday Thursday Friday Injury Designation Micah Parsons* Edge Knee DNP DNP PUP – OUT Josh Jacobs* RB NIR DNP DNP CE List- OUT Luke Musgrave TE Neck DNP DNP PUP – OUT Jordan Riley DT Achilles DNP DNP PUP – OUT Aaron Banks* LG Knee LP LP Zach Bako-Bewele* RT Knee LP LP Warren Brinson DT Calf DNP DNP Ty’Ron Hopper LB Achilles DNP DNP Javon Hargrave* DT Knee LP LP Jordan Morgan* LT Knee LP FP Devonte Wyatt* DT Ankle LP LP Barryn Sorrell EDGE Foot LP LP Injury Report Terms and Glossary FP = Full participant in practice. LP = Limited participant in practice. DNP = Did not participate in practice. NIR = Not injury related. PUP = Physically unable to participate list. IR = Injured reserve. Note: only starters on IR are listed. CE List = Commissioner’s exempt list. Player Name* = Starter. Injury designation definitions: Probable = the league defines a Probable injury designation as a 75% or greater chance of playing. Historically, 95% of players designated probable are active and played on game day. Questionable = the league defines a Questionable injury designation as being ‘uncertain’ of whether the player will play or not. This replaces the former definition of having a 50% chance of playing. Historically, 70-75% of players with a Questionable injury designation were active and played on game day. Doubtful = The league defines a Doubtful injury designation to mean the player is unlikely to participate in the game. In practical terms, teams use the designation when a player has less than a 50% chance to suit up, and active game appearances from this designation remain rare. Historically only around 6% of players with a Doubtful designation are active and played on game day. Out = will not play. Players with this designation are not active on game day and league rules prohibit them from playing. Notes on Injured Players For the Packers, Micah Parsons, Luke Musgrave, and Jordan Riley are all on the PUP list and will miss the first four games of the season. Josh Jacobs is on the Commissioner’s Exempt list following an offseason incident until further notice. The Packers also have three starting offensive linemen and two starting defensive linemen on their injury report, which isn’t ideal to start the season. Zach Bako-Bewele (formerly Tom) is recovering from offseason knee surgery to repair a partially torn patellar tendon. He said he plans to start on Sunday. Aaron Banks has been dealing with chronic tendinitis in his knee and has missed practice time because of it during training camp. It’s unclear if he’ll be able to go on Sunday or not, but Jager Burton, a rookie fifth-round pick, would be the likely starter at left guard if he can’t go. He continues to be limited so whether he’s able to be a full participant on Friday will be insightful into his availability on Sunday. Would not be surprised to see him listed as questionable. Starting left tackle Jordan Morgan was a surprise addition on Wednesday as a limited participant due to a knee injury. Unclear if this is a minor issue- which seems more likely- or if it more significant. Morgan was upgraded to full participation in Thursday’s practice so he was likely working through something minor and is unlikely to have an injury designation for Sunday’s game. Starting defensive tackles Javon Hargrave and Devonte Wyatt are both dealing with lingering injuries that aren’t likely to keep them out of Sunday’s game, but they could be limiting during the game. I suspect both players are taking it easy as they prepare for Sunday. I would not be surprised if both play on Sunday. Defensive tackle Warren Brinson, who rotates as a backup, seems less likely to be active on Sunday. His second day of not participating in practice makes it more likely he’s not active on Sunday. For the Vikings, no starters on their injury report and the issues with the two Thomas’ are unlikely to keep them out of Sunday’s game. Jakobe Thomas being upgraded to limited is a positive sign in that regard. Caleb Tiernan may or may not be active for the game based on his status on the depth chart as much as the ankle injury he has been dealing with for a couple weeks now. That’s all for today. I’ll have an update again tomorrow with final injury designations. Follow me on X/Bluesky @wludford

title: Daily Norseman Roundtable: 5 Burning Questions to Start the Season
summary: We’re just about ready to start the 2026 season. Well, as Minnesota Vikings fans, anyhow. If you’re a New England Patriots or Seattle Seahawks fan….what are you doing here in the first place? Kidding aside, there are plenty of questions for a Vikings team that hasn’t won a playoff game since Jan. 5, 2020. That’s […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - JANUARY 4: Harrison Smith #22 of the Minnesota Vikings is interviewed after the game against the Green Bay Packers at U.S. Bank Stadium on January 4, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’re just about ready to start the 2026 season. Well, as Minnesota Vikings fans, anyhow. If you’re a New England Patriots or Seattle Seahawks fan….what are you doing here in the first place? Kidding aside, there are plenty of questions for a Vikings team that hasn’t won a playoff game since Jan. 5, 2020. That’s right — before COVID. So we asked the experts from Daily Norseman in our latest edition of the roundtable: Who surprised you most by making the team? Brandon Warne : I’m going with Brett Thorson. Not because I think he didn’t deserve it, but because I thought with how the team is currently constructed, they’d go with the veteran at punter, too. I also thought that if they really regarded Thorson that highly, he probably could have been stashed on the practice squad. I was wrong. They regarded him even more highly. Christopher Gates : As for who I’m most surprised made the team, I think I’d have to go with Zemaiah Vaughn. For those saying “Who,” that shows how few spots were really up for grabs on this roster going into this season. Vaughn currently sits as CB5 on the roster, and I wasn’t sure if he was as good this preseason as Da’Veawn Armstead was, but the Vikings decided that Vaughn was the guy to take that spot. I suppose when you get that far down the depth chart, it’s sort of interchangeable, but that was a bit of a mild upset in my opinion. Warren Ludford : Ben Yurosek. I would think with Josh Oliver and Max Bredeson, they wouldn’t need a third blocking TE/H-back on the roster. Dave Stefano : Jacob Thomas. UDFA out of James Madison, and Flores was giving him flowers in pressers while he was lining up veterans like Jay Ward. That’s not supposed to happen. Brett Thorson beating Hekker is a close second — cost and leg win, but cutting a proven holder/punter that late still feels like a Teasley/O’Connell “we actually mean the youth movement” statement. Four TEs and Max Bredeson also landed heavier than I projected heading into Sunday. Shawn C : Brett Thorson. While there were a few unexpected moves, the only thing that truly surprised me was Thorson beating out Johnny Hekker. There’s a lot on the line this season, and I assumed the proven vet – especially one with Hekker’s resume – would be a foregone conclusion. It’s a huge responsibility for an undrafted rookie, serving as punter and holder for Will Reichard. Who surprised you most by not making the team? BW : By proxy, I guess I have to say Johnny Hekker, right? But he remains unsigned, so I suspect he’s their fallback plan if for some reason Thorson is a disaster. If we know one thing as Vikings fans, it’s that the kicking game rarely matters much in games. /s CG : I’m pretty surprised that Walter Rouse isn’t on the team right now, honestly. Not just because I thought he played pretty well this preseason, but because I thought he offered a lot of versatility along the offensive line. He had gotten some time at both guard and tackle, and given the injury issues that the Vikings have had on the offensive line in recent years, I thought that sort of versatility may have been something they could have found valuable. But, like Vederian Lowe a couple of seasons ago, Rouse is in New England now, so apparently the coaching staff saw things differently than I did. WL : Walter Rouse. Although I get they were able to trade him and probably knew Keegan and/or Samac, or others they liked better, would be available. DS : Johnny Hekker, then Tavierre Thomas [yes, he is on the practice squad now]. Hekker wasn’t clearly beaten on tape; they just preferred the cheaper, bigger-leg IPPP kid. Tavierre had a two-year extension and lived on special teams last year — cutting him because Jacob Thomas ate his lunch is the kind of cold roster math I respect, but I didn’t have it as a lock. Zavier Scott losing the RB3 job to Claiborne is less shocking once you watch the preseason tape. Walter Rouse getting moved instead of just waived was the “wait, they’re actually getting a sixth for that?” surprise. SC : Tavierre Thomas. The easiest choice because they signed him to a two-year extension in the offseason, with $1.95 million guaranteed. He saw significant field time last year and was a proven special-teamer (and, I believe, the unit’s lead tackler). I’m glad to see him back on the practice squad. What practice squad player do you think makes the biggest contribution this season? Editor’s note : For the sake of discussion, we have omitted the most obvious answer of Kyle Van Noy. BW : I’m going with Dillon Bell. I just love the total talent package and he initially made the roster before some finagling had to be done. If he can add some value on special teams, I could see him being active on game days in short order. CG : I’m going to go a bit out of left field and go with DeeJay Dallas. Aaron Jones isn’t getting any younger, and even though he did manage to play all 17 games last season, he has shown a propensity for getting banged up. Dallas showed some flashes as a runner early in his career in Seattle, and could step into the backfield as an option should anything happen to Jones or Jordan Mason. He also has some skills as a returner, too, so he could potentially make an impact on that front as well. WL : Tavierre Thomas. But it depends on injuries and who gets called up. Thomas could get called up for special teams duty. Not really expecting much from any of the practice squad guys, though. DS : I hope this doesn’t happen, but Minnesota’s 53-man backfield is Jones, Mason, Claiborne, and fullback Bredeson. That is a good room until it isn’t. Jones is 31. Mason is a between-the-tackles hammer who has never been asked to carry a full-season passing-down load here. Claiborne is a rookie who won the RB3 job over Zavier Scott. If either starter — or both — goes down for multiple weeks, you do not want the next man up to be “hope the kid is ready” plus a fullback. That is why Teasley put Dallas on the practice squad on Sept. 2 instead of leaving the taxi squad as a pile of camp bodies. Dallas is not a secret feature back. He is a 27-year-old, 5-10, 225-pound fourth-round pick (Seattle, 2020) with 84 career games, 124 rushes for 538 yards (4.3 YPC) and four TDs, 64 catches for 407 yards and two scores, and 89 kickoff returns at 25.3 yards with a 96-yard touchdown in Arizona in 2024. That kick-return average is still among the best of any active back. He also has punt-return work from the Seattle years. That is not a “change-of-pace flyer.” That is a grown man who has already played in this league on Sundays when someone else got hurt. SC : Dillon Bell. Huge fan of Bell’s, and I was excited to see him make the initial 53-man roster and then return to the practice squad. He’s got a diverse skill set ideal for 11-personnel and special teams, is a strong blocker, and would be the call-up if any wide receiver misses time. I wouldn’t be shocked if he saw significant snaps this season. Harry the Hitman is back; on a scale of 1-100, what is your surprise level? What are your expectations for him? BW : I’ll say….60. I figured he’d be back, but the further we went into training camp and the preseason without a helicopter flying out with Ryan Longwell, Steve Hutchinson and Jared Allen out to get him, the more I became convinced he might just be done. I think he’s going to play maybe half the snaps — maybe even as a subpackage guy as the season goes on — and will be just as valuable in the classroom/film room, if not more, than he is on the field. CG : I’ll go with a 22. (See what I did there?) I think that when he didn’t announce his retirement around the same time that C.J. Ham and Adam Thielen did last season, the suspicion was that he was going to be back. He…

title: Gabe Jacas shows improvement in regular season debut
summary: New England Patriots second-round draft pick Gabe Jacas played 19 defensive snaps in his NFL debut Wednesday night. For the most part, head coach Mike Vrabel liked what he saw. “Continues to improve. I thought he was active, set some good edges in the run game. Good to see him make a nice play for […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - SEPTEMBER 9: Gabe Jacas #50 of the New England Patriots celebrates after a play during the third quarter of an NFL football game against the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field on September 9, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images New England Patriots second-round draft pick Gabe Jacas played 19 defensive snaps in his NFL debut Wednesday night. For the most part, head coach Mike Vrabel liked what he saw. “Continues to improve. I thought he was active, set some good edges in the run game. Good to see him make a nice play for a tackle for a loss,” Vrabel said. “Some good things. Some things we’ll have to coach and correct, and fix things on special teams. Thought it was an improvement.” Jacas showed his motor by chasing down Seahawks quarterback Drew Lock for his first career sack in the second quarter. Coming out of halftime, Jacas flashed his athleticism by getting into the backfield for a tackle for loss. But another play caught the eye of his head coach, with Jacas diagnosing a run play against an unbalanced look and chasing down the ball carrier to record a tackle. “Thought his most instinctive play since he’s been here was the unbalanced play in the red zone,” Vrabel explained. “They went for a speed break, tackle over in a little bunch to the boundary. They tried to block down on him and he just kind of reacted across the guys’ face and made a tackle for just a few yard gain. “That was probably the play I was most pleased with. Said this a guy just out here playing.” Mike Vrabel on Gabe Jacas: “Continues to improve. He was active, set some good edges in the run game… Thought it was an improvement.” Calls the play vs. unbalanced look (1:05) the most instinctual play he’s made since being here. https://t.co/LIqVE0a3H3 — Brian Hines (@iambrianhines) September 10, 2026 After missing the entire spring and start of training camp due to a procedure and contract dispute, things were expectedly moving quickly for Jacas upon his return. That included some consistent issues in the preseason when it came to play recognition. The struggles left many wondering if Jacas’ Week 1 role would be diminished. But those inside the building noted that the extra preparation time ahead of the season opener was beneficial to Jacas and other younger players across the roster. Jacas felt similarly. “The preseason definitely helped. Then coming into the game, the preparation that we had, like a week or two to prepare for this game. I was comfortable out there and just playing football,” he said post game. The Patriots edge group — which currently features just four players on the active roster — was the position with the most question marks on the roster ahead of the season. The group got off to an overall strong start as free agent addition Dre’Mont Jones impressed in his Patriots’ debut, leading the team with seven pressures. The early flashes from Jacas were then promising, and the 23-year building on that performance would be a welcomed development for the edge group. “Not bad. I mean, there’s a lot of stuff I can clean up,” Jacas said of his performance. “First sack, first game. Not too bad, just look at the film when I get back and work on the things I need to work on. You know, just continue to improve as weeks go on.”

title: Patriots injury analysis after season opener vs. Seahawks
summary: Their season opener against the Seattle Seahawks did not go the way the New England Patriots would have hoped. Not only did they let a 10-0 lead slip out of their grasp behind a three-interception performance from their starting quarterback, they also lost one of their most important offensive skill position players to what projects […]
full_text: Their season opener against the Seattle Seahawks did not go the way the New England Patriots would have hoped. Not only did they let a 10-0 lead slip out of their grasp behind a three-interception performance from their starting quarterback, they also lost one of their most important offensive skill position players to what projects as a multi-week injury. Obviously, all eyes are on A.J. Brown and his sprained ankle coming out of the game. But as a look at our weekly injury analysis shows, he was not the only Patriot to get banged up during the 13-10 defeat on Wednesday night . Patriots injury analysis: NFL Week 1 CB Carlton Davis III: Davis was shaken up midway through the first quarter while helping to blow up a run play. He remained down on one knee, but jogged off with members of New England’s training staff shortly thereafter. Following a brief stay in the blue medical tent, he returned to the sidelines and eventually reentered. the contest on the next defensive series. TE Hunter Henry: Henry took a hard hit on the first play from scrimmage in the second half, landing on his back after a 13-yard reception. He left the field under his own power and entered the medical tent for further evaluation, but returned to the game a short time later. WR A.J. Brown: The big one. Brown remained on the ground after an incomplete third-down attempt, with medical personnel and even head coach Mike Vrabel checking in on him on the field. He limped off the field into the medical tent, and later gingerly walked back to the locker room albeit under his own power. Follow-up evaluation done on Thursday found out that he had suffered a high-ankle sprain . C Jared Wilson: The Patriots’ starting center had to be evaluated on the sideline after suffering an apparent cut on his right snapping hand during the first series of the second half, the same that saw Henry and Brown get shaken up. He ended up playing all 71 offensive snaps. RT Morgan Moses: During his Monday press conference, head coach Mike Vrabel listed Moses among other players suffering injuries in the game. There was no obvious moment an injury might have occurred, however, and he did end up playing 100% of New England’s offensive snaps. What this means for the Patriots Losing A.J. Brown just 31 snaps into his Patriots debut is an obvious blow to an offense that already had a hard time stringing consistent plays together versus the Seahawks with him on the field. Now, the unit will have to find a way to operate with Romeo Doubs, DeMario Douglas, Mack Hollins, Kyle Williams and Efton Chism as its primary wide receivers — a group that will be in the spotlight over the coming games. Based on Wednesday and his role throughout the summer, Williams in particular should see an uptick in reps as the primary X-receiver. Hollins, who does have some good chemistry with Drake Maye, also will continue to be heavily involved. For how long Brown will be out remains to be seen. According to reports, the expected recovery range for his type of sprain is somewhere between four and six weeks. This means that short-term injured reserve, which would sideline him for a minimum of four weeks, appears to be a realistic if ultimately disappointing possibility. As for the other players listed above, they do not appear to have suffered any long-term issues. “Morgan Moses was able to return. Hunter Henry was able to return. Carlton Davis III was able to return,” said Mike Vrabel on Thursday. “Probably some bumps and bruises, but I do not think anything that would keep anybody out. A.J. Brown is one we will have to monitor.” Coming off their season opener, the Patriots will enjoy a 10-day break before their home opener against the Pittsburgh Steelers.
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Patriots vs. Seahawks: The good, the bad, the s—t that gets you beat
summary: Ahead of his first training camp as Patriots head coach in 2025, Mike Vrabel explained that he was judging his team’s performances by three distinct categories: the good, the bad, and the s—t that gets you beat. If Vrabel looks at his team through those specific categorizations, we shall follow his lead. To New England […]
full_text: Ahead of his first training camp as Patriots head coach in 2025, Mike Vrabel explained that he was judging his team’s performances by three distinct categories: the good, the bad, and the s—t that gets you beat. If Vrabel looks at his team through those specific categorizations, we shall follow his lead. To New England Patriots losing their season opener was not entirely unexpected; as far back as the NFL schedule release in May, we already pegged their Week 1 game in Seattle as a potential loss. The issue was not that the Patriots lost to the Seahawks for a second time in seven months, it’s how they lost: after taking a 10-0 lead, to a backup quarterback, with their own MVP runner-up effectively throwing the game away. With that all being said, let’s dive into our weekly breakdown of the good and the not-so-good from the 13-10 defeat on Wednesday night . The good: Christian Gonzalez Even though the end result was most definitely underwhelming, the Patriots saw a few positive contributions against the Seahawks. Will Campbell showed some positive strides, as did Gabe Jacas; Mack Hollins stepped up after A.J. Brown’s reported high-ankle sprain; Andy Borregales hit his lone field goal from 50 yards out. Ultimately, though, none of them had the same level of consistency as Christian Gonzalez. Fresh off signing a four-year, $135 million contract extension , the highest-paid cornerback in NFL history looked the part: with the exception of a dropped interception in the second quarter and slightly tipping his hand on a corner blitz on the Seahawks’ long 4th-and-1 touchdown, he was near-flawless. On five targets, he gave up one 4-yard catch (to tight end A.J. Barner) and had two pass breakups. He also locked down NFL Offensive Player of the Year Jaxon Smith-Njigba whenever lined up across from him. Every time that JSN and Christian Gonzalez matched up last night 🍿 @jaxon_smith1 @chrisgonzo28 pic.twitter.com/joH2p0wBPf — NFL (@NFL) September 10, 2026 According to NFL Next Gen Stats, Gonzalez and Smith-Njigba faced each other on 10 total snaps with both of the passes thrown their way ending up incomplete. For comparison, JSN was targeted on nine of 18 routes against all other Patriots defenders. The bad: Coaching decisions Speaking of Christian Gonzalez, his usage was curious. Despite showing himself up to the task of taking on the Seahawks’ most dangerous player, he only did so on 10 occasions throughout the game, including on seven man coverage snaps. All eight of Smith-Njigba’s catches for 122 yards and a touchdown, meanwhile, came against zone. He faced man coverage on only nine of his routes for a rate of 32.1% — a number that was 70% versus Gonzalez and only 11% against every other defender. Ultimately, the Patriots only gave up 13 points which in a vacuum is a solid defensive outing. That said, one has to wonder how a different plan for Gonzalez and the rest of the secondary would have impacted that number. That coaching decision was not the only head-scratcher. On offense, coordinator Josh McDaniels’ insistence on running the ball on early downs repeatedly created unfavorable downs and distances. Obviously, three interceptions on the last three drives distort the picture but even before those issues began the Patriots had only scored on two of their six possessions. The game plan seemingly meant to keep Drake Maye out of pressure situations did not exactly create plenty of scoring opportunities either. The s—t that gets you beat: Drake Maye’s decision making “We’re trying to be aggressive and obviously win the football game, but not reckless,” said Vrabel during his post-game press conference when asked about the Drake Maye interception that ended the Patriots’ hopes for a comeback late in the fourth quarter. That recklessness was what ultimately doomed the team on Wednesday night. Yes, it didn’t help that the defense gave up that long touchdown or allowed Drew Lock to complete 72.7% of his passes, but at the end of the day, the Patriots were let down by their most important player. He knows it, too . “We had the game under control. I thought we had a good plan to try to start chipping away and be patient; I lost patience, and it cost us,” Maye said. “[They were] decisions that cost us the game on my part. I’ve asked myself to be better and realize it’s a long season, but at the same time, can’t have those.” Entering the fourth quarter, Maye had completed 17 of 22 passes for 127 yards and a touchdown. His 5.8 yards per attempt was low, but purposeful: the Patriots did not want to run long-developing pass plays against a pass rush capable of giving them all sorts of fits. And while the results especially coupled with the aforementioned early-down runs were not always pretty, they did allow the team to take control of the game and enter the final period with a 10-3 lead. Then, the wheels came off. An unnecessary deep shot intended for Romeo Doubs into disciplined coverage, followed by too much aggressiveness on a third-and-long, followed by a head-scratching lack of situational awareness while in field goal range. Three passes, three picks. That’s all it took to turn what had been a quite solid performance into one of the worst of Maye’s career, and to lose the Patriots the game.

title: A.J. Brown injury update: Patriots WR expected to miss at least 3 weeks
summary: Update 9/10/2026: A.J. Brown to miss at least 3 weeks with reported high-ankle sprain New England Patriots wide receiver A.J. Brown did indeed suffer a high-ankle sprain on Wednesday night against the Seattle Seahawks. An MRI taken on Thursday confirmed the initial diagnosis and according to a report by NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport suggests that […]
full_text: Update 9/10/2026: A.J. Brown to miss at least 3 weeks with reported high-ankle sprain New England Patriots wide receiver A.J. Brown did indeed suffer a high-ankle sprain on Wednesday night against the Seattle Seahawks. An MRI taken on Thursday confirmed the initial diagnosis and according to a report by NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport suggests that the 29-year-old “[is] expected to be out at least four weeks.” A follow-up report by NFL insider Jordan Schultz put the projected recovery time at around 3-6 weeks, with internal discussions whether or not a move to injured reserve will be necessary. Original story 9/10/2026: A.J. Brown suffered high-ankle sprain against Seahawks, per report The New England Patriots will be without their No. 1 wide receiver for the foreseeable future. A.J. Brown, who exited Wednesday’s loss to the Seattle Seahawks in the third quarter, is believed to have suffered a high-ankle sprain. According to a report by NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport and Mike Garafolo, how much time he will miss will be determined by an MRI on Thursday. X-rays did come back negative for a fracture of the injured right ankle, though. Brown, 29, joined the Patriots in a trade with the Eagles this offseason. He promptly took on a starting role, and as such was on the field for 31 of New England’s first 35 snaps against Seattle. He caught three passes for 26 yards along the way and drew a 34-yard pass interference penalty to set up his team’s lone touchdown. However, he remained on the ground following an unsuccessful target in the third period. Brown eventually got up under his own power before limping to the blue medical tent on the sidelines. He departed for the locker room shortly thereafter, and was eventually ruled out for the remainder of the game. In his place, New England relied heavily on fellow wideout Mack Hollins while also giving Kyle Williams a handful of reps in the X-receiver spot. “We don’t blink at all. It’s always been the-next-man-up mentality,” said offensive tackle Morgan Moses after the game. “We know in that room we have some dogs. It’s not just one guy. When you have a room like that, full of guys that can make the play, you’re never thinking on one guy. The opportunity for the other guys to step up was there, and they did what they needed to do. A.J.’s a professional, and he’ll do what he needs to do to get back.” Coming out of their season opener, the Patriots will enjoy a mini-bye before their next game on Sept. 20 against the Pittsburgh Steelers.

title: Lan Larison, Mitch Wishnowsky revert to Patriots’ practice squad following season opener
summary: Lan Larison and Mitch Wishnowsky reverted to the New England Patriots’ practice squad on Thursday after having a hand in the 2026 season opener. The running back and punter served as standard elevations for what became a 13-10 loss to the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field. Larison, 24, made his NFL debut as part of […]
full_text: Foxborough, MA - August 25: New England Patriots running back Lan Larison runs with the ball during practice at Gillette Stadium on August 25, 2026. (Photo by Danielle Parhizkaran/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images Lan Larison and Mitch Wishnowsky reverted to the New England Patriots’ practice squad on Thursday after having a hand in the 2026 season opener. The running back and punter served as standard elevations for what became a 13-10 loss to the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field. Larison, 24, made his NFL debut as part of a backfield that included starter Rhamondre Stevenson and recent trade acquisition Corey Kiner. With TreVeyon Henderson ruled out due to an ankle injury, the UC Davis product saw three snaps on offense and six snaps on special teams in the Super Bowl LX rematch. Converting one first down, he caught a pair of passes for nine yards and averaged 24.5 yards per kickoff return. Signed by the Patriots as an undrafted free agent in 2025, Larison redshirted his rookie year on injured reserve after suffering a foot injury . He proceeded to score his second preseason touchdown last month. And at the 53-man roster deadline, the 5-foot-11, 209-pound running back was waived and retained on the initial practice squad after going unclaimed. Wishnowsky, 34, joined New England’s practice squad at its formation as incumbent Bryce Baringer landed on injured reserve to begin the regular season. The 6-foot-2, 220-pound veteran specialist soon served as the holder and punter in the Pacific Northwest alongside 2025 draft picks in long snapper Julian Ashby and kicker Andy Borregales. From there, he played a part in a 50-yard field goal while averaging 44.3 yards per punt and 42.0 net yards per punt across four opportunities. A trio of inside-the-20 efforts and no touchbacks were notched against past Pro Bowl and All-Pro returner Rashid Shaheed. Entering the NFL in the fourth round of the 2019 class at No. 110 overall, Wishnowsky spent six years with the San Francisco 49ers before stints with the Washington Commanders and Buffalo Bills. Released at the latest cutdown deadline, the former Ray Guy Award winner by way of Australia, Santa Barbara City College and the University of Utah now stands 106 games into his career. Two standard call-ups remain for the two reversions before an official move to the active roster would be required to take the field. In Week 2, the Pittsburgh Steelers will visit Gillette Stadium. The home opener is set for 1 p.m. ET on Sunday, Sept. 20.

title: Fan Notes from the Patriots’ loss to the Seahawks
summary: We all know Overreaction Monday. Welcome to Overreaction Thursday. And if you think Overreaction Monday is bad, you might want to hole up somewhere without internet for a while. I’m going to do my best not to buy into the hype and acknowledge that it’s a long, long season. I’m probably feeling the same way […]
full_text: We all know Overreaction Monday. Welcome to Overreaction Thursday. And if you think Overreaction Monday is bad, you might want to hole up somewhere without internet for a while. I’m going to do my best not to buy into the hype and acknowledge that it’s a long, long season. I’m probably feeling the same way as a lot of you this morning, based on what happened last night. But I’m nothing if not rational, logical, and objective — and a damn good liar to boot. So let’s get to it. First thing’s first: Wednesday Night Football can go kick rocks. I don’t know how long it’s going to be before there’s an NFL game on every day of the week, but I can’t imagine we’re that far out. It’s a horrible idea, but that hasn’t stopped the NFL in the past. I would also imagine that it won’t be that long before you’re going to need 16 different subscriptions if you want the option of watching every game at home in your underwear. But then again, we’re never going to stop watching. We have all proven time and time again that there literally isn’t a single thing that a player, coach, or league executive could do that will make us stop watching this sport. So I don’t know why I find myself harping on this nonsense year in and year out. Speaking of nonsense… I shouldn’t be as upset about this loss as I am. And I’ll likely be over it soon. You figure opening night of the season, in Seattle, banner-raising ceremony, prime time… not sure how you get a much tougher ask for the very first game than that. I feel like most of us had this one pegged as an L right when the schedule first came out. But the way in which the Patriots lost, from getting completely outcoached to our quarterback getting completely outplayed to the overall lackluster performance and overall rustiness of the squad, just left a bad taste in my mouth. Maye as well rip the band-aid off. See what I did there? Drake Maye is a major reason why the Patriots lost last night. He began the game with efficient, smart play, but something happened in the third quarter and he couldn’t get out of his own way. The pick he threw to end the game might be the worst decision of his career, and he made more than a few wrong reads. And you can’t blame the line this time. I think that the offensive line play was, for the most part, one of the bright spots of the night. I wonder how much freedom Maye has to switch the play at the line, because as much as the execution was on him, I think what has my ass most chapped this morning is the way the Patriots seemed to approach the game once Darnold was out. There was no urgency, no creativity, and there seemed to be a belief on the sidelines that 3-0 was probably enough to win the Patriots the game. The Seahawks were clearly on their heels with the loss of their QB and had their guard up in the corner of the ring trying to figure out what to do next, and the Patriots could have stepped on their throat. Instead they decided to let Rhamondre Stevenson step over his own feet for 1.9 yards a clip on every single first and second down. What’s really weird about last night is that you can almost pinpoint the unraveling to the moment A.J. Brown went down. It’s like Seattle changed their coverage schemes or Maye lost his faith in the offense or something. I really, really don’t think that’s what it was, but it’s an odd coincidence. I should probably bitch a little more about the playcalling, how vanilla and conservative it was, and how little the Patriots seemed able to adjust once Seattle got themselves back together. The 2025 Patriots adopted the bold strategy of letting their opponents score on almost every opening drive without breaking a sweat or needing a third down to do it. I wonder if the 2026 Patriots are going to try their hand at calling an HB Dive up the gut on every first and second down of the first half. This would have been a great TreVeyon Henderson game, I think. He has more explosive speed around the edge, and I think he would have done well as the passing back. When one of your offensive highlights is a nine-yard Lan Larison catch and run and your starting RB is your second-leading receiver, I can’t help but think the Patriots could have used Henderson’s speed and ability as a receiver. The other offensive highlight of the day was a horribly underthrown pass to A.J. Brown that drew a DPI call. I’d like to hope that Joe Flacco saw that pass last night and shed a single tear of nostalgic joy. I wish they’d fix that. There’s nothing to be done there by the DB. It’s the NFL equivalent of a litigation-happy driver slamming on his brakes so he intentionally gets rear-ended for a cheap payday. But I don’t have any kind of solution to offer. Nobody can even figure out what a catch is, so there’s no way I want the NFL leaving the word “uncatchable” in the hands of the refs. I used to always associate Seattle with some of the best music this country has ever produced. I’m starting to associate them with sadness now. And I’ll tell you what really isn’t helping in that department. I was always very aware of my middle age, but I didn’t realize that, until very recently, I was in denial over what that actually entails. Then I learned about a whole new genre of music called Divorced Dad Rock. It’s basically all the music I listened to in high school. And while I’m neither divorced nor a dad, I’m a Divorced Dad Rock guy. The angle of the sun on the opening kickoff had me thinking that the NFL was using some kind of new red ball. All of this bellyaching aside, I think that the Patriots are going to be fine. That Seattle defense is still as good as ever, and Week 1 is always weird. They need to move past this right away and get ready for the Steelers in what has suddenly become a Week 2 game that carries way more importance than it should. Even tougher than coping with last night’s game was having to break the news to the wife that the Patriots no longer have Marte Mapu or Kayshon Boutte on their roster. One of her favorite Sunday activities used to be asking me “is Mapu doing that thing with Boutte?” There’s a reason why she married me. Speaking of Boutte… kinda coulda used him last night. That said, Romeo Doubs is going to be fine. Remember that multi-fumble Mondre game last year where we all thought he should be benched? I’d absolutely love to use the NFL application of the word “questionable” to my everyday life. Alec Shane is questionable to report to work today. Alec Shane is questionable to take out the trash. Alec Shane’s return from the bathroom is questionable. Probably the MVPs for both teams last night are the punters. Mitch Wishnowsky had himself a game last night. And the nickname potential is simply phenomenal. I forgot how much people absolutely despise the Patriots. Unreal levels of creativity in the hate. And I imagine that they’re having an absolute field day today—as they should. The team looked terrible, the coaching was terrible, Drake Maye was terrible, and the folks who harped on The Schedule are probably feeling great right now. But that’s OK. If you don’t have haters, you’re irrelevant in this sport. I’ll end things on a positive note, because I really do believe it: the Patriots are going to be one of the better teams in the AFC. They’re going to figure things out. Drake Maye is going to settle, and the starters will gel and get more reps with each other, and things are going to go well. It’s never fun to get slapped around by a backup quarterback, nor is it fun to lose your big offseason acquisition for what looks to be at least a few weeks. But the NFL is lousy with teams who looked terrible in September and unstoppable in December. We’ll get there. Time to get ready for Thursday Night football. I know h0w long we’ve all been wondering why the NFL doesn’t play a game in Australia, so it’s wonderful that they’re addressing it tonight.

title: Romeo Doubs vows to be better after disappointing Patriots debut
summary: Maybe Romeo Doubs just wanted to get his annual no-catch game out of the way early. The New England Patriots wide receiver, who arrived in the offseason via a four-year, $68 million free agency deal, did not haul in a single one of his targets on Wednesday night against the Seattle Seahawks. It was his […]
full_text: Maybe Romeo Doubs just wanted to get his annual no-catch game out of the way early. The New England Patriots wide receiver, who arrived in the offseason via a four-year, $68 million free agency deal, did not haul in a single one of his targets on Wednesday night against the Seattle Seahawks. It was his fifth catch-less game in five years in the NFL. He had one in 2022, one in 2023, one in 2024, and one in 2025. Now, he also has one in 2026. Based on that fact alone, happier times should be ahead for the 26-year-old. At his locker after Wednesday’s 13-10 defeat , however, happiness was in short supply. Accountability, on the other hand, was not. “I just wasn’t locked in,” Doubs told reporters. “That’s all. I mean, the video speaks for itself. I’ll be better moving forward.” Doubs was one of two high-prized wide receivers brought in by the Patriots in the spring; the former Packers fourth-round draft pick joined in free agency, A.J. Brown as a trade acquisition from the Eagles. The season opener in Seattle was an opportunity for both to finally leave their mark on New England’s offense. Both their nights ended in an underwhelming fashion. Besides Doubs finishing with no catches, Brown left the game with an ankle injury in the third quarter after three receptions for 26 yards. Doubs could have had similar numbers, but none of the three passes thrown his way ended up as completions. The first was picked off, the second was dropped to negate what would have been a sizable gain, the third fell incomplete on third down. “I just put that on my end,” Doubs said. “I’ll just be able to move forward. That had nothing to do with Drake [Maye]. That was 150% me, and I’ll be better.” Like his quarterback, who ended the day with three total interceptions, Doubs also received encouragement from his teammates after the game. “He’s the definition of a leader,” said team captain Morgan Moses. “All of us got some things that we look in the mirror at ourselves and say, ‘Hey, we can get better.’ Going back to the drawing board. I think Game 1 is always the hardest, because you never know what they’re going to throw out there. But you just go play football. You line the football up wherever you line it up, and you go out there and you play football. There’s some things that you want to get back that you can’t get back, but it’s going to make you a better player for the rest of the season.” For Doubs, the goal for the rest of the season is clear: live up to the trust the organization showed in him when it brought him aboard in March. Despite the outcome against the Seahawks, he seems confident in his ability to be able to do so. “Part of my job as a player is to make this team better,” he said, “and I’ll be better moving forward.”
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Patriots express confidence in Drake Maye after Seahawks loss
summary: The New England Patriots see Drake Maye as the face of their franchise. On Wednesday night, he was relegated to being the face of their defeat. Going up against the same Seattle Seahawks team that beat him and his team in Super Bowl LX seven months earlier, the third-year quarterback played one of the worst […]
full_text: The New England Patriots see Drake Maye as the face of their franchise. On Wednesday night, he was relegated to being the face of their defeat. Going up against the same Seattle Seahawks team that beat him and his team in Super Bowl LX seven months earlier, the third-year quarterback played one of the worst games of his career. Maye threw interceptions on each of the Patriots’ final three possessions, playing a critical part in a 10-0 lead turning into a 13-10 defeat . Maye himself was critical of his performance, calling the three picks “unacceptable” during his postgame press conference. The rest of his team, meanwhile, was not that harsh on the 24-year-old. “We have nothing but the utmost confidence in him and everybody on this football team,” said head coach Mike Vrabel. “He’s going to make a lot of plays for us.” Maye did just that on Sunday, even after his interception woes began. Following his first two picks, which allowed Seattle to take a lead for the first time all day, he marched the Patriots into the red zone on what very well could have been the game-winning drive. Along the way, he showed his trademark playmaking ability as both a passer and a runner. However, that series, like the two previous ones, ended with a costly mistake by the former third overall draft pick. And yet, his teammates made sure not to pin the defeat on Maye. “It’s not on one person at all,” said running back Rhamondre Stevenson. “This is a team game. We win together and we lose together. I wouldn’t pinpoint on one single person in that room. We all have to get better. Back to the drawing board and figure it out.” “I have the utmost confidence in him,” added wide receiver Romeo Doubs, the target on the first of Maye’s three INTs. “I know what he can do. I’ve watched him and what he’s done in this league a long time, and, like I said, this doesn’t define him. It’s just this league, it’s always a pendulum in this league.” The message of support did not only come out of the offense. The Patriots defense echoed those remarks as well. “We have all the confidence in the world in Drake,” said cornerback Carlton Davis. “He’s our guy. We are going to stick together right now, and we’ll move forward.”
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: 10 things we learned from Patriots vs. Seahawks
summary: The New England Patriots lost their season opener in Seattle on Wednesday night, and the defeat was somehow worse than anyone could have predicted. The Patriots jumped to a 10-0 lead in the third quarter, but gave up 13 straight points down the stretch — in large part due to three straight interceptions from quarterback Drake […]
full_text: The New England Patriots lost their season opener in Seattle on Wednesday night, and the defeat was somehow worse than anyone could have predicted. The Patriots jumped to a 10-0 lead in the third quarter, but gave up 13 straight points down the stretch — in large part due to three straight interceptions from quarterback Drake Maye — to lose 13-10. Here is what the defeat taught us. It’s simple: Drake Maye just collapsed When talking about this game, we have to start with Drake Maye. The Patriots’ quarterback was playing smart for three quarters, taking what the defense gave him and not putting the ball in harm’s way. In the fourth quarter, he completely collapsed. Yes, he was let down by his receivers at times, but all three of his picks, which were exclusively thrown in the fourth period, were clearly on him. This is, by his own admission, unacceptable and cannot continue to happen for a third-year player considered to be one of the best quarterbacks in the NFL. The concerning part is that this is not the first time this has happened in his career either. Losing to Drew Lock is embarrassing I know that Sam Darnold is not an elite quarterback. I know that the Seahawks don’t run around him. It still hurts to see Drew Lock be the quarterback to not just beat you, but also outplay your own MVP runner-up quarterback along the way. Regardless of what else happens in the game, that simply cannot happen. And yet, it did. It’s a big reason why the Patriots left Seattle as losers. The Seahawks coached circles around the Patriots Mike Macdonald is one of the best defensive coaches in football, and he showed that again on Wednesday night. The Patriots were never comfortable pushing the ball down the field, Maye looked rattled, and, once the Seahawks adjusted to the swing pass to beat the blitz, the Patriots had almost no consistent offense to speak of. To make things worse, the Seahawks offensive was led by a rookie coordinator who found a way to move the ball consistently in the second half with a backup QB . The Patriots’ lack of adjustments was obvious, and the home team flat out smashed them in the coaching matchup. Mike Vrabel, Josh McDaniels and Zak Kuhr are all very good coaches, but they were far from good enough on Wednesday night. The Patriots have had the coaching advantage in a lot of games since Vrabel took over as their head coach, but in the last two games they have played, they have simply been outcoached. The Patriots were dominated on the line of scrimmage The Patriots spent a lot of money and resources in the offseason trying to make their running game more effective, and, for Wednesday night at least, they did not seem to be successful. They were unable to get almost any consistent push on the offensive line, or open up real holes for their backs until the last drive of the game. If their identity is going to be a physical, smash-mouth football team, this is going to have to vastly improve moving forward. Averaging 2.6 yards per carry between Rhamondre Stevenson and Corey Kiner is just nowhere near good enough. On the defensive side of the ball, Seattle was able to run the ball effectively, though they didn’t do it a ton. The Patriots did end up with a pair of sacks, but the pressure was far from consistent, and too often Drew Lock had a clean pocket to make an easy throw. There is no sugar-coating it either. The Patriots need to be much better on both sides of the line to give themselves a chance to win more games, because what they got on Wednesday was simply not good enough. That said, I do think that the pass blocking overall was much improved outside of a miscommunication or two, so at least that was a positive to take away from what was mostly a rough game from the trenches. The A.J. Brown injury is a serious concern A.J. Brown went down with an ankle injury and left the stadium in a walking boot, and I don’t think it’s a coincidence that the Patriots offense went off the rails after that happened. The concern is this potentially being an injury that sidelines Brown for an extended period of time. If that’s the case, they are going to need a whole heck of a lot more out of every receiver not named Mack Hollins. The Patriots gave up a 2028 first-round pick to get Brown, and they were hoping to make him the focal point of the offense. Losing him would be a massive blow. I would also like to mention that I advocated for the Patriots to include conditions to the pick they sent to the Eagles that revolved around playing time and performance. Hindsight is 20/20, but they might end up kicking themselves for not doing that if this injury ends up being of the serious variety. Romeo Doubs has a rough debut The Patriots shipped Kayshon Boutte out of town because, besides trading for A.J. Brown, they also went out and signed Romeo Doubs away from the Packers in free agency. In his first game with his new team, he was targeted three times, with one target being an interception, one being a bad drop that led to an interception on the next play, and the third falling incomplete on a third down. Doubs looked slow, showed off bad hands, and couldn’t get open all night. Other than that, how was the play Mrs. Lincoln? In case Brown is going to miss time due to his ankle injury, the Patriots are going to need Doubs to step up in a big way. Mack Hollins looked roughly better than Doubs on Wednesday, and that simply cannot happen given the investment made in the latter. Gabe Jacas plays well Gabe Jacas basically looked like he didn’t belong on an NFL field for most of training camp and preseason. In his first regular season game, however, he finished with a sack and two tackles for loss. He did have a bad penalty on special teams, but he showed some promise along the edge, and that is exactly what the Patriots are going to need from him moving forward. Of all the negatives in this game, Jacas wasn’t one of them, and that’s a good thing. Will Campbell plays well Speaking of positives, Campbell was much-maligned in the playoffs and Super Bowl, and people like me told you that it was because he was injured and that he would be better. I’m happy to report that, at least for one game, the glass-half-full outlook appears to be the correct one. Campbell received a questionable holding call and had a correct block in the back call, so it wasn’t perfect. Unlike the Super Bowl, however, he held his own against a very good Seahawks defense. It was a definitive step in the right direction. Maybe the Patriots should have played their starters in preseason Of all the criticisms, the most obvious one is that New England simply should have played its guys in the preseason. And there is an argument for that, just ask ex-Patriot Jason McCourty: You can tell starters didn’t play in the preseason!!! — Jason McCourty (@JasonMcCourty) September 10, 2026 The Patriots looked rusty and uncomfortable at times out there. The offensive operation was clunky, and Drake Maye certainly needs more time to develop chemistry with his new receivers. Now, did they lose this game because they didn’t play their starters in the preseason? Absolutely not, but I am always an advocate for giving players at least a series or two to get them back to full-speed and full-contact football. Joint practices are fine, but they are not tackling, and they can’t hit the quarterback. It’s a different feeling when you have 11 guys bearing down on you trying to knock you out, and it seems that Maye could have used those reps. Mini-bye awaits The Patriots are going to have 10 days to let this one settle, as they don’t play again until September 20 when they host the Steelers for their home opener. As poorly as the Patriots played, it’s important to remember that it was against a fantastic football team. The Steelers, on the other hand, are a good bounce-back opportunity. If Drake Maye plays like he did in the fourth quarter, then the Patriots could lose to any team in the NFL. However, they have plenty of time…
author: Pat Lane

title: Our defense vs. their offense: Detroit Lions
summary: On Sunday, both the New Orleans Saints and Detroit Lions will begin their 2026 regular season at Ford Field as a long offseason comes to a conclusion. Ahead of what will likely be a competitive NFC battle, let’s take a look at what the New Orleans defense will be up against this weekend. Saints’ defensive […]
full_text: On Sunday, both the New Orleans Saints and Detroit Lions will begin their 2026 regular season at Ford Field as a long offseason comes to a conclusion. Ahead of what will likely be a competitive NFC battle, let’s take a look at what the New Orleans defense will be up against this weekend. Saints’ defensive coordinator Brandon Staley lost a couple of key pieces from his 2025 group. Talented veteran players such as CB Alontae Taylor and LB Demario Davis departed from the Big Easy by way of the free agency market. While New Orleans has young guys with potential on the current roster, it is difficult to replicate the vocal nature and consistent presence these leaders provided. While areas on the defense remain weak, the Saints have made some key additions on top of retaining All-Pro DE Cam Jordan. LB Kaden Elliss and DT Christen Miller made their way to New Orleans via free agency and this year’s NFL draft, respectively. With Jordan still recovering from a hamstring injury sustained late in the offseason, it will be critical for New Orleans to get some pressure on Lions’ QB Jared Goff while keeping their offense backed into long down-and-distance situations. Detroit has explosive playmakers at just about every offensive skill position. Sharing the backfield with Goff, tailback Jahmyr Gibbs can attack defenses both in the run and passing games. The Lions also possess one of the better WR duos in the league with Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jameson Williams, but just when you think everyone is covered, TE Sam LaPorta can stretch the field and make a linebacker look silly. Last year, the Lions had a top five offense in the league averaging just under 375 yards per game. When your offense has the capabilities of moving the football up and down the field like Detroit does, putting points on the board becomes much easier. Detroit scored an average of 28.3 (Saints fans laugh here) points a contest in 2025. If New Orleans expects to have any shot at overcoming the Lions on the road, their defense will have to anchor down and disrupt an offense that can find a rhythm quickly.
author: Jason Watson Jr

title: Week 1 Prediction: New Orleans Saints vs. Detroit Lions
summary: There’s no easing into the 2026 season for the New Orleans Saints. They will open the season on Sunday afternoon on the road against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field, facing a team that is very eager to put last year’s disappointing 9-8 record behind it. For the Saints, it’s an opportunity to show just […]
full_text: There’s no easing into the 2026 season for the New Orleans Saints. They will open the season on Sunday afternoon on the road against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field, facing a team that is very eager to put last year’s disappointing 9-8 record behind it. For the Saints, it’s an opportunity to show just how much progress they’ve made entering Year 2 under head coach Kellen Moore. New Orleans finished 6-11 a year ago, but the team closed the season with four wins in its final five games and enters 2026 with considerably higher expectations. Quarterback Tyler Shough has emerged as a leader, while the Saints made several offseason additions designed to give him more help. But the Saints will have their work cut out for them Sunday. Detroit is a difficult place to open a season, and the Lions have plenty of firepower on both sides of the football. Aidan Hutchinson is coming off a career-high 14.5-sack season, establishing himself as one of the NFL’s top edge rushers and earning second-team All-Pro honors. The Saints also won’t have a completely healthy roster. Running back Alvin Kamara, who has been limited in practice all week, could miss the opener with an MCL injury, meaning offseason addition Travis Etienne will be taking on a significant workload. First-round wide receiver Jordyn Tyson will also miss the first four games after landing on injured reserve with a hamstring injury. Defensively, New Orleans will be without defensive end Cam Jordan, who is battling a hamstring injury and was ruled out Wednesday as well as defensive tackle Bryan Bresee, who was placed on injured reserve in early August. Still, there are several reasons to believe the Saints can make this interesting. Detroit will also be without two key defensive backs, Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph, who will miss at least the first four games as well as the uncertainty of DB Christian Izien, DE Derrick Moore and DL Mekhi Wingo, who have all been limited this week in practice. That could give Shough some opportunities to attack a secondary that isn’t at full strength. The biggest question for New Orleans may be whether the offensive line can protect Shough and whether the Saints can establish enough of a running game to keep Hutchinson and the Lions’ pass rush from taking over. If they can, I expect this to be a competitive game into the fourth quarter. Detroit has the home-field advantage, a talented offense and a defense capable of creating problems for a young New Orleans offense. The Lions are favored by 6.5 points entering the week, and I think they find a way to make enough plays late. Prediction: Lions 27 – Saints 24 However, if Tyler Shough proves capable of making the big throws in a hostile environment, New Orleans could quickly make it clear that this is a very different team from the one that finished 6-11 last season. title: Saints rookie report: Week 1 preview
summary: Welcome to the Week 1 edition of the New Orleans Saints rookie report! A quick preview before we start: this will be a bit different from last year because of injuries and playing time. The Saints relied on their rookies early last season, and although it took time for other players to start, nearly the […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 22: Bryce Lance #18 of the New Orleans Saints during warm up before a preseason game between the New Orleans Saints and the Los Angeles Rams at SoFi Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Harry How/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to the Week 1 edition of the New Orleans Saints rookie report! A quick preview before we start: this will be a bit different from last year because of injuries and playing time. The Saints relied on their rookies early last season, and although it took time for other players to start, nearly the entire class was important to this team. To start this year, many of these players likely won’t play. But I’ll talk about scenarios where they can start and what happens if they are brought into the lineup. Health-wise, I’ll list the injured players at the end. DT Christen Miller For our first player, his playing time will be interesting to watch in Week 1. The Saints clearly view Christen Miller as a nose tackle, and from what we saw in preseason, he looks really good in that spot. Davon Godchaux is the starter, and the expectation is that he can play better as the Saints try to run a 3-4 defense more than last season. But with his age, the Saints may need to sub him out throughout the game, and Miller can step in when that happens. This becomes even more of a focus due to the Saints’ opponent. Detroit Lions RB Jahmyr Gibbs is one of the best RBs in the NFL, and he is about to give the Saints defensive line arguably their biggest test of the season. So much effort will go into stopping Gibbs, and that could be why we see Miller more in this game. TE Oscar Delp As of now, it seems Oscar Delp will play despite a hamstring issue. Personally, I would not rush the young TE, especially after seeing other hamstring issues plague the roster and because Delp is the third-string TE. Still, if he does play, it’s going to be really exciting to see him on the field. The Saints want to use the TE position more in 2026, so all three TEs will get to see the field throughout games. Also, in the run game, Delp is a really good blocker. Again, rushing him should never be in the cards, but if all is good, Delp could have some winning moments against the Lions. OG Jeremiah Wright For our first rookie that will likely not play, Wright is going to be behind Cesar Ruiz for game 1. He’s likely not going to play, but Ruiz has not had the healthiest time in the NFL, so if an injury does happen, Wright would likely step in. Regarding Ruiz’s play on the field, even if he does struggle (which may not happen), I doubt the Saints will make the change. WR Barion Brown Although Bryce Lance was selected before Barion Brown, which is how I determine the order of the rookie report, I wanted to talk about Brown first. Going into game 1, due to Jordyn Tyson’s injury and Brown just flat-out being impressive all offseason, the former LSU Tiger will be in the WR3 spot against Detroit. Also, as the punt and kick returner, Brown is going to have a chance to significantly help the Saints on special teams. On offense, Brown’s presence will bring really nice flexibility to the WR group. While the Lions may put most of their focus on stopping the run or Chris Olave, Brown will have a better chance of beating Detroit deep with his speed. Also, the Lions are missing both of their starting safeties due to injury. Brown is more of a WR than just a deep ball specialist, but I would not be surprised to see Kellen Moore try and get a big play early. WRs Bryce Lance With Brown being WR3, Lance is slotted right into that WR4 spot, and he should still see a good role in Week 1. Lance’s blocking is too good to overlook, and he also has that serious deep threat that Moore could utilize. Also, Lance’s ability after the catch could make him a really good WR on screens. OT Mason Murphy On the depth chart, Mason Murphy is listed as the backup to Taliese Fuaga, and as we saw last year, that is a very important role. Fuaga has dealt with lingering injuries, so having a competent backup will be important for the Saints. As with Ruiz, hopefully no injury occurs, but if it does, Murphy will likely be called upon. Injured players: WR Jordyn Tyson DB Lorenzo Styles Jr.

title: Saints draft position: Entering Week 1
summary: With the New Orleans Saints not having played a game yet, projections are the only way the draft order can be made going into Week 1. According to those projections, the Saints are set to select at pick 9 in the NFL Draft. So, for the first draft position of the season, that is what […]
full_text: NORMAN, OKLAHOMA - SEPTEMBER 20: Defensive tackle David Stone #0 of the Oklahoma Sooners encourages the crowd to cheer on a defensive stand against the Auburn Tigers late in the fourth quarter at Gaylord Family Oklahoma Memorial Stadium on September 20, 2025 in Norman, Oklahoma. Oklahoma won 24-17. (Photo by Brian Bahr/Getty Images) | Getty Images With the New Orleans Saints not having played a game yet, projections are the only way the draft order can be made going into Week 1. According to those projections, the Saints are set to select at pick 9 in the NFL Draft. So, for the first draft position of the season, that is what I’m going to go off of. Also, since it’s early in the college football and NFL year, the focus will be more on the Saints’ roster than the player. Here are two potential selections that would make too much sense for the Saints at pick 9. Texas EDGE Colin Simmons If the Saints are selected in the top 10, EDGE has to be a priority. The Saints’ not adding a sure-thing starting pass rusher across from Chase Young is a worry, but the team believes in attacking that position with a committee instead. The group of Cam Jordan, Tyree Wilson, Anfernee Jennings, and even Kaden Elliss could do some damage in 2026, but that may not work out, and the long-term plan for that position is nonexistent. So, at pick 9, Texas’ star pass rusher Colin Simmons must be the choice if he’s available. Simmons is extremely athletic, had 9 sacks in 2024 and 12 in 2025, can win in a number of different ways against offensive linemen, and is not a liability against the run. Simmons perfectly fits as that 3-4 OLB that the Saints could put across from Young, and the future on the defensive line would look much brighter than it currently is. Oklahoma DT David Stone Sticking with the defensive line, if the Saints don’t go with a pass rusher, I wouldn’t be shocked to see them pivot to a DT. Just like the EDGE group in this draft class, the DTs are extremely talented, and at the top of that list is David Stone. The big DT is an all-around defensive lineman who can make winning plays against the run and in pass rush. His versatility on the defensive line will make defensive coordinators in the NFL salivate at the idea of selecting him, and on the Saints’ defense, he could be an incredible addition. Before getting to his fit, I do have to say one thing. If the Saints view Stone as a primary nose tackle, which could happen, they will likely not make this pick. Christen Miller is the future at that spot. Although if Miller ends up playing some 3-4 DE and doing well, that could make the pick a possibility. If the Saints do view Stone as a potential 3-4 DE to put next to Miller, that would instantly create one of the most exciting DT groups in the NFL. Miller and Stone could make the Saints’ run defense elite.

title: Our offense vs. their defense: Detroit Lions
summary: Tyler Shough and the New Orleans Saints are finally set to begin their 2026 campaign on the road against the Detroit Lions this Sunday. After a relatively disappointing season that finished with a positive swing in momentum last year, expectations and vibes surrounding the team are now higher than they’ve been in over five years. […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TEXAS - AUGUST 28: Noah Fant #87 of the New Orleans Saints runs on the field during the first half of the 2026 NFL preseason game against the Dallas Cowboys at AT&T Stadium on August 28, 2026 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Sam Hodde/Getty Images) | Getty Images Tyler Shough and the New Orleans Saints are finally set to begin their 2026 campaign on the road against the Detroit Lions this Sunday. After a relatively disappointing season that finished with a positive swing in momentum last year, expectations and vibes surrounding the team are now higher than they’ve been in over five years. Ahead of this weekend’s kickoff, let’s take a look at the offensive matchup for the Saints. Detroit’s defense will be down a couple of key players in its secondary as CB Kerby Joseph and SS Brian Branch both landed on the injured reserve list, meaning each will be out at least the first four weeks of the season. The Lions’ defense had a down year in 2025 after giving up an average of over 330 yards per game. Luckily for the Lions, DE Aidan Hutchinson is still an elite edge rusher and with Dan Campbell’s defensive background, the Michigan product should be able to make an impact in the backfield even if just hurrying the processing time of the offense. Although the Saints will have limited options at the WR position available on Sunday due to injuries and roster cuts, Shough’s ability to build chemistry with his pass catchers early on could become a critical factor in New Orleans’ chances to steal a win in the Motor City. New Orleans’ initial depth chart for this weekend showed just three options at wideout to go along with the typical three tight ends. New Orleans struggled to put points on the board last season, averaging just 18 per contest, a mark that ranked 28th in the league. Now, with a full offseason under their belts in the Big Easy, head coach Kellen Moore and Shough will seek to improve the team’s efficiency when in possession of the football, especially when inside of the redzone. With new additions to the Saints such as RB Travis Etienne Jr., OL David Edwards, TE Noah Fant, and more, it is seemingly likely that New Orleans will find more success for their offensive production between the tackles. This, in turn, should allow other areas such as the play action passing game to open up further.
