title: NFL Week 1 picks, predictions: BBV staff split on Giants-Cowboys outcome
summary: Can the New York Giants go against history and upset the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday night? Below, find the Big Blue View staff predictions for that and the rest of the remaining Week 1 slate of NFL games. Chris Pflum Bottom line up front: I’m picking the Giants here. I also have no clue exactly […]
full_text: Can the New York Giants go against history and upset the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday night? Below, find the Big Blue View staff predictions for that and the rest of the remaining Week 1 slate of NFL games. Chris Pflum Bottom line up front: I’m picking the Giants here. I also have no clue exactly how this game is going to play out. There are a ton of unknowns on both sides of the ball. We don’t know exactly what the Cowboys’ defense will look like, and we don’t know what the Giants’ offense or defense will look like between roster and coaching turnover. A year ago I believed that the Giants’ roster was about to hit a critical mass of talent that would allow them to compete week in, week out, without needing to out-scheme their opponents or rely on lucky breaks to win. The results weren’t there, but I do believe the overall talent on the roster put the Giants in position to win more often than not. What I didn’t count on was a lack of accountability and attention to detail from the top down with the Giants’ coaches. This year, I believe the roster is stronger given the continued development of the 2024 and 2025 classes. Ultimately, given all the unknowns in this game, I have to think it will come down to which squad is better prepared for Week 1. And while the Giants’ veteran coaching staff is barely mentioned at the national level, I think they’ve been methodical in how they’ve approached the start of the season. I’m going to trust their experience and clear vision to have the team ready to go on Sunday night. I have no doubts that this is going to be a tough, hard-fought match-up. But I’m going with the Giants starting the season with a statement. Pick: Giants Tony DelGenio 22 years ago, the Giants played their first game under a new, no-nonsense head coach who had almost gotten his team to the Super Bowl a few years earlier. The Giants took a 7-0 lead against the division rival Eagles, but three Donovan McNabb TD passes to Terrell Owens later, Philadelphia won going away. Things eventually worked out, but not in Tom Coughlin’s first season. I expect something similar to happen Sunday, because I feel that the Giants match up poorly with Dallas. The John Harbaugh Giants want to establish the run, but with Quinnen Williams and Kenny Clark inside and Rashan Gary outside, that won’t be easy, and the Giants’ middle of the OL is its weakest part at least until rookie Sisi Mauigoa establishes himself. It is also the place from which I expect the Cowboys to generate the most pressure on Jaxson Dart. Dart in principle should be able to do more business through the air, but that depends on his ability to read Dallas’ disguised coverages and whether a thin receiving corps with a lot of question marks can get open and hold onto the ball often enough. On defense I expect more from this Giants team than last year’s. Dennard Wilson’s defense has to be more effective than Shane Bowen’s was. The Cowboys’ offensive line is missing Pro Bowl guard Tyler Smith, and with the Giants’ revamped linebacking corps I expect Dallas’ running game not to be the weapon against the Giants that it has been in the past, even though we haven’t yet seen D.J. Reader and Shelby Harris in Giants blue. My real concern is the secondary. CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens feasted on Giants’ defensive backs last year. We have absolutely no idea how this year’s group, with reclamation projects Deonte Banks and Greg Newsome starting, will fare. And the underrated Dak Prescott always feasts on the Giants’ D and has fun doing it. Coughlin started his Giants career 6-10 in 2004. I expect something similar from Harbaugh, say 7-10, with the first two losses sadly being in Weeks 1 and 2. Pick: Dallas James Hickey The Giants start the 2026 season seeking to replicate a formula that is in many ways the DNA for that has won them four Super Bowls: a defense who success is based on rushing the quarterback and a physical offense with a quarterback who has a knack for making the plays when needed. When it comes to the Giants defense matching up against the Dallas offense it comes down can Brian Burns, Abdul Carter and Kayvon Thibodeaux get to the quarterback against a banged up Cowboys offense line. Because if given time, Dak Prescott will undoubtedly pick apart a secondary that is starting Tae Banks Week 1. To slow down the Dallas offense, the Giants will need to control the clock with their running game. That brings into the spotlight John Michael Schmitz, the third-year center who has not developed into a top center as hoped. Schmitz will be facing the best defensive tackle tandem in the NFL— Kenny Clark and Quinnen Williams. Since 2016, the four Giants head coaches have split their first games coaching— Ben McAdoo in 2016 Won his debut, 20–19 over the Cowboys and Brian Daboll lead the team to victory in over the Titans in 2020 by a score of 21–20 as Randy Bullock’s 47 yard field goal was wide left as time expired. Pat Shurmur (2018) and Joe Judge (2020) both lost in their debuts. John Harbaugh is not a first-time head coach and will have his team ready for the national Sunday night game. We will see if Dennard Wilson brings an aggressive defense that brings out the best of the players and if the offensive coaching staff can help Jaxson Dart take that proverbial next step. I believe the talent is there and will shine this Sunday. Pick: Giants 27, Dallas 21 Valentine’s View As many years as I have been covering the Giants, and making predictions about them, I should know better. I do know better. I should make the Giants prove they can win games before I pick them to do that. But, while Mrs. Big Blue View would probably disagree, I prefer to be optimistic. I always want to believe that things are going to turn around for the Giants, that things will get better. When I reflect, I can see why things went sideways under Ben McAdoo, Pat Shurmur, Joe Judge, and Brian Daboll. All of them were trying to learn how to be head coaches, and ultimately proved they weren’t cut from the right cloth. John Harbaugh is different. He has already been there and done that. He doesn’t have to prove his head-coaching credentials to anyone. Harbaugh has brought something different to the Giants. He has raised the expectation for everyone — players, front office, the maintenance guys who put together the players’ temporary locker room quarters. To be honest, maybe even the media covering the team. I am going to believe that the last few months of the entire organization going to Harbaugh University will pay off on Sunday night. Pick: Giants
author: Ed Valentine

title: NY Giants’ OC Matt Nagy will call plays from upstairs vs. Cowboys
summary: After experimenting during the preseason with calling plays from the sideline and upstairs in a booth high above the field, New York Giants offensive coordinator Matt Nagy said Thursday he will work from upstairs Sunday night against the Dallas Cowboys. “I’m excited about it. I think that I’ve always been down on the field. When […]
full_text: Matt Nagy | Getty Images After experimenting during the preseason with calling plays from the sideline and upstairs in a booth high above the field, New York Giants offensive coordinator Matt Nagy said Thursday he will work from upstairs Sunday night against the Dallas Cowboys. “I’m excited about it. I think that I’ve always been down on the field. When I was a quality control coach, I was up in the box for one year,” Nagy said on Thursday. “So, I wanted to experiment with that in the preseason, and I was able to do that. I really liked it. You can see a lot more from up there.” The tradeoff, of course, is giving up the personal interactions and feeling the game from the sideline. “It takes away a little bit of the on the field element of being able to communicate and talk all the time, but there’s a calm in the box,” Nagy said. “And for me, first time in this role as a play caller, OC being up in that box, I just feel like I can see things a lot better and then have the ultimate trust in the staff and being able to see things so that they can communicate to me what they’re seeing. And we’ve got the telephone, too, so I can always jump on the phone with (quarterback) Jaxson (Dart) if I need to. But I’m excited about that opportunity.” Here are more takeaways from Nagy’s Thursday media availability. On the Giants’ offensive scheme … “What I would say to that is, we talk about, Coach Harbs (Head Coach John Harbaugh) talks about principles and methods and what that means and you can relay that to an offense is, I learned this game through Andy Reid, (former NFL coach) Marty Morningweg when I was in Philadelphia. And I learned that foundation of this offense and that offense for me. Took it to Kansas City, took it to Chicago, and now here I am. And again, this opportunity that I have is a first for me. So, being here to be able to take some of the things that we do as a staff and make it ours, that’s been some of the times for me selfishly, it’s been fun just putting this thing together. So, I’m excited to see how this thing goes this year, because I think you’re going to see it’s our offense. It’s no other offense from prior history. You know, it’s ours.” On what he wants to see from Jaxson Dart … “We want Jaxson to be able to play fast. We want him to be himself. He’s a special talent. And it’s our job as coaches to take all this time that we’ve had to do it. And that’s what we’ve put together is a game plan that we think is to his strengths. But at the same point in time too, we got to make sure that there’s going to be times in the game where we just got to let him cut it loose and continue to build every week. This isn’t, there’s going to be good plays, there’s going to be bad plays, but how does he keep that up? It’s going to be an emotional time. Sunday night football against the Cowboys, a lot of emotions going on. He’s a competitor. So, I want him to stay calm, extremely confident, play fast and execute and just be a complete leader, but also just be himself, man. Cut it loose and have fun.” On where Dart has grown … “Probably just the confidence and understanding of the concepts that we’re doing, both run and pass. There was probably some frustration early on because sometimes you don’t know, it’s the first time you’re running a play, you don’t really know the play. And now when we’re out here, he knows the play, he has multiple reps. And so, we can build off of that. We can teach off of that. Now we’ve got to transfer it to the game and some unscouted looks. And so, I think for him, again, his growth, and he’s so mature for being 23 years old and having limited experience in the NFL, super mature, very calm, but he’s really good. So, we got to make sure we use his strengths.” On Odell Beckham’s acceptance of his role … “He hasn’t brought that up at all as far as that part of it, which is probably hard. Odell has come to me at times and we’ve had some good conversations where he’ll almost come to me like I’m the conduit between him and Jaxson because he wants to be careful and gentle with how much he gets in Jaxson’s ear, with how he, he’s played a lot of football. He’s seen a lot of things. And so, what I can do is I can balance some of the questions he has and filter it to Jaxson. And then the other times he goes to Jaxson. But what I find really professional about Odell is that he doesn’t want to put too much on Jaxson’s plate mentally. And I think he’s in a good spot too. You guys see what he can do. He can do a lot of good things, but we also have a lot in this offense and there’s details. So, every now and then, if he screws up an assignment, the biggest thing we say is don’t do it again. And he’s done a good job with that.”
author: Ed Valentine

title: NY Giants’ rookie placekicker, long-snapper have earned the team’s trust
summary: When John Harbaugh was hired as New York Giants’ head coach, it figured that a makeover of the kicking game would follow. Harbaugh, after all, is a former special teams coach who has always emphasized that part of the game. The Giants’ kicking game in recent seasons has been lackluster. The Giants made Jordan Stout […]
full_text: Jordan Stout (15) and Dominic Zvada (34) watch a field goal sail through the uprights. | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect When John Harbaugh was hired as New York Giants’ head coach, it figured that a makeover of the kicking game would follow. Harbaugh, after all, is a former special teams coach who has always emphasized that part of the game. The Giants’ kicking game in recent seasons has been lackluster. The Giants made Jordan Stout the game’s highest-paid punter, bringing one of the best in the league at that job from the Baltimore Ravens, Harbaugh’s former employer. No surprise there. The other two kicking-game specialist roles belong to undrafted, with Dominic Zvada as the placekicker and Ben Mann as the long-snapper. That could be considered a surprise. Zvada won a competition with veteran Jason Sanders, who was released during the spring, and Ben Sauls, who was went 8 of 8 as the Giants’ placekicker at the end of last season. After Casey Kreiter left for the Arizona Cardinals in free agency, the Giants signed Mann and journeyman Zach Triner. They quickly released Triner in the spring, and never brought in other competition for Mann. Zvada appreciates Harbaugh’s trust. “There’s a certain level of trust that he [Harbaugh] has,” Zvada said recently in the Giants’ locker room. “Obviously, bringing in two rookies, that’s how you have to go at it. But it also shows, at least from what I see, his knowledge of specialists. “Ben’s done a great job. I think I’ve done a really good job. Obviously, Jordan’s been doing a really good job for the last few years. So, he seems confident in who he wants to bring in. I think we’re a great group, and we’re going to do really good this year.” Zvada and Mann will be roommates this season. Mann said he finds it “amazing” that he gets to partner with Zvada. “I’ve definitely thought about it, and I’m just so grateful for the opportunity because I definitely do think about it,” Mann said. “I think it’s amazing. There’s only so many rookies that start every year at these two positions, and for us to be here together is obviously a great thing. For the coaches to be putting that much trust in the players we are now and the players we’ll develop into really means a ton.” Zvada added that it is “kind of nice going through it with somebody who’s in the same situation. I talked to some other guys around the league that were in my class. And they don’t have this sort of thing. So, it’s very nice to have this.” Stout, a 2025 All-Pro who is in his fifth NFL season, revealed that Harbaugh and special teams coach Chris Horton, who had that role for 12 years in Baltimore, sought his input when sifting through placekicking and snapping specialists. “Chris and Harbaugh were both extremely diligent with finding the right person,” Stout said. “They were talking to me through the whole process, asking me to look at specific guys and who do you like, who do you not like? “Chris and Harbs have been with the best in the world. They’ve been with [placekicker] Justin Tucker, they’ve been with [long-snapper] Nick Moore, who’s an incredible long snapper. They had [punter] Sam Koch in Baltimore for 16 years. I mean, they know what greatness looks like. These guys, they were the best out there and they are really, really talented and it’s gonna be a lot of fun to play with them.” Zvada ‘thankful’ for opportunity Coming off a season at Michigan that was not the best of his four-year college career, Zvada just wanted a chance. “Really, all I wanted was an opportunity and Coach Harbaugh gave me that opportunity,” Zvada said. “I was able to show up and do what I wanted to do, or do what I needed to do. Be able to prove myself and Coach Harbaugh gave me that opportunity. So, I was really thankful for that. It’s worked out so far and I’m going to keep going with it.“ Zvada, 22, had two exceptional collegiate seasons, and two so-so seasons. He said his focus is “just getting better at being consistent.” “I mean, for me, it’s all focused on this season,” Zvada said. “I think. I’ve done a good job so far and I think at the beginning of every year I want to lay out a plan of how I want to attack each part of the year. And so far, where I’m at, I’m very happy with how things have gone so far. “It’s all about staying consistent. It’s all about going into the season with the momentum, having a good preseason, having a good camp, those sort of things. And those things start with having good momentum during the summer. So, it all kind of ties together.” Horton said Zvada achieved the consistency he was looking for. “Dom just showed consistency from the day he walked in,” Horton said. “There’s just been a lot of consistency, and going out there, and kicks being made, right? We started with the process. Again, we broke down everything, how he kicked, how he wanted the ball. We talked to (punter) Jordan (Stout) a lot about, like, let’s fine-tune these things to help him, to give him the best chance. Really, to give both guys the best opportunity, but since he’s walked in this building, he’s been very consistent.” The swirling winds of the Meadowlands have given many placekickers fits. Zvada is confident he can figure them out. “I played in the Big Ten. I don’t know how it is here, but I’ve played in elements before,” Zvada said. “Certainly, the practice field here in the Meadowlands is windy. “For me, you know, it’s the same sort of thing with the yardages. I would go out there and I’d pretend the wind’s not even there. Unless it’s a side wind, then you’ve got to play it. But, I’m going to hit it the same way.” Zvada made a handful of kicks beyon 60 yards during training camp. So, what is his range? “I’ll say deep,” Zvada said. “That’s all I’ll say.” Mann: ‘A complete dream come true’ No matter who else called, Mann was not saying no when an offer came from the Giants. “Playing for the Giants is a complete dream come true,” Mann said. “Growing up in the Northeast, starting in Pennsylvania, going to school in Connecticut and then Boston .. it’s a team I kind of grew up rooting for. “My grandfather [Chuck Mercein] was drafted here a long, long time ago. And if you told me I’d have an offer from all 32 teams, I think the Giants are the team I would choose. With everything that’s going on here, the opportunities, on and off the field, the new coaching staff, everything, there’s so many factors that would draw me to this team.” Mann did not intend to make long-snapping a career. He was a tight end and defensive end in high school, as well a lacrosse and basketball player. He went to Yale to play tight end, with snapping as a secondary skill. Mann and his coaches quickly realized he was a better snapper than tight end, and soon enough that was all he was doing. “It was funny, it was definitely a transition for me. Because when I first got to Yale, I committed, at least in my mind, as a tight end that kind of did long snapping on the side,” Mann said. “And I quickly found out I was better than I realized at long snapping. “And once I was a starting long snapper, they took away my role as a tight end. And I wasn’t really practicing as much. I was standing on the sidelines doing my snaps, not playing scout offense. And it drove me wild for a while, because I went from a three-sport athlete, came in what I thought was a tight end, and then I kind of got, I fell into my role as a long snapper. And I was just out there restless.” While it took time to accept and adjust to his new reality, Mann has ended up “grateful” for the decision. “I definitely went back and forth with my coach about it, but I always knew they were doing what was best for me and what was best for the team,” Mann said. “And it drove me nuts, but they were right. “So, I always thank them and I’m grateful for them.” Mann finished his collegiate career at Boston College in 2025, and then landed with the Giants. When the Giants released Triner, Mann didn’t take for granted that the job was his. “It was…

title: NY Giants news: Malik Nabers’ status, C.J. Okoye, Jaxson Dart, more
summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know on a day we remember those that we lost 25 years ago today. Big things expected from John Harbaugh’s Giants | ESPN.com This is Harbaugh’s program. He’s hoping building a bigger, more physical team pays immediate dividends because the schedule doesn’t […]
full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know on a day we remember those that we lost 25 years ago today. Big things expected from John Harbaugh’s Giants | ESPN.com This is Harbaugh’s program. He’s hoping building a bigger, more physical team pays immediate dividends because the schedule doesn’t let Harbaugh’s Giants ease into the flow. The Giants face an unusually big game in Week 1 considering they get the Super Bowl favorite Los Angeles Rams on the road next Monday night. It makes their matchup in Week 1 with a division rival that has owned them for years that much more critical. But nobody seems to be giving Harbaugh the sort of grace period new head coaches generally receive. Instead, the rhetoric is to turn it around immediately, even though the Giants won seven games combined the past two seasons. “I get it from the standpoint of expectations, but of course we expect to win,” Harbaugh said. “How do you go out there and compete at this level if you don’t expect to win? If you don’t expect to win, you certainly aren’t going to. I’ve said this before, we expect and we plan to and we’ll be playing to win every single one of our games this year. That’s our expectation, that’s our plan, that’s what we’ll be striving for. We think we can [win], we believe we can [win], wholeheartedly.” Giants-Dallas is a hot ticket Think Giants fans are excited for their first game with John Harbaugh as head coach? The current get-in price for Sunday night vs. the Cowboys at @TickPick is $242 and the average purchase price is $369, the highest ever at MetLife in TickPick’s history (since 2011). #Partner pic.twitter.com/MDYnJMhtyI — Field Yates (@FieldYates) September 10, 2026 2026 NFL offensive line rankings: Broncos, Eagles and Buccaneers open in top three | PFF 23. New York Giants. Andrew Thomas was arguably the Giants’ best player last year, as his 90.3 PFF grade tied for a career high. His issue has been staying healthy, having missed significant time both in 2023 and 2024. New York drafted Francis Mauigoa in the first round, and if he can hit the ground running, then the unit looks a lot stronger. But, it’s a group that just might be another season away from making a bigger impact. How Giants are molding Jaxson Dart into savior they need him to be | The Athletic Harbaugh oversaw one of the best Year 2 leaps in NFL history while in Baltimore. After making seven starts as a raw rookie in 2018, Lamar Jackson blossomed into an MVP while leading the Ravens to an NFL-best 14-2 record in his second season. No one is banking on that type of breakout season for Dart. But there is at least a blueprint for the coaching staff to follow as Dart transitions into his second season. “I think the approach has been similar from the basic idea that we’re trying to build an offense for Jaxson Dart that is amenable to his skill set,” Harbaugh said. “We did the same thing with Lamar. But they’re different people, different quarterbacks — all those kinds of things are different.” Unexpected Match: John Harbaugh & Jaxson Dart’s Obsession Could Be Enough To Fix Giants | FOX Sports On paper, it’s a mismatch. The 63-year-old coach with a somewhat stoic, all-football demeanor and the flashy 23-year-old who seems to love everything that comes with being a celebrity in New York. Dart is a showman, whether it’s on Instagram, at parties or on celebrity row. Harbaugh, on the other hand, seems more at home in a film room with the lights down low. But what Harbaugh quickly learned was that Dart’s appearance was deceiving. The old coach spent hours talking with the young quarterback before he took the Giants job. That’s where he first learned of Dart’s “obsession” with the details, with becoming a better quarterback, and with the hard work he knew he had to put in to get there. And just in case he wasn’t convinced, he took calls from former Giants coach Brian Daboll, Eli Manning, and several others raving about Dart’s football acumen and work ethic, too. Jaxson Dart’s 10-word text to Giants linemen reveals QB’s bold intentions before facing Cowboys | New York Post The text was sent Tuesday night. Late. “It was kind of just random, out of nowhere,’’ left guard Jon Runyan Jr. told The Post. Jaxson Dart has several different text chains within the Giants locker room, and this particular one was with the five starting offensive linemen. The message was transmitted into the phones of Runyan, Andrew Thomas, John Michael Schmitz Jr., Francis Mauigoa and Jermaine Eluemunor. Giants’ Darius Slayton replacement ready for big shot vs. Cowboys: ‘Pressure is a privilege’ | NJ.com John Harbaugh, the Giants’ new coach and football czar, sent Darius Slayton packing because he believes he has better options to play opposite Malik Nabers. And those two outside receiver options — who both now face significant pressure — are seventh-year pro Darnell Mooney and intriguing third-round rookie Malachi Fields, a big-bodied red-zone weapon. So what does Fields think about being thrust into a significant role immediately, starting with Sunday night’s enormous season opener at home against Dallas? title: NY Giants’ C.J. Okoye says landing in New York ‘a really good outcome’
summary: EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J — NFL players don’t usually admit to reading the tea leaves and trying to figure out whether or not they fit on a roster as cutdowns to 53 players approach. New York Giants defensive tackle C.J. Okoye, though, is an unusual NFL player. During an exclusive interview with Big Blue View on […]
full_text: C.J. Okoye with the Ravens during the preseason. | Getty Images EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J — NFL players don’t usually admit to reading the tea leaves and trying to figure out whether or not they fit on a roster as cutdowns to 53 players approach. New York Giants defensive tackle C.J. Okoye , though, is an unusual NFL player. During an exclusive interview with Big Blue View on Wednesday, Okoye admitted he had been looking at the Baltimore Ravens depth chart this summer and trying to figure out if the Ravens — a team he played 13 games for last season — had a spot for him. “My [defensive line] room back in Baltimore was a deep room, but I had a great camp coming out,” Okoye said. “I was like, if they’re gonna cut me, I know I’m gonna have to go somewhere else.” Being traded to the Giants right before roster cuts was a best-case scenario for the Nigerian-born 6-foot-6, 365-pound 24-year-old. “That morning, it was like a shock to me, but it wasn’t a shock,” Okoye said. “I was kind of happy, like it was a trade, you know what I mean? So, it was, it was a good, it was a good outcome. “It was a really good outcome.” Giants head coach John Harbaugh and defensive line coach Dennis Johnson were familiar with Okoye from last season in Baltimore. In need of defensive line depth, they turned to the Ravens to find it. After the trade, Harbaugh said this about Okoye : He’s a guy that we got to know recently last year, came in, was with the Chargers actually with my brother [Jim] for a couple years in the international program,” Harbaugh said. “So a guy who had been a developmental-type guy, learning the game and tremendous physical skills, hard worker, has really dedicated himself over the last few years to learning the game really because he didn’t play it growing up and made great strides, made great strides with Dennis Johnson, our defensive line coach last year. That’s where he kind of broke through and had a really good season. “We see him as an inside defender, a defensive tackle, A gap, B gap player, run stopper, pocket pusher in terms of the past game and just a really big physical player,” Harbaugh said. “So kind of a type of guy we’ve been looking for and we’re really excited to get him up here.” Okoye is thrilled to be back under Johnson’s tutelage. “Coach Dennis, he’s my guy; he’s the one that, like, he’s one of the people that brought, like, that brought CJ out, you know what I mean?,” Okoye said. “So, yeah, so, I was really happy that I’m coming to a system I knew already.” No matter where it is on the defensive line that the Giants ask him to play, Okoye just wants to play. “Right now, I don’t know [how he will be used] and I don’t care,” Okoye said. “Just line me up, mano a mano. Just line me up. So far as I know the play, if you want me to play anything, anything the team wants, I’m here.” Okoye’s journey Okoye’s journey to the NFL began when he attended an International Pathway Program camp in Africa run by former Giants great Osi Umenyiora. Until then, Okoye had been a basketball player. “I learned about football through a movie,” Okoye said. The movie? ‘The Game Plan’ starring Dwayne ‘The Rock’ Johnson. “That’s when I learned about football,” Okoye said. “I was playing basketball before then, the whole thing, then the camp came, and I didn’t even know, I thought it was like a, that [it] was one of those charity events or something like that, but I went through, made the camp, saw it was real, the rest is history, but I had never played football. My first snap of football was in the league.” Okoye was impressive enough that he ended up being allocated to the Los Angeles Chargers for the 2023 season. He spent two seasons learning the game on the Chargers’ practice squad. Okoye recorded a sack in his first-ever NFL game, a 2023 preseason contest against the Los Angeles Rams. It is a story he has recounted many times, but Okoye did not know what he had done. “I thought it was a tackle for loss. I didn’t even know it was a sack because I didn’t know, like I was playing the game,” Okoye said. “I didn’t even know what I was doing.” If you have ever watched little kids play basketball and get thoroughly confused when the teams switch ends of the court after halftime, you will empathize with the other “welcome to the NFL” story Okoye told about that game. “After the first quarter, they were switching,” Okoye said. “I’m like, why are you guys switching? I didn’t even know why they were switching. I’m like, okay, we’re switching now. They said, yeah, we switch every quarter. I’m like, okay.” Okoye learned something else important that day. He learned he could play football at the highest level despite his inexperience. “I knew I can play this game because as someone that had never played, if I can still whoop ass like that, imagine when I have like five, seven years of this,” Okoye said. Okoye switched quickly from offensive to defensive line after joining the Chargers. “I like it better,” Okoye said. “I’d rather be the aggressor than sit and absorb. “I’d rather just go and knock somebody back than try to absorb somebody knocking me back, you know what I mean?” ‘I’m never going to be satisfied’ Okoye played 214 defensive snaps and 41 special teams snaps for the Ravens last year, the first regular-season action of his career. Entering his fourth season, where does Okoye think he is in terms of his development and understanding? “I’ll say I’m still behind,” Okoye said. “I look at myself like that because I’m playing catch-up. I’m never going to be satisfied, you know what I’m saying? Because I always feel like the person I’m going against went to college, and he’s more prepared than me. “So it makes me want to work more. It makes me want to go out there and prove myself, you know what I’m saying? So just because of him going to college, I feel like he, he thinks he got the edge over me.” Okoye praised veteran defensive tackles D.J. Reader and Shelby Harris for sharing their knowledge. He said Reader and Harris are “no doubt” more forthcoming with information than his veteran Ravens teammates were. “They’re both amazing guys,” Okoye said. “I feel like I’m going to learn here more. I’m going to add to my play here more than Baltimore because they’re ready to like give you everything, like as much as you can, as much as you can like learn, they are willing to teach.” The Giants, of course, are hoping that Okoye’s ascension continues and that he becomes a true force on their defensive line.

title: NY Giants-Cowboys matchup: New York to unveil new-look, physical offense
summary: The New York Giants are looking to start the John Harbaugh era off with a bang, and come away from their season-opening Sunday Night Football game with a win over the Dallas Cowboys. The matchup between the Giants’ offense and Cowboys’ defense is one of the most intriguing of the weekend. The Giants’ offense will […]
full_text: Malik Nabers catches a touchdown against the Dallas Cowboys. | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New York Giants are looking to start the John Harbaugh era off with a bang, and come away from their season-opening Sunday Night Football game with a win over the Dallas Cowboys. The matchup between the Giants’ offense and Cowboys’ defense is one of the most intriguing of the weekend. The Giants’ offense will look significantly different from a year ago, with Jaxson Dart at quarterback, Darnell Mooney , Odell Beckham Jr. , and Malachi Fields at receiver, Isaiah Likely at tight end, Patrick Ricard at fullback, and a new coaching staff. The Cowboys, meanwhile have a reshuffled roster of their own and a completely new scheme under Christian Parker. As things stand now, we simply don’t quite know what either unit will look like or how they’ll play. So what can we expect when Jaxson Dart and the Giants’ offense takes the field against the Cowboys’ defense? Let’s start with what we do know and then make some educated guesses. What will the Giants’ offense look like? This has been, perhaps, the most beguiling question hanging over the Giants’ offseason — at least for me. The Giants having four former offensive coordinators on their staff (OC Matt Nagy, QB coach/passing game coordinator Brian Callahan, senior assistant Greg Roman, and tight ends coach Tim Kelly) may not be unprecedented, but it is unorthodox. We won’t really know how it will work until the game is well under way. However my personal speculation has been that Nagy will serve as the master distiller who blends various aspects of Roman, Callahan, and Kelly’s philosophies into a single product. It could blow up in the Giants’ faces, or the various twists on existing schemes could present defenses with unexpected looks or combinations of concepts. That said, we might be able to use context clues to define the negative space and get a rough outline of what the Giants want to do on offense. Power running game – This one became blatantly obvious when the Giants hired John Harbaugh and painfully obvious when they hired Greg Roman as “Senior Offensive Assistant”. Harbaugh has always favored a run-heavy offense, while Roman loves a down-hill rushing attack and is among the best in the NFL at scheming one up. The Giants will likely attempt to displace the defense vertically and force them to crowd the box. We’ll also likely see Jaxson Dart used as a runner more than those fearing the Blue Tent would likely prefer. After all, John Harbaugh was once called the “Prince Of Analytics” by ESPN, and forcing defenses to play true 11-on-11 football is typically confers an analytic advantage for the offense. Heavy sets – Again, this one is pretty obvious based on John Harbaugh’s past preferences. It was only reinfoced when the Giants released Darius Slayton and left themselves with just four receivers. That doesn’t mean the Giants will forego the passing attack, but rather they’ll be getting their tight ends and backs heavily involved as pass catchers. Isaiah Likely was Jaxson Dart’s most common target in training camp, while Theo Johnson flashed brilliance (in addition to frustrating drops) in his second season. Likewise, each of the Giants’ four running backs are dangerous pass catchers. Former receiver Tyrone Tracy is the obvious standout, however Cam Skattebo, Najee Harris, and Devin Singletary all have upside as pass catchers. Precision passing game – Teams often like contrast between their running and passing game. So if the Giants want a downhill rushing attack, we could see that paired with a passing attack that uses precise route running to set receivers up for yards after the catch. This is where Brian Callahan’s influence (may) come in. Where Matt Nagy is a traditional West Coast Offense guy, having learned under Andy Reid, Callahan comes from the “New West Coast” tree. In other words, we could see influences from the “Kubiak-Shanahan-McVay” school of offense. In that vein, it’s notable that the Giants’ four remaining receivers are all talented route runners. Even 6-foot-4, 220-pound rookie Malachi Fields is far more nimble than his frame would suggest. The release of Slayton may also suggest that Malik Nabers is trending toward being ready to play Week 1. There will certainly be a vertical aspect to the offense, Lamar Jackson was tied for the fourth-highest intended air yardage in the NFL last year (9.1 yards downfield), while Matt Stafford was third with 9.2 intended air yards. So while much of the passing attack may be to set Malik Nabers and Darnell Mooney up with YAC opportunities, we should also expect to see the Giants attempt to generate chunk plays. Condensed sets – Modern NFL offenses like to weaponize every aspect of play design, including formation width. While spread formations can be conducive to running the ball (by forcing defenses to spread out an lighten the box), condensed sets are coming into vogue. The Giants featuring tight ends and a fullback suggests that they’ll go with that trend, though perhaps not for the reason fans expect. Condensed sets certainly make it easier to insert receivers or detached tight ends into gaps as blockers for inside runs. But they also allow offenses to create traffic for their passing concepts. That, in turn, makes play-action passes to the intermediate area even more effective and can force teams to pay for playing a base defense. The Fangio factor In addition to not knowing quite what to expect from the Giants’ offensive scheme to start the season, we also don’t know quite what to expect from the Dallas defense either. The Cowboys fired their previous defensive coordinator after fielding a historically bad defense for much of the 2025 season, and hired former Philadelphia Eagles Passing Game Coordinator and defensive backs coach Christian Parker. Parker spent 2024 and 2025 with the Cowboys after spending 2022 and 2023 as the Denver Broncos’ defensive backs coach. Parker is considered one of the bright young minds on the defensive side of the ball and is a disciple of Eagles’ DC Vic Fangio. In other words, we should expect the new-look Cowboys’ defense to be similar in structure to what the Eagles run. The Fangio scheme is based on quarters coverages, man-match coverage rules, nickel sets, and post-snap rotations. Coverage rotations are a signature aspect of Fangio’s scheme, usually starting out in quarters coverages and rotating to a Cover 3 look, or to Cover 6 and Cover 8 looks. Cover 6 and Cover 8 are hybrid coverages that mix Cover 2 and Cover 4 principles. The primary difference is that Cover 6 plays the “quarters” side to the passing strength, while Cover 8 plays the “quarters” away from the passing strength. The purpose of the rotations is to disguise rotations, help simulate pressure, and allow nickel sets to play heavier than they appear on paper. Speaking of nickel sets, while the “Fangio” defense is based in the 3-4, his primary alignments are 4-2-5 Nickel and 3-3-5 Penny sets. In either case, STAR Caleb Downs will be a key piece for the Dallas defense as the third DB. He’ll be playing a similar role as Cooper DeJean does in Philly, and be Dallas’ primary “Pivot” player who changes the look between Quarters, Cover 6, and Cover 8, as well as changing how Dallas defends gaps up front. The Giants will likely want to go back and study last year’s Week 8 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles in preparation for this game. The Giants trounced the Eagles just two weeks prior, however that game featured Fangio abandoning his usual tendencies to attack the rookie QB with blitzes. Jaxson Dart comported himself well in that game, but struggled once Fangio returned to his usual defense in Week 8. Dart will need to prove that he can decipher the Ultimately, there are two big questions with respect to the Cowboys’ defense: First, whether they have the personnel to properly run a Fangio-adjacent defense. It’s one of the most popular schemes in the NFL for a…

title: Three things I’m looking at in the Jets vs Titans Game
summary: It’s an honor to be featured on Gang Green Nation, and I can’t wait to talk Jets football with you all season! In a world full of emotional recollections and irrational takes, I aim to be the purveyor of truth for this passionate fan base. While I wholeheartedly root for the team day in and […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TN - SEPTEMBER 29: Geno Smith #7 of the New York Jets is hit while throwing a pass by Jurrell Casey #99 of the Tennessee Titans at LP Field on September 29, 2013 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Wesley Hitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s an honor to be featured on Gang Green Nation, and I can’t wait to talk Jets football with you all season! In a world full of emotional recollections and irrational takes, I aim to be the purveyor of truth for this passionate fan base. While I wholeheartedly root for the team day in and day out and yearn for the day they can reward me as my Knicks have, my pieces are grounded in logic, reason, and provable data. I’m going to use those three principles to assess the three things I discuss in this article about the Jets/Titans game. Of course, there are plenty of obvious storylines here (revenge game, anyone!?), but two things I will guarantee in my weekly previews are that I will never just echo the mainstream narrative, and you will always learn at least one new stat you’ve never seen before. The mainstream narrative here is revenge, and that’s fair. This is more than Robert Saleh looking to spite the owner who fired him mid-season; it is more than Aaron Glenn trying to prove Woody was right to choose him instead of sticking with Saleh. A whopping 20.7% of the total players rostered in this game are preparing to face either their old team or old coach this Sunday. The revenge angle will be heavily prevalent throughout the game, but let’s look at things that are more easily measured than vengeance: Geno Smith Under Pressure A lot of the eyes on Geno will be looking to answer the question, “Is this Seahawks Geno or Raiders Geno?” I regret to inform you that they’re the same person. He can put up yards with high usage, and he throws picks with his fearless nature – these things have rung true all four years as a starter in his 30s. Another constant from that entire four-year span is how badly he folds under pressure. Last year in particular, he had the single worst drop in PFF grade when pressured vs clean pocket in the entire NFL. His 79.9 grade dropped all the way down to 28.8 for the 212 dropbacks in which he was pressured. There were several QBs who had their grades drop 40+ when pressured, but Geno was the lone QB in the NFL to drop 50+. Six of his league-leading 17 interceptions came from plays where he was under pressure. The Jets offensive line is coming off a year where they were the only team in the NFL to have exactly one combination of linemen start for all 17 games. They replaced John Simpson with Dylan Parham, extended Joe Tippmann, and seem poised to take another step together as one of football’s younger ascending units. Will this line, Frank Reich’s game-planning, and Geno’s pre-play diagnoses abolish all instances of pressure? Statistics (and common sense) say probably not, as Saleh has consistently been one of the best minds in the sport at this exact skill. In 2023, Saleh’s Jets led the league in Sack %, and they were 2 nd in the league five weeks into 2024 before he was shown the door (they fell outside of the top 5 under Jeff Ulbrich’s watch). Armed with equally motivated ex-Jets Jermaine Johnson II, John Franklin-Myers, and the established Titans All-Pro DT Jeffery Simmons, I’d imagine he’s looking to continue his efficiency in this stat. Perhaps the greatest aspect of Saleh’s defensive scheme is the ability to create pressure without blitzing. They rush with four, have seven in coverage, and make it that much more difficult for opposing QBs to make good decisions. Geno has been struggling so much with pressure vs. teams that actually blitz, meaning there are five or six players in coverage and he’s making the wrong decision. How much will that be amplified if he’s under pressure and there are seven players in coverage? I’m extremely curious to see how much pressure Saleh’s Titans can generate, and even more curious to see how Geno and the Jets respond. Will there be more calamity? Has Frank schemed up some outlet/checkdown options? Can Geno play with poise and make smart decisions? I have my popcorn ready! All Stuffed Up? I don’t especially enjoy Kool-Aid, so I don’t often drink it, but I might be in on the Kool-Aid for T’Vondre Sweat. There just aren’t too many guys his size that move that quickly, and I love the sneak peek we got vs. the Giants in preseason a couple of weeks ago. One of the clearest issues for the Jets last year was the run defense – the Jets allowed the 4th most rushing yards per game on the 10th most yards per carry, and after Quinnen Williams was traded, there was no answer for the opposing running backs. This season, Darren Mougey signed David Onyemata, secured a trade for T’Vondre Sweat, and brought in a desperately needed veteran presence in the linebacker room in Demario Davis. I cannot overstate how impressive it is that 15-year veteran Demario Davis is coming off a season in which he had his career-high in tackles (143). He also had a career-high 16 run stuffs and 6 tackles for loss. The combination of his physical skill set with his football intellect will be perfect for Jamien Sherwood, who was still a tackling machine last year (154) but looked lost at times. With Cam Ward a sophomore QB learning a new system and young, developing weapons, we can say with absolute certainty that Titans OC Brian Daboll will look to run the football. Between Tony Pollard, Tyjae Spears, and Nicholas Singleton, they feel good about their options in the room. Pollard is coming off a 1,082-yard campaign with five touchdowns and 4.5 yards per carry, which are all better than Breece Hall’s 2025 numbers. There’s a lot of attention on a “Cam vs Geno” discussion, but I truly believe that in these first two points, we have established the actual two keys of the game. The Jets will need Geno to survive the inevitable pressure when it comes, and the Titans will need to somehow get Tony Pollard and Tyjae Spears consistently running past their former teammate T’Vondre Sweat. The Dark Cloud If you’re a Jets fan, you know about the dubious interception stat that is clouding the Aaron Glenn Jets era. The three-time Pro Bowl cornerback-turned-defensive coordinator-turned-head coach spearheaded the first team in NFL history to record zero interceptions in a full season. Fun fact: seasons used to be 16 games long; they were previously 14 games long, and teams still managed to grab an interception during the season. 17 games, and Aaron Glenn’s team was completely empty-handed. Until they get one, this dark cloud will loom over them. Glenn could fire all the coaches he wants, make all the excuses he needs to feel better, but nothing can erase this embarrassing 2025 record, and until they get one in 2026, the monkey will still be on their back. The good news is that this regime knows this! They signed Nahshon Wright, who tied for second last year in most interceptions (5), Dane Belton, who had a pick last year (and is a tackling machine), drafted star cornerback D’Angelo Ponds, and traded for All-Pro Safety Minkah Fitzpatrick. It should be inarguable that the personnel in the secondary is much more equipped to catch interceptions than last year’s bunch. It should also be noted that the earlier point about Geno Smith throwing picks in duress works for lots of other teams as well. If the Jets can generate pressure much more efficiently than they did last year, then perhaps a young QB (say, like Cam Ward) would panic under pressure and throw it directly to the Jets’ secondary. They made a huge upgrade there by drafting David Bailey second overall and signing Joseph Ossai and Kingsley Enagbare. Ossai’s not healthy, so we can omit him for this Sunday preview, but let’s see what the second overall pick can do in his NFL debut. With Will McDonald IV on the other side, there should be opportunity to get after the quarterback and force mistakes, but I admittedly said the same thing last year with…

summary: Breece Hall is ready for takeoff. We all held our collective breath when Hall went down with a non-contact injury back in August. Now we can breathe a sigh of relief. The talented tailback has been a full participant for the last two days of practice. “I feel great,” Hall told the media on Thursday, September 10. […]
full_text: Sep 15, 2024; Nashville, Tennessee, USA; New York Jets running back Breece Hall (20) scores over Tennessee Titans linebacker Kenneth Murray Jr. (56) during the second half at Nissan Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Steve Roberts-Imagn Images | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con Breece Hall is ready for takeoff. We all held our collective breath when Hall went down with a non-contact injury back in August. Now we can breathe a sigh of relief. The talented tailback has been a full participant for the last two days of practice. “I feel great,” Hall told the media on Thursday, September 10. “It was actually a very good, like two-week vacation. Yeah, so I could have been out there a little earlier, but the team thankfully was very cautious with me, and it was a really good vacation. I feel really fresh now.” The Jets will be running the football a ton in 2026. Hall is a straw that stirs the drink. He got paid like one of the top running backs in football. Now it’s time for him to play like one. Coming off this injury, the Jets will likely be cautious with Hall’s usage, as they should be. If I were running the operation, 99% of his touches would come in the screen game. We witnessed it when Robert Saleh was here with the Jets. The Kryptonite of Saleh’s aggressive attack-style defense is their over-pursuit, which makes them vulnerable to the screen game. After the Jets got killed by it for years, it’s only right to return serve and kill Saleh and the Titans with that same strategy. I’d be remiss if I didn’t mention that today is the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. title: Iron Men: Hidden strength in a violent world
summary: The New York Jets face a second half schedule in 2026 that, at least on paper, looks formidable. The last nine games of the season the Jets face the Kansas City Chiefs, the Buffalo Bills (twice), the Los Angeles Chargers, the Miami Dolphins, the Denver Broncos, the Arizona Cardinals, the New England Patriots, and the […]
full_text: FLORHAM PARK, NEW JERSEY - JULY 29: Will McDonald IV #9 of the New York Jets, Demario Davis #56 of the New York Jets and Jowon Briggs #91 of the New York Jets during training camp at Atlantic Health Jets Training Center on July 29, 2026 in Florham Park, New Jersey. (Photo by Adam Hunger/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New York Jets face a second half schedule in 2026 that, at least on paper, looks formidable. The last nine games of the season the Jets face the Kansas City Chiefs, the Buffalo Bills (twice), the Los Angeles Chargers, the Miami Dolphins, the Denver Broncos, the Arizona Cardinals, the New England Patriots, and the Minnesota Vikings. On paper, that looks like four games against legitimate Super Bowl contenders (the Bills twice, the Patriots and the Broncos) and another three teams that could contend for playoff spots (the Chargers, Chiefs and Vikings). Even the two games against what look like bad teams (Dolphins and Cardinals) are both on the road. That looks like a tough way to end a season, with the caveat that every season brings plenty of surprises, so we don’t really know for sure how easy or difficult any schedule will be before the season begins. The NFL is a violent world. As the saying goes, over the course of a season the injury rate in the NFL is 100%. That is exaggerating things a bit, but injuries are the rule, not the exception. Often the battle for playoff spots down the stretch comes down to a war of attrition, favoring the teams that are the healthiest. A team that looks like a shoo-in for a deep postseason run can collapse down the stretch due to injuries. Long time Jets fans are familiar with this phenomenon. In 1986 the Jets were riding high at 10-1, looking like a legitimate Super Bowl contender, when it all came crashing down. Injuries crushed the team that year. Joe Klecko missed five games, Marty Lyons missed four and Mark Gastineau missed six. That’s virtually the Jets entire pass rush, wiped out by injuries. Star linebacker Lance Mehl missed eight games and starting cornerback Russell Carter missed three. On the offense, Freeman McNeil, arguably the most talented Jets running back ever, missed four games and running mate Johnny Hector missed three, while starting right tackle Reggie McElroy missed eight games. The Jets were playing a bunch of backups down the stretch and it showed. After looking like the number one seed through 11 games, the Jets limped into the playoffs, losing their last five games of the regular season. They managed to secure a wild card spot but lost to the Cleveland Browns in the divisional round. If head coach Aaron Glenn is fighting for his job this season, the back stretch looks like it could spell trouble for him. However, Glenn and general manager Darren Mougey have seemingly built in a hidden strength for this team that could, in theory, even the odds a bit. Over the past year the Jets front office has seemingly prioritized acquiring players with the one trait that is often called the best ability: availability. Looking at the Jets 2026 draft, the Jets selected eight players. None of the eight missed more than one game over the last two years. All eight missed a total of just three games combined over the last two years. That’s a remarkable collective record of durability. In addition to the rookies, the Jets also have a large number of veterans who have made themselves available at a high rate in their careers. On offense, Geno Smith missed a total of four games over the last four years. Joe Tippmann: one game in three years. Josh Myers: one game in four years. Olu Fashanu: two games in two years. Armand Membou: zero games. Dylan Parham: four games in four years. That’s a remarkably durable starting offensive line, a very good thing to have for an offense. Breece Hall has missed a total of two games over the last three years and Isaiah Davis has missed one game in two years. Garrett Wilson had a major injury last year, but he had never missed a game in the prior three years combined. Adonai Mitchell missed one game over the last two years. On defense it’s more of the same. Brandon Stephens missed four games in five years. Jamien Sherwood has not missed a game over the last four years. Demario Davis remarkably has never missed more than one game in any season over a 14 year career. Just call him Iron Man. Kingsley Enagbare has never missed a game in his career. Dane Belton has missed zero games over the last three years. Will McDonald has missed just two games over the last two years. David Onyemata missed three games in the last four years. Harrison Phillips missed zero games over the last four years. There is one key exception to this group of players who are almost always available: Minkah Fitzpatrick. He missed 10 games over the last three years. If Fitzpatrick were to go down for any length of time in 2026, the back end of the Jets defense would be in a world of trouble. There is a large element of random chance to injuries in the NFL. The knee that is caught up in traffic and bent at an unnatural angle and the ankle that is rolled up on don’t care if the player they are attached to has a pristine track record. However, to the extent that some players are less prone to serious injuries than others, the Jets appear to have intentionally built a roster of players who are unusually available. If availability is indeed the best ability, the Jets may find themselves in the back half of the schedule in the enviable position of being near full strength, facing squads that are ravaged by injury. Should that happen, we may find a surprisingly competitive Jets team giving seemingly superior rivals all they can handle. We’ll see how this plays out, but maybe, just maybe, the Jets surprise everyone and go on a run to end this season.

title: Eagles News: Saquon Barkley poised for another big season
summary: Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! Saquon Barkley looked pretty good in training camp this summer. The Eagles’ offense was uneven as a whole but they looked their best when they leaned into the running game. It’s not hard for me to envision Barkley having another big […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - DECEMBER 20: Saquon Barkley #26 of the Philadelphia Eagles runs with the ball during an NFL football game against the Washington Commanders at Northwest Stadium on December 20, 2025 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! Saquon Barkley looked pretty good in training camp this summer. The Eagles’ offense was uneven as a whole but they looked their best when they leaned into the running game. It’s not hard for me to envision Barkley having another big season. Obviously not easy to project him to reach his 2024 numbers. And him looking good won’t matter if the blocking doesn’t hold up, as we saw last season. But I tend to think things will come together in the run game more than they did in 2025. Can Saquon Barkley recapture his 2024 dominance? – ESPN Not only is the offensive line in a better place but Barkley is as well. He shot past his career high in carries (345) during the regular season in 2024 and added 91 more rushes in the postseason. That number fell to 280 last season. And while the wild-card playoff exit against the San Francisco 49ers was disappointing for the Eagles, it gave everyone more of a physical and mental break this offseason, including the 29-year-old Barkley. “Huge,” said running backs coach Jemal Singleton, on the benefits of the longer layoff. “He could take the time from the offseason and get his rest but then come back and start working. So I feel like he’s in a really, really good place now. … It’s going to be exciting to kind of see him go.” Singleton can see it most in the conditioning part of it where Barkley, who shares a backfield this season with a pair of capable backs in Tank Bigsby and Will Shipley, has stayed on the field for more plays during long drives while looking “explosive.” Put the fresh legs with a revitalized offensive front in this run scheme, and there is optimism Barkley can ascend to the top of the running back class once again. “Being a better playmaker,” Barkley said on what he wants to improve from last season. “That’s why I was brought here, that’s what I feel I’m one of the best in the league [at] and just bringing that back.” Can Saquon Barkley defy the RB age curve? His favorite back’s best season came at 29 – The Athletic The Eagles made a major scheme change this offseason that will be apparent in the running game. Quarterback Jalen Hurts will more frequently line up under center. The Eagles installed a wide-zone running scheme. Barkley said he’s “always been intrigued with this kind of system” while observing the success of players from afar. He spoke to Peterson about the depth he should align before the snap, ranging from six yards to eight yards. The landmarks in the running game are different. Barkley said he must be more of a one-cut runner. He believes the protection is friendly to a running back. “I feel like I have a chance to be really good in this system,” Barkley said. “I feel like it’s going to open things that I may have not been able to show in my career.” “He can be good in any system, let’s be honest,” running backs coach Jemal Singleton added. “But I think this is one that allows him to do some things that I think is going to be fun. It’ll be fun to watch him work, and he’s one of those guys that dives into everything. He reaches out to former players that have played in the system like this.” Barkley connected with Todd Gurley, who was offensive coordinator Sean Mannion’s teammate in Los Angeles. Gurley’s two best seasons came in this offense, making first-team All-Pro both years. (Gurley is also an example of a running back who did not age as Barkley intends; Gurley’s final season was at age 26.) Singleton, who coached in this system elsewhere, raved about Barkley’s offseason. Barkley has made cuts in practice that left new teammates dumbfounded. For old teammates, it’s a reminder of Barkley’s 2024 greatness. “We kind of take that stuff for granted a little bit,” Singleton said. “It’s like the ‘wow’ factor. It’s Saquon Barkley. Let’s not forget, and he’s done some amazing things, and he still can.” Eagles vs. Commanders Game Preview: 5 questions and answers with the Week 1 enemy – BGN The Philadelphia Eagles are beginning their 2026 season with a home game against the Washington Commanders. Nick Sirianni and Jalen Hurts are aiming to reach 6-0 in Week 1 games together. In order to preview this NFC East matchup , I reached out to our enemies over at Hogs Haven . The affable Andrew Y kindly took the time took the time to answer my questions about this upcoming battle. Let’s take a look at the answers. NFC East Mixtape Vol. 188: Week 1 Preview – NFC East Mixtape We have FINALLY reached Week 1 of the 2026 NFL season and to start things off we have all four NFC East teams taking on another member of the division. Which two will emerge as winners? Which two will hate everything and want to start over? RJ Ochoa and Brandon Gowton discuss in true Mixtape fashion… plus Big Blue View’s Ed Valentine joins for perspective on the G-Men! You can see that we have a BRAND NEW NFC East Mixtape YouTube Channel so make sure to subscribe as the show will live here exclusively in video format. Lots of Questions – Iggles Blitz So the experts have the Eagles missing the playoffs, as a wild card team or making it back to the Super Bowl. That’s quite a range of outcomes. The lack of faith in the Eagles is all about the offense. AJ Brown is out and a new scheme is in. People have doubts about how good Jalen Hurts will be in the new scheme. It is absolutely fair to have concerns about the offense. I’m buying the Eagles as a contender because of Saquon Barkley, better OL play and an elite defense. That is a winning formula. Hurts should have time to grow into the new offense and for his receivers to work into their roles. Why Sean Mannion decided to call plays from the booth this season – NBCSP While Mannion explained that there are pros and cons of both locations, the 34-year-old ultimately decided to head up to the booth as he enters his first season as the Eagles’ offensive coordinator. “When you’re in the box, obviously you have a little bit more space,” Mannion explained on Thursday afternoon. “You’re not pacing around. You have the tablet. It’s a little bit like sitting at a desk, but I think just the vision is a little bit unique there, the higher vantage point. “Honestly, I felt comfortable with both, and really, I just felt like the vision type of thing really led me to the decision. Ultimately, the other part of it is we have a great staff. They communicate really well on the sideline. There’s been constant lines of communication, and I think all of that led to the decision.” This decision is a departure from the way the Eagles have done things for a long time. Franchise quarterback Jalen Hurts noted earlier this week that this will be his first time with a play caller upstairs since his days in college. It can make communication a bit tricky between Hurts and Mannion because it’ll have to be over the red phone on the sideline. Is Sean Mannion ready for his big moment with the Eagles? He’s been preparing for it for years. – Inquirer Mike Riley and Sean Mannion were having one of their catch-up calls when Mannion, who played quarterback at Oregon State under Riley, told his former coach the latest project he was working on during the nascent days of his own coaching career. Mannion, the most prolific passer in Oregon State history, told Riley that he was putting together and digitizing all of the passing concepts he could find dating back to the 1960s. “This is what he does in his spare time,” Riley explained recently. Mannion is just 34 years old and only three years removed from his playing career. He has never called plays in the NFL before and now is tasked with turning around an Eagles offense that was too stagnant in 2025 under another…

title: Eagles-Commanders Film Preview: Philadelphia needs to take advantage of Washington’s offensive line
summary: Hello! I’m back this year with BGN, as always, and I’ll have two review articles and two preview articles every week. If you missed the first preview of the year, make sure you check it out here. The same Week 1 warning applies here. Washington’s new offensive coordinator, David Blough, has never called an NFL […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - DECEMBER 20: Moro Ojomo #97 of the Philadelphia Eagles lines up against the Washington Commanders during the first half of the NFL game at Northwest Stadium on December 20, 2025 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images Hello! I’m back this year with BGN, as always, and I’ll have two review articles and two preview articles every week. If you missed the first preview of the year, make sure you check it out here . The same Week 1 warning applies here. Washington’s new offensive coordinator, David Blough, has never called an NFL offense, so there is no real film that tells us exactly what Vic Fangio will be preparing for. We can make educated guesses based on Blough’s background and what Blough has said publicly, but anyone claiming to know precisely what this offense will look like is guessing. David Blough and Jayden Daniels It’s really hard for me not to spend the whole article comparing Sean Mannion and David Blough, but the similarities are so obvious. Blough only stopped playing quarterback recently and spent the past two seasons as Washington’s assistant quarterbacks coach under Kingsbury. Before that, his playing career put him around a wide range of offensive coaches, including Ben Johnson in Detroit and Kevin O’Connell in Minnesota. Washington has also been open about wanting to move away from some of the philosophical elements of Kingsbury’s offense, particularly by becoming more balanced and using more under-center play action. Sound familiar?! Blough’s challenge is deciding how much to change. Daniels has already spent two seasons getting comfortable in Kingsbury’s system, particularly operating from shotgun, using tempo, and using his legs a lot. Daniels looks like someone suited to a shotgun, spread-heavy RPO offense. Let Jayden Daniels COOK 🧑‍🍳 Daniels unstoppable on the RPO! pic.twitter.com/bw9yCJIgHx — MyBookie – Bet With The Best (@MyBookie) December 30, 2024 Throwing all of that away would make very little sense. At the same time, Washington didn’t change coordinators because it wanted the exact same offense, so I would expect the eventual structure to keep some of the shotgun and RPO elements Daniels already excels at while adding more motion, heavier personnel, under-center formations, and a more connected run and play-action game. Once again… sound familiar?! Ben Johnson has always done an excellent job making the run and pass game look identical. Daniels has spent most of his career seeing the defense from shotgun. It is a different world from under center. Turning your back to the defense and then having to relocate safeties and underneath defenders is a different skill. I thought Johnson handled a similar situation intelligently when he began working with Caleb Williams. Rather than forcing every element of his offense on a young quarterback immediately, he simplified some early play-action concepts and gradually added more as the season progressed. Blough would be wise to do something similar. I expect Week 1 to be a transition to a new offense, but not something totally different. That is what makes Washington difficult to predict. The sensible approach would be to keep plenty of consistency for Daniels early in the season and gradually layer in the new ideas. However, Blough is also a young first-time coordinator who will understandably want to put his own stamp on the offense (similar to Mannion! OK, I’ll stop comparing them now). If Washington wants Daniels under center more frequently, I expect Fangio to test his comfort level immediately by rotating the secondary after the snap and forcing him to process a different picture once he turns around from the run fake. Daniels remains the biggest problem regardless of scheme because his athleticism can erase mistakes. He is also a quarterback who has never been shy about taking hits, which Washington will want to manage over a long season, but it can create defensive issues. From the Eagles’ perspective, Fangio cannot allow the pass rush to become reckless because Washington’s quarterback is too dangerous once the structure breaks down. Maintaining rush-lane integrity will be every bit as important as creating pressure in this game. Skill Positions Washington has built a fairly interesting collection of skill players around Daniels. Terry McLaurin remains the obvious focal point and is still the receiver the Eagles need to account for first. He has had success against Quinyon Mitchell a couple of years ago. Eagles rookie cornerback Quinyon Mitchell had the most plays in the NFL this year for any CB without giving up a TD. But that comes to an end. Terry McLaurin beats him. pic.twitter.com/QoJWUqf1FT — John Clark (@JClarkNBCS) December 22, 2024 However, last year Quinyon bossed him. He totally erased McLauin out the game. Quinyon Mitchell lined up against Terry McLaurin on 36 of his 48 routes (75%), aligning in press coverage on half of those matchups. Mitchell allowed just one reception for 7 yards on 4 targets against McLaurin, including a fourth quarter interception. #WASvsPHI | #FlyEaglesFly pic.twitter.com/umbdPA5yNJ — Next Gen Stats (@NextGenStats) January 26, 2025 Stefon Diggs gives the offense another experienced target who can move between the slot and outside, while rookie Antonio Williams is talented but still unknown. They also have Dyami Brown, who can threaten vertically; Treylon Burks, who has a ton of physical talent; and Jaylin Lane, who gives them another speed option. That collection makes sense if Blough wants to use more play action. McLaurin and Brown can threaten defenses vertically once the run fake pulls defenders forward, while Diggs can work underneath and in the intermediate areas of the field. Williams gives the offense another player who can move around the formation rather than being tied to one spot. The Commanders have enough versatility to make the passing game hard to predict, even if they don’t have a superstar WR1. The tight end room also supports the idea that Washington could become heavier and more multiple. Chig Okonkwo is the main receiving threat, John Bates is a good run blocker, and Ben Sinnott has enough versatility to do elements of both. Washington can play 12 and 13 personnel without necessarily declaring whether it intends to run or pass, which is exactly what you want if the offense is trying to marry the run game with play action. In the backfield, Jacory Croskey-Merritt is expected to carry the bulk of the early-down workload, while Rachaad White should be involved in passing situations if healthy and Kaytron Allen gives the Commanders a more physical short-yardage option. None of them are individuals I expect to create explosives consistently on their own, so I think this backfield’s success will depend heavily on the blocking structure Blough creates. Offensive Line This is the matchup the Eagles need to win. Washington entered the season expecting Laremy Tunsil to protect Daniels’ blind side, and losing him changes the entire look of the line. Brandon Coleman is expected to move back outside to left tackle. This will leave Chris Paul at left guard, Nick Allegretti moving to center, Sam Cosmi remaining the standout at right guard, and Josh Conerly Jr. continuing at right tackle. There is talent here, so I don’t want to make the mistake of describing the whole line as poor. Cosmi is one of the better guards in football, and Washington has every reason to believe Conerly can take a significant step forward. Conerly and Cosmi on the right side could become a real strength. Cosmi already plays at a high level, while Conerly has the athletic traits to improve significantly after his first season. If Washington gets the expected development from him, the Eagles are not going to simply dominate every matchup across the line. However, the issues are much more concentrated on the other side and in the middle. I’ve used a lot of Brandon Thorn’s work here , and he had Tunsil…
