title: 3 quick takeaways from the 49ers dominant Week 1 win: Is this a true Super Bowl contender?
summary: The San Francisco 49ers dominated the Los Angeles Rams in every facet of the game on Thursday evening, winning 27-7 in Australia as they were in control for all of the second half in a strong opener. The 49ers entered the game as 3.5-point underdogs with rep questions about Nick Bosa and George Kittle, who […]
full_text: The San Francisco 49ers dominated the Los Angeles Rams in every facet of the game on Thursday evening, winning 27-7 in Australia as they were in control for all of the second half in a strong opener. The 49ers entered the game as 3.5-point underdogs with rep questions about Nick Bosa and George Kittle, who were both coming off injuries, while the Rams were ready to debut their new-look addition on defense. They turned out not to be much of a factor, as San Francisco cruised on offense, aside from a Brock Purdy interception, and started off Week 1 on a great note. Here are three quick takeaways from the 49ers Week 1 win over the Rams on Thursday. Run game flourishes Entering the game, one of the questions I had was about the run game for the 49ers, which was quite inefficient with Christian McCaffrey last year. A lot of the same infrastructure was returning, apart from the addition of Kaelon Black, and it wasn’t clear how much of a timeshare there’d be at running back. Well, the 49ers showed their comfort level with Black, getting him in early and often in the first half, as he led the team with 14 carries. The duo combined for 133 yards on 24 carries, while Brock Purdy and Deebo Samuel added 29 and 12 yards on their own, respectively. The 49ers ran the ball 30 times for 174 yards on a very respectable 5.8 yards per carry. And they did so against one of the NFL’s best defensive lines. I thought the 49ers offensive line played extremely well. And both of their backs looked explosive, as McCaffrey looked very fresh with the running back split. It was a real good day on the ground for the 49ers. Linebackers lead physicality charge on defense Fred Warner had a heck of a game, recording 11 tackles and really making his presence known everywhere on defense, but especially in the run game. Warner flew into lanes, didn’t miss a tackle, and brought the physicality to a rivalry game on defense. But the 49ers as a whole exceeded my expectations in a big way on defense. I thought they’d struggle to defend the run, which happened at times. But the Rams finished with 122 yards on 4.2 yards per carry, as Kyren Williams had just 3.7 yards per carry on 11 attempts, while Blake Corum had 5.4 yards per carry on 10 rushes. I thought San Francisco’s cornerbacks were also quite physical with Puka Nacua and Davante Adams, as Matthew Stafford looked quite off. It was a very good showing from the players, and a very quality start for Raheem Morris. Money down The 49ers were the NFL’s best on third downs offensively last year, and they picked up where they left off on Thursday, extending that to both sides of the ball. San Francisco went 7-of-12 on third downs on offense, which led to scoring drives of 15, 9, and 11 plays. Meanwhile, the Rams were just 2-of-9, as they had just one drive over seven plays outside of the final drive in garbage time. The 49ers controlled the time of possession and felt in control throughout the second half as they extended drives and played their style of football. I also thought they did a great job on 1st and 2nd downs to make 3rd downs much more manageable. They had just one third down with a to-go distance of more than five yards, which they converted. It was a good sign for Kyle Shanahan’s offense, as the Niners consistently won in big situations.
author: Rohan Chakravarthi

title: 49ers News: Nothing more grouse than a Victory Friday
summary: No matter what happens, I’m just hoping that De’Zhaun Stribling is able to come back strong and still go on with his career at a high level after this injury. I don’t even care that he’ll miss time, I just saw such a talented dude that seemed super smart and committed to the game. You […]
full_text: MELBOURNE, AUSTRALIA - SEPTEMBER 11: Brock Purdy #13 of the San Francisco 49ers throws the ball during the NFL football game at the Melbourne Cricket Ground on September 11, 2026 in Melbourne, Australia. (Photo by Morgan Hancock/Getty Images) | Getty Images No matter what happens, I’m just hoping that De’Zhaun Stribling is able to come back strong and still go on with his career at a high level after this injury. I don’t even care that he’ll miss time, I just saw such a talented dude that seemed super smart and committed to the game. You always want to see people like that win. He had an interview with his high school paper that I found on the internet one time and even at that age you’re like, how could you not root for the guy? Prayers up man. That being said… My favorite part of the game was the feeling of going to war with Brock freaking Purdy. He had this Ben Shelton-like intense look in his eyes in the second half, coming back from the pick, and he just started dealing in the third quarter. I don’t know if it’s the play calling or how well the other players executed, but he just looked so locked in, so dialed, just flow state quarterbacking and did what he wanted. The Rams are a good defense on paper and I’m curious if he keeps it up the next few games and later on against the Broncos. The Broncos will have similarly bad linebackers in the passing game but also some absurd talent elsewhere. Defense also looked solid. You love to see it. Happy Friday y’all! 49ers’ Brock Purdy looked like a quarterback out to silence his critics “I thought Brock played so well,” Shanahan said after the game. “He had one play I know he wants to take back, the interception to [Rams S Quentin] Lake, but he made some big-time plays, some big-time throws.” ….Purdy said, “…I think Kyle was doing a great job with dialing up the right play calls, and obviously not being aware of when we want to take a shot and go deep and stuff, but the [Rams] defense was giving us our ones and twos in the progression. So, just trying to take that….And then, obviously, when it wasn’t there, I think that was the time in the game where I started using my legs a little bit. And then guys did a great job on the scramble drill, obviously hitting Deebo late.” … Shanahan said,. “The 99-yard drive, there were so many plays there that he had to take off-schedule, where there wasn’t an answer, and he moved the chains with his legs. And I think he found Deebo on one—that was a big off-schedule for the touchdown. So Brock was unbelievable today.” Hutchinson: The 49ers needed this a lot more than the Rams (paywall) “Los Angeles was able to Duo the hell out of the 49ers. They employed double-team runs through their gut while CJ West frequently flailed around and forgot he is not meant to be used as a bowling ball for the opposing team. Despite this issue — one I felt would be crucial to defining the 49ers’ success — the secondary was tremendous. Nick Bosa and Fred Warner were omnipresent. Raheem Morris decided he’d rather trust his four best corners than dare go to big nickel. He used dime more than nickel! The 49ers got rewarded for it against a team that should have theoretically demolished the 49ers with their love of heavy personnel. But the Rams used 13 personnel as a changeup, not as a primary mode of extracting pain. They overwhelmingly stuck to 11 personnel despite their success (5-for-5, 96 yards, +1.06 EPA per SumerSports) in 13….On the other side, the Rams barely ran any man coverage despite having Jaylen Watson and Trent McDuffie, who … bodybagged Deebo Samuel and the 49ers in the 2023 Super Bowl with a heavy dose of man. The 49ers played more man than they did!….They suddenly have a No. 2 back in Kaelon Black who is a human pistol shrimp. He may not have any interest in reading the flow of the offensive line. But he will shoot through a hole and get positive yardage. If you give him an inch, he’ll take a yard. Shanahan used unique wrinkles from the last few seasons — dash, jet, bump and ghost motions — and bizarre, offset alignments, including a few pre-snap bumps and shuffles to put receivers in the slot, but about 5 yards of depth. He created opportunities for easy throws for Purdy.” Maoicco: What we learned as Purdy, Evans fuel 49ers’ opening win over Rams in Australia “Odighizuwa pressured Stafford relentlessly in the first half with three quarterback hits. Bosa, in his first game back after tearing his right ACL in Week 3 last season, turned up some pressure, too. Cornerback Renardo Green came up with a big play in the first half when he intercepted Stafford’s pass intended for Puka Nacua. But when the 49ers needed a big goal-line stand near the end of the third quarter, it was rookie Gracen Halton and Warner who stopped Stafford for no gain on a push up the middle….And, even more surprising, Aaron Donald had about as much impact on the game as Myles Garrett. Through three quarters of action, Garrett was completely shut out from the stat sheet. He had no tackles, no sacks, no nothing. Donald, who recently came out of retirement and stayed back in California for the Week 1 game, had the same stat line. The 49ers game-planned around Garrett to do their best to make sure he did not wreck the game. Garrett was the NFL’s Defensive Player of the Year last season while with the Cleveland Browns. The Rams acquired him in an offseason trade following his 23-sack season.” Cohn: Grading the 49ers After Their 27-7 Win Over the Rams in Australia “First, let’s praise defensive coordinator Raheem Morris. He didn’t sell out to stop the Rams’ running game. He conceded 5.1 yards per carry, which seemed risky, but he was making sure that Stafford wouldn’t beat him. In fact, Morris owned Stafford, just like last season when Morris was the Falcons head coach and they beat the Rams in Week 17. Morris used to be the Rams’ defensive coordinator, so he has faced Stafford countless times in practice and clearly has his number. What a hire for the 49ers. Next, let’s praise Kyle Shanahan. He made all the right calls on this trip. He was right to bring his players out to Australia more than a week before the game. He was right to stop calling passes for Kittle after giving him a chance to show he was ready. He was right to feature Evans. He was right to split carries between McCaffrey and Black. And he was right to hire Morris. As a result, the 49ers just destroyed the team that lots of people predicted to win the Super Bowl. Of course, this one game doesn’t mean the 49ers will win the Super Bowl. Remember, they beat the Seahawks Week 1 last season, and then the Seahawks went on to win the Super Bowl. But that Week 1 win was fluky and close. This one was decisive and embarrassing for the Rams. They deserved every bit of the humiliation the 49ers gave them. They cheated the process of preparation and disrespected the 49ers and Australia by showing up yesterday. Enjoy that long flight home tonight. The 49ers sure will.” ’ Shanahan, McVay brush off travel plans as factor in Niners’ win over Rams “It was definitely worth it coming a little bit early,” receiver Mike Evans said. “I felt like we got acclimated. … We didn’t complain. We actually enjoyed being out here in Melbourne.” The 49ers landed in Melbourne on Sept. 4. They stayed at the Park Hyatt Hotel, where the team arranged for everything from meeting and film rooms, and the 49ers’ chefs prepared meals at the restaurant. The players had access to a nearby spa for various recovery tools such as a cold plunge and red light therapy. When they weren’t planning for the game, the Niners explored the city, trying the various coffee shops and going to group dinners at local restaurants. Running back Christian McCaffrey even got a haircut and was told that his hair “looks cracker,” which he was then informed means it looks good. “Melbourne was sick,” tight end George Kittle said. “I had a great time here. I’m real excited, the fact that we came out early and were…

title: 49ers receive some good news about De’Zhaun Stribling’s injury
summary: The San Francisco 49ers’ injury luck couldn’t have been worse coming into the season. It’s a team that consistently has been among the worst in the NFL in adjusted games lost. Unfortunately, that trend is continuing in 2026. De’Zhaun Stribling left the game early on, but shortly returned. When he did come back, Stribling was […]
full_text: Photo by Robert Cianflone/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers’ injury luck couldn’t have been worse coming into the season. It’s a team that consistently has been among the worst in the NFL in adjusted games lost. Unfortunately, that trend is continuing in 2026. De’Zhaun Stribling left the game early on, but shortly returned. When he did come back, Stribling was carted off the field. It was a non-contact injury in which Stribling couldn’t put any pressure on his left leg. The 49ers immediately ruled him out, which is never a good sign. 49ers rookie WR De'Zhaun Stribling was carted off the field after suffering an apparent leg injury. (📺 Netflix) pic.twitter.com/rtcwZQcqLH — ESPN Fantasy Sports (@ESPNFantasy) September 11, 2026 Stribling played 21 snaps before he left with an injury. The 49ers relied on Jacob Cowing and Deebo Samuel in Stribling’s absence. They’ll likely use Demarcus Robinson more moving forward. A wide receiver core that looked promising a month ago is now without two of its top three targets with Stribling’s injury and Ricky Pearsall out for the season. Tight end Jake Tonges was also carted off with a lower leg injury. He’s questionable to return, but this does not seem like somebody who is coming back: Jake Tonges being carted off pic.twitter.com/GwuH83fKhu — John Chapman (@JL_Chapman) September 11, 2026 Luke Farrell and Kyle Juszczyk are playing in Tonges’s place. Kyle’s update, 8:49 p.m. PT: Kyle Shanahan said Stribling injured his ankle, and Stribling’s Achilles is still intact. We’ll have updates when they’re available, but that means there’s still a chance he can return this season, as opposed to what it appeared to be. Jake Tonges has an MCL injury. Shanahan said his injury “wasn’t good.” More tests to come to determine the injury.
author: Kyle Posey

title: 49ers embarrass the Rams for the entire world to see
summary: The San Francisco 49ers defense was on the field first, and it didn’t take long for Fred Warner and Nick Bosa to make an impact. Bosa hit Los Angeles Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford on his first dropback. He followed that up with a tackle for loss on the ensuing drive. Warner broke up the intended […]
full_text: Photo by Quinn Rooney/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers defense was on the field first, and it didn’t take long for Fred Warner and Nick Bosa to make an impact. Bosa hit Los Angeles Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford on his first dropback. He followed that up with a tackle for loss on the ensuing drive. Warner broke up the intended pass to Puka Nacua. After Deommodore Lenoir made a tackle, the Rams went three-and-out. Brock Purdy used his shiny new toy on his first third down of the game. Evans beat Quentin Lake for a seven-yard reception to move the sticks. It came after an inexplicable drop. Purdy played with fire on the first drive, after a Drake Maye impersonation. Purdy threw off his back foot, and the throw was nearly intercepted just shy of the end zone. Thankfully, Trent McDuffie landed out of bounds. When Purdy needed somebody, he went to Evans. The veteran had three receptions for three first downs to begin the game. Evans came off the field on third and goal. Shanahan tried to get Purdy outside of the pocket, but to no avail. Instead of going for it on 3rd & goal from the two, Shanahan elected to go for a 20-yard field goal. Eddy Pineiro’s kick was good, but it was a disappointing result after an incredible 15-play, 65-yard drive that took over seven minutes off the clock. After picking up a first down on the second drive, Stafford was off-target twice to Puka Nacua on the second drive. Shanahan stuck to his word, as we saw Kaelon Black on the field on the first drive of the game. Black had a reception and a carry. His catch helped keep the drive alive. Black was the first running back to start the second drive. The offense went three-and-out after McCaffrey dropped a pass on 3rd & 2. On the same drive, De’Zhaun Stribling limped into the blue medical tent. You knew the Rams wouldn’t stay down for long. Ji’Ayir Brown took a gamble and lost. It resulted in a 41-yard Puka Nacua reception. It’s a risk you cannot be wrong about in that situation. Unfortunately, Brown was, and it gave the Rams the ball in the red zone. Stafford connects with Puka for a big gain! SFvsLAR on Netflix pic.twitter.com/AQsQhquXO8 — NFL (@NFL) September 11, 2026 Dre Greenlaw’s tackling wasn’t much better. Kyren Williams capped the drive off with a touchdown, and just like that, the Rams took the lead 7-3. Deebo dropped a pass to begin the next drive, but Evans made up for it with a first-down reception. After running for a first down, Purdy threw it over the middle to Kittle, but it was Quentin Lake who intercepted the pass. It was a costly turnover, as the 49ers were driving and in a position to put points on the board. The 49ers’ defense: After gains of 5, 6, 10, and 13, McVay abandoned the run, and that was just what the doctor ordered for the 49ers. Odighizuwa had a pressure on second down. Renardo Green picked Stafford off on third down, and the Rams failed to score. Stribling went left on the next drive with a non-contact injury. He was not putting any pressure on his left leg. That didn’t prevent the 49ers from finding the end zone. Purdy found Demarcus Robinson streaking down the middle of the field on a post behind the Rams’ quarters coverage for a walk-in touchdown: PURDY GOES DEEP FOR THE TOUCHDOWN!!! SFvsLAR on Netflix pic.twitter.com/SCggzxjqLo — NFL (@NFL) September 11, 2026 That was the longest air-yard completion of Purdy’s career, as it traveled 44 yards. The Rams took over and moved the ball, but Keion White drew a holding call, which made it 3rd & 13. Morris drew up a beautiful design out of dime personnel. He took Greenlaw off for cornerback Jack Jones. Stout and Warner blitzed, and Jones nearly came up with another interception. The Rams were forced to punt. Brock Purdy took a big helmet-to-helmet blow on the two-minute drive. That inched the Niners closer to midfield. Mike Evans dropped a third-down pass, and the offense was forced to punt. The 49ers were 5-for-8 on third downs compared to the Rams’ 1-for-5 in the first half. They had double the first downs, but also threw an interception, had four drops, and came up empty on a goal-to-go situation. Yet they took the lead into halftime and got the ball back to open the second half. Deebo Samuel ignited the first drive with a 45-yard kickoff return. McCaffrey picked up 14 and 16 yards. Before you knew it, the Niners had another goal-to-go situation. A perfect fade pass to Mike Evans gave the Niners a 17-7 lead. But you knew the Rams wouldn’t go away. Puka got behind Lenoir on one play, which led to an illegal contact penalty. Another chunk play allowed by Lenoir put the Rams inside the red zone. Fred Warner and Jaden Dugger made a stop on second and goal. Lenoir did just enough on third down to prevent Nacua from scoring. Then, on fourth and goal, the Niners stood tall for the second year in a row to force a stop. The worry was that, with the offense backed up, they’d give the ball right back to Stafford. Purdy had other ideas. He found Farrell for a first down, then Deebo for 13. Purdy scrambled for 18 yards to flip the field. Purdy’s legs were the theme of the drive. He extended another play before finding Samuel in the end zone. That extended the lead to 24-7. As the Rams were driving, Fred Warner forced a fumble. However, the offense didn’t capitalize. Eddy Pineiro’s 56-yard field goal was good, and the Niners took a 27-7 lead. It was a dominant performance. Myles Garrett was held without a pressure for the first time since 2018. He had as many tackles as Kyle Shanahan. It was the fewest points the Rams have scored with Stafford as a starter. Stafford was held to his lowest EPA per dropback as a Ram. It was Los Angeles’s first double-digit loss since 2024.

full_text: (Photo by Jordon Kelly/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images According to Matt Maiocco, the San Francisco 49ers will start second-year pro Connor Colby at left guard over rookie Carver Willis. Maiocco said Willis, who is active, could rotate with Colby. That’s the correct decision, in my opinion. It’s a question that was posed on a podcast yesterday: Who will start at left guard once the dust settles- Colby or Willis? 1:16:21 After we both agreed it’d be Colby, here are some of the quotes: “He has the experience. We’re forgetting about the 55 starts that he came into the NFL with.” “He’s a really good athlete, too. He’s not a bad athlete. In my mind, he overthinks himself. He gets into his own head. title: 49ers inactives: 6 players on their rookie contracts won’t suit up vs. Rams
summary: The San Francisco 49ers’ first inactive list of the season is out. They’ll lean into the veterans on the roster tonight, as every player on the inactive list is on a rookie contract: QB Kurtis RourkeCB Ephesians PrysockRB Jordan JamesWR Jordan WatkinsLB Tatum BethuneOT Enrique Cruz The 49ers having only two running backs active suggests […]
full_text: (Photo by Quinn Rooney/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers’ first inactive list of the season is out. They’ll lean into the veterans on the roster tonight, as every player on the inactive list is on a rookie contract: QB Kurtis Rourke CB Ephesians Prysock RB Jordan James WR Jordan Watkins LB Tatum Bethune OT Enrique Cruz The 49ers having only two running backs active suggests Deebo Samuel will play a pivotal role out of the backfield. Expect him to be an option still in the passing game, but it likely comes from the running back alignment. If anybody knows how to take on a heavier workload against the Rams, it’s Deebo. It’s also a sign that the team is comfortable giving Kaelon black touches. Kyle Shanahan said this past offseason that he regrets not involving more running backs last season. It means you’re taking Christian McCaffrey off the field, so it’s understandable. Still, the goal is to keep McCaffrey fresh for the last stretch of the season. With Watkins inactive, Mike Evans, De’Zhaun Stribling, Demarcus Robinson, Jacob Cowing, and KhaDarel Hodge are the wideouts. If Samuel’s role is more underneath, we’ll see whether that means Cowing has a role as the receiver who stretches the field for the offense. It wouldn’t be surprising to see Brock Purdy spread the ball around. We haven’t heard much from Robinson with Stribling’s ascension, but Shanahan relying on a veteran in Week 1 makes far more sense, based on his history. It’s a mild upset that Bethune is inactive, but Brant Boyer clearly wanted a different body type on specific special teams units than Bethune. It’s no surprise to see the rookies inactive. Those players weren’t drafted to contribute in 2026.

title: 49ers elevate Ogbo Okoronkwo and a receiver from the practice squad
summary: We’re a few hours away from the San Francisco 49ers kicking off their 2026 season against the Los Angeles Rams. Ahead of Week 1, the team officially placed defensive tackle Alfred Collins on the season-ending Injured Reserve List. No matter how you slice it, it’s a bummer for Collins. The second-round pick from a season […]
full_text: (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’re a few hours away from the San Francisco 49ers kicking off their 2026 season against the Los Angeles Rams. Ahead of Week 1, the team officially placed defensive tackle Alfred Collins on the season-ending Injured Reserve List. No matter how you slice it, it’s a bummer for Collins. The second-round pick from a season ago was slated to be an integral part of Raheem Morris’s defense. Collins battled a shoulder injury that kept him out of the first block of training camp practices . He was gun-shy. Collins never looked comfortable, and it led to passive play. The idea was he’d play more, gain more confidence, and shake off the rust while playing himself into shape all in one. But a patellar tendon injury ended the chances of Collins getting a chance to play through those struggles. The 49ers elevated defensive lineman Ogbo Okoronkwo from the practice squad. He will wear No. 59. He’s a veteran who knows what to expect against a Sean McVay offense after practicing against it for the first three years of his career. Okoronkwo also has overlap with Raheem Morris during their time with the Rams. Okoronkwo was the lone defensive lineman elevated from the practice squad. Leaving Sebastian Valdez and Kevin Givens on the practice squad is likely a combination of things. The most significant being that Morris is comfortable with the rotation he can put onto the field. Maybe that is because a player like Jaden Dugger can hold his own at the line of scrimmage. It’s a good sign that Gracen Halton and James Thompson Jr. are healthy enough to play a role if needed. It also signals that Nick Bosa’s pitch count might be closer to 70 than 50%. It’ll be fascinating to track who plays where among CJ West, Halton, Osa Odighizuwa, Keion White, Romello Height, and Khalid Kareem. That’s who the 49ers are rolling with in Australia against the Rams up front. The 49ers also elevated wide receiver KhaDarel Hodge. He’s No. 86. Hodge was with the Falcons from 2022 through 2025. He was drafted by the Rams in 2018. Hodge played 219 special teams snaps across five different units last season. That’s how undrafted free agents stick on rosters. Hodge had six special teams tackles, but also missed five last year.
author: Kyle Posey

title: Deebo Samuel is a vintage performance away from a piece of 49ers history
summary: Deebo Samuel has had a number of memorable performances against the Los Angeles Rams over the course of his 49ers career. After an unsuccessful year away with the Washington Commanders in which he did not face the Rams, he will renew acquaintances with them as the Niners face their division rivals in Melbourne. Samuel will […]
full_text: Credit: Jayne Kamin-Oncea-USA TODAY Sports | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con Deebo Samuel has had a number of memorable performances against the Los Angeles Rams over the course of his 49ers career. After an unsuccessful year away with the Washington Commanders in which he did not face the Rams, he will renew acquaintances with them as the Niners face their division rivals in Melbourne. Samuel will naturally be determined to mark the historic occasion of the first regular-season game in Australia by once again proving a thorn in the Rams’ side. And there is extra incentive for Samuel to do so as he stands close to writing his name into the 49ers’ history books with a strong Week 1 showing. Samuel will enter the game with 5,935 scrimmage yards to his name for the 49ers. He needs 65 yards to become the 12th player to reach 6,000 for San Francisco. He would become just the fourth wide receiver to achieve that feat, following in the footsteps of Jerry Rice, Terrell Owens, Dwight Clark and Gene Washington. With Mike Evans, George Kittle and Christian McCaffrey also likely to command targets, Samuel will not be the focal point of the 49er attack, so there is a chance he does not receive the kind of workload to hit that number. Regardless of how he performs in Week 1, Samuel — provided he avoids injury — will get to the 6,000 mark this year. But it would be extra sweet for Samuel to achieve the feat against the 49ers’ NFC West foes, and a strong performance from him would likely mean a very good night for the San Francisco offense. San Francisco will take a win over Los Angeles in any fashion, but there would be no better way to start the season than with a vintage Samuel performance against the Rams, which would give the 49ers reason to be even more confident about their star-studded offense for the rest of the campaign.
author: Nicholas McGee

title: 49ers-Rams preview: Familiarity, new looks, and aggressive QBs
summary: By now, you’re sick of everybody with a platform predicting that the Los Angeles Rams will not only beat the San Francisco 49ers in Week 1, but also shift into cruise control after their inevitable victory en route to a Super Bowl win where nobody challenges them. That’s how football works, right? The best teams […]
full_text: (Photo by Harry How/Getty Images) | Getty Images By now, you’re sick of everybody with a platform predicting that the Los Angeles Rams will not only beat the San Francisco 49ers in Week 1, but also shift into cruise control after their inevitable victory en route to a Super Bowl win where nobody challenges them. That’s how football works, right? The best teams win every year. The preseason Super Bowl favorites waltz through their schedule without any speed bumps along the way. That happened in 2025, when the three preseason favorites, the Ravens, Bills, and Eagles, looked like juggernauts. Or in 2024, when the Niners made a deep playoff run. And who could forget the epic postseason from the preseason champs, the Philadelphia Eagles, in 2023? None of those things occurred in any of those seasons. Acting like the red carpet will be rolled out for the Rams for a Super Bowl run would make sense if we didn’t have years of history showing how football actually works to disprove that notion. But we’re here to talk about Week 1. A game that features two teams that have had Super Bowl aspirations entering each of the previous five seasons. The 2026 version for each team could very well be the best iteration of themselves this decade. However, a Week 1 showdown between two teams who know each other like the back of their hand gets another injection of familiarity by adding Raheem Morris — the Rams defensive coordinator from 2021-23 — into the mix. Raheem Morris vs. the Rams in ‘25 We don’t have to go far to find an example of a Morris (Jeff Ulbrich) defense against Sean McVay. The Falcons faced the Rams in Week 17 last year. In that game, Matthew Stafford had the third-lowest EPA per dropback and completion percentage of the season, to go along with his worst QB rating — by 18 percentage points — and three touchdowns. Stafford was sacked three times, despite being pressured on 26.8% of his dropbacks (for reference, the Nick Bosa-less 49ers pressured Stafford on 27% and 25% of his dropbacks in two games last season). It wasn’t as if the Falcons blitzed like madmen all game. It was the third-lowest blitz rate he faced all season. In fact, it was the opposite approach. Atlanta was heavy upfront, played it safe on the back end, and dared Stafford to either beat them deep into double coverage or be a checkdown merchant for most of the game. There’s always some luck involved when playing against a quarterback of Stafford’s caliber. The Rams dropped a couple of first downs. But Stafford is a proven risk-taker. Three of his interceptions came from clean pockets. The 49ers will have their opportunities. Whether they catch the ball is another story. Atlanta not only forced three turnovers, but also held the Rams to 6-for-17 on third and fourth downs, despite only three sacks, and held them to 1-for-3 in the red area. The most impressive thing the Falcons did in that game was limit the Rams’ running game. Their running backs had 20 carries for 115 yards. Kyren Williams had three carries that went 15+ yards. On a down-to-down basis, the Rams’ ground attack was bottled up. Despite those 15+ yard carries, Williams had a 38.5% success rate with a -.20 EPA per rush. Blake Corum had a 16.7% success rate with a -.32 EPA per rush. Neither ran into stacked boxes more than 25% of the time. The Falcons did it by creating 5-man surfaces with their base personnel: Tonight, the 49ers will miss Mykel Williams’s ability to reduce into a 4i (inside eye of the offensive tackle) and be disruptive as a run defender. Whether it’s a Tite front, like the one above, to take the B-gaps away, or a different front where the defensive line reduces to the strong or weak side, we can expect multiple 5-man surfaces out of Morris tonight to make things congested and the reads blurry for the Rams’ running game. The give and take of 5-man fronts If you’re using seven bodies to stop the run, it means you’re trusting four other players to hold their own in coverage. The Falcons were fortunate to have a veteran like Kaden Elliss sniff out a couple of concepts that could very well expose rookie Jaden Dugger tonight. That’s who Sean McVay will put under the microscope. Dugger will see patterns, different motions, and all kinds of eye candy to distract him. The player Dugger thinks he’s supposed to defend will be different by the time the ball is snapped. In Dugger’s case, the goal is to minimize damage. Make open-field tackles against the running backs. If a tight end gets behind you, catch up and make the tackle so your defense gets to live to fight another down. It won’t be easy, as Dugger will be stressed in ways he never has in his life. Tight ends Colby Parkinson and Terrance Ferguson had field days against the Falcons’ third linebacker and safeties. That was true in Week 10 for those two against Luke Gifford and Ji’Ayir Brown. The hope is that Dugger’s athleticism allows him to run with the tight ends down the field. And if he’s in position, he has an opportunity to contest the pass. Another counter would be to add a defensive back and remove a linebacker from the equation. A 5-man front can turn into a “Penny” look if you don’t trust one of the linebackers in coverage. Safety Malik Mustapha was not listed on the injury report , while Renardo Green was upgraded to a full participant. That means Morris can use Mustapha or Jack Jones as an extra coverage player if he plans on being aggressive with his pass rush. Inevitably, the way teams use 5-man surfaces against the Rams leaves their safeties exposed on the back end. Even in a game where Jessie Bates and Xavier Watts had interceptions in Week 17, they still allowed explosive plays, touchdowns, and first downs, and it would’ve been worse had it not been for drops. Puka Nacua had a quiet outing, with 47 receiving yards on 10 targets, and only two first downs — the Falcons actually broke up three passes his way. Davante Adams didn’t play. I suspect the tight ends will be a bigger factor than the receivers for the Rams tonight. Night and day from a year ago The 49ers front-7 the last time they took the field against the Rams consisted of Bryce Huff, Kalia Davis, Jordan Elliott, Sam Okuayinonu, Tatum Bethune, Dee Winters, and Luke Gifford. Stafford’s EPA per dropback in that game was +0.56 (his highest of the season), and he had 3.12 seconds to throw, the second-longest mark of 2025 for Stafford. Twenty of Stafford’s 24 completions went for first downs. On the ground, Williams averaged 5.2 yards per carry with a +0.14 EPA per attempt and a 57.1% success rate. Blake Corum had a 61.5% success rate. Nothing went right for the Niners defensively that day. This time around, the 49ers will send out this guy named Nick Bosa. Next to Bosa, it’ll be CJ West, Osa Odighizuwa, Keion White, Fred Warner, Dre Greenlaw, and Jaden Dugger. That’s right, seven different players from Week 10. The 49ers should be more disruptive by throwing different fronts at the Rams and by being decisively more athletic. West can eat blocks and hold his ground against the run in ways Davis and Elliott could not. Odighizuwa’s first step is closer to Bosa’s. His length will come in handy. White weighs about 40 pounds more than Huff. We discussed the kind of night Dugger will be in for. The other two linebackers need no introduction. Dre Greenlaw has returned twice in his career from injuries to face the Rams, and put on two of the most impressive performances this decade in those games. Warner has not forced a fumble in his career against the Rams. He has one interception, which came in 2019. He’s due. Brock bolting out of danger Myles Garrett was a full participant in the previous two practices. Byron Young, Kobie Turner, and Braden Fiske complete a fierce group of four that’ll rival any pass rush in the league. All four are athletic. Garrett makes the other three dangerous with all of the attention he’ll command. Unprompted, Brock Purdy told the media that he was prepared to run more this…

summary: The Tampa Bay Buccaneers enter the 2026 season with plenty of uncertainty, and our staff predictions reflect it. The Bucs scored 380 points but allowed 411, finished […]
full_text: TAMPA, FL - AUGUST 06: Tampa Bay Buccaneers Head Coach Todd Bowles looks out toward the main building and sees a recognizable face approaching during Training Camp on August 06, 2026 at the AdventHealth Training Center at One Buccaneer Place in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Cliff Welch/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Tampa Bay Buccaneers enter the 2026 season with plenty of uncertainty, and our staff predictions reflect it. Tampa Bay finished 8-9 in 2025 after a 6-2 start, losing seven of its final nine games and missing out on the NFC South title through a tiebreaker. The Bucs scored 380 points but allowed 411, finished 3-3 inside the division and went just 1-4 over their final five games. There is reason for optimism, particularly after Baker Mayfield signed an extension that gives Tampa Bay stability at quarterback. Mayfield has become the unquestioned leader of the offense and gives the Bucs a proven veteran to build around. But much of that optimism could disappear quickly if the defensive backfield struggles. Questions in the secondary remain one of the team’s biggest concerns, and against a schedule featuring several dangerous passing attacks, breakdowns on the back end could turn winnable games into losses. That makes the range of predictions from our staff interesting. Evan has the Bucs finishing 8-9, an exact repeat of last season. Mike sees a slight improvement at 9-8, while Will is the most optimistic of the group at 10-7. I’m on the other end, predicting a 7-10 finish. Collectively, that puts our average prediction at exactly 8.5 wins and 8.5 losses — essentially a .500 football team. Tampa Bay’s schedule could make separating from that middle difficult. The Bucs open on the road against Cincinnati before playing three straight home games against Cleveland, Minnesota and Green Bay. Later matchups with Detroit, Baltimore, the Chargers and Rams add more potential hurdles. For Tampa Bay, turning close games into wins may determine whether Will looks prophetic or my prediction proves closer to reality.

summary: After minicamp, OTAs, training camp and the preseason, the Tennessee Titans finally begin their 2026 NFL campaign on Sunday. They’ll host the New York Jets at Nissan Stadium in Week 1. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images After minicamp, OTAs, training camp and the preseason, the Tennessee Titans finally begin their 2026 NFL campaign on Sunday. They’ll host the New York Jets at Nissan Stadium in Week 1. Head coach Robert Saleh will officially make his debut, marking the start of a new era in Tennessee. Coach Saleh needs multiple players to step up versus the Jets, his former team, in Week 1. We’ve identified five in particular. Jeffery Simmons, DT Jeffery Simmons is the best defensive tackle in the NFL. He needs to apply pressure to Jets quarterback Geno Smith, who is a mistake-prone quarterback when under duress. Smith leads the NFL in interceptions across the 2024-25 seasons combined. Cam Ward, QB This entire fanbase will be monitoring Cam Ward’s progress as a sophomore quarterback. After a pair of lackluster showings in the preseason, fans want a heat-check on Ward as a quarterback. A big-time showing versus the Jets would ease any lingering concerns. Carnell Tate, WR Rookie No. 4 overall pick Carnell Tate will make his official regular season debut. The Titans drafted Tate for him to be Ward’s go-to playmaker. After failing to register a catch in the preseason, Titans fans want to see Ward pepper him with targets. Alontae Taylor, CB The Titans paid Alontae Taylor roughly $20 million per season to be the defense’s No. 1 cornerback. Taylor and the entire first-team unit struggled in the preseason, allowing multiple explosive touchdowns. He needs a better showing versus Garrett Wilson and the Jets’ potentially underrated passing attack. Tony Pollard, RB Tony Pollard has enjoyed four consecutive 1,000 yard seasons. The Titans’ reliable bellcow is both underrated and underappreciated. Pollard appears primed for another big season in Tennessee as the lead ball carrier. Tyjae Spears will spell him, and both backs are expected to catch more passes in Brian Daboll’s offense.

full_text: PITTSBURGH, PA - AUGUST 21: Geno Smith #7 of the New York Jets warms up before the game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium on August 21, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Justin K. Aller/Getty Images) | Getty Images Tennessee Titans head coach Robert Saleh will officially begin his era on Sunday . The Titans are hosting the New York Jets in their Week 1 opener of the 2026 NFL season. Coach Saleh will be debuting his new-look defense. Saleh is a defensive-minded coach. General manager Mike Borgonzi built the defense in his vision. Saleh was especially allowed to revamp the defensive line, acquiring players he had coached before like Jermaine Johnson II, John Franklin-Myers, Solomon Thomas, Jacob Martin, and Jordan Elliott. One area of emphasis for this new-look Titans defense is 2026 will be to force more turnovers. The 2025 Titans were -5 in turnover differential last year. They notched just 14 total takeaways, tied for fourth-last in the NFL. They only had six interceptions, third-fewest. New Jets starting quarterback Geno Smith is a gunslinger. He led the league in interceptions throughout the 2025 season with 17 despite playing just 15 games. In 2024, Smith’s 15 interceptions were tied for second-most in the NFL. He loves testing tight throwing windows. The Jets have weapons. Garrett Wilson and Breece Hall are proven playmakers. They used two first-round picks on a pair of rookie pass catchers in Kenyon Sadiq and Omar Cooper Jr. They also expect Mason Taylor and Adonai Mitchell to continue getting better. Smith will attempt to sling the ball around. Saleh’s San Francisco 49ers defense also struggled to record interceptions last year. They actually tied the Titans with six. We’ll see if acquisitions like Cor’Dale Flott and Alontae Taylor help. Safety Amani Hooker uncharacteristically had zero interceptions in 2025 after registering a career-high five in 2024. Saleh brought his aggressive defense to the Titans. Hopefully it yields better results in the turnover department. The Titans will see a mistake-prone Smith at quarterback in Week 1. Hopefully the new approach pays dividends.

title: Washington Commanders vs Philadelphia Eagles Week 1: Five Questions with Bleeding Green Nation
summary: It’s week 1 of the NFL season and the Washington Commanders will be facing an Eagles team on the road at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, PA on Sunday at 4:25 p.m. ET. The Eagles have now done the improbable and won the NFC East Championship two years in a row, though they flamed out […]
full_text: Philadelphia Eagles running back Saquon Barkley celebrates a first down against Washington Commanders safety Will Harris (3) during the first half of an NFL football game, Saturday, Dec. 20, 2025, in Landover, Md. | AP Photo - Nick Wass It’s week 1 of the NFL season and the Washington Commanders will be facing an Eagles team on the road at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, PA on Sunday at 4:25 p.m. ET. The Eagles have now done the improbable and won the NFC East Championship two years in a row, though they flamed out of the playoffs last postseason to an injury-riddled 49ers team in the Wild Card round. Still, the Eagles are the most accomplished team in the division in recent years and the betting favorites to win the division . On offense, the Eagles have switched OC again after an underwhelming stint from OC Kevin Patullo last year. The Eagles offense this year will be helmed by OC Sean Mannion, formerly of the Packers. Similar to Washington’s OC David Blough, Mannion was a player as recently as 2023 and only served a couple of years coaching QBs for the Packers before being hired by the Eagles to run their offense. Mannion is expected to run a Shanahan-style outside-zone run game with heavy use of under-center formations and play-action fakes. It is also an offense that typically features an emphasis on passes to the middle of the field, though this seems to conflict with the preference of QB Jalen Hurts, who threw just 28 times between the hashmarks last season . This was both a career high for Hurts and the fewest amongst QBs who played 14+ games in 2025. Hurts seems to prefer to throw to the sidelines, an area where X-receiver AJ Brown thrived. Brown was traded away in the offseason, but former 1st-round pick DeVonta Smith will try to reprise Brown’s role and become the boundary X. Meanwhile, 2026 1st-round pick Makai Lemon (who battled hamstring injury during training camp, but is now fully healthy) will try to fill that important between-the-hashes role. On defense, the Eagles are in their third year with Vic Fangio at DC. Fangio typically runs a 3-4 front and 2 deep safeties to limit explosive plays. He also typically runs a light box, relying on stout defensive linemen to stop the run, while dropping most of his players back into coverage. It is a defense designed to limit big plays and slowly suffocate offenses into punting. Quite frankly, the Eagles defense is well coached and stacked with good or great players at multiple levels. It will be in contention for best defense in the NFL this year and should be comparable to last year, when it was ranked 13th in yards allowed and 5th in points allowed . However, if it has a weakness, it seems to be at the safety position, which has received little attention in the offseason . I asked Brandon Lee Gowton of Bleeding Green Nation five questions to better understand the state of the Eagles and what to look for in this game. 1) Jeff Stoutland was one of the all-time great OL coaches in the NFL and retired this offseason. What does this mean for the Eagles and what do you expect to be different in the Eagles’ OL blocking this year? “Retired.” The Eagles purportedly wanted him back … but only as their offensive line coach and NOT their run game coordinator, which is a title he was granted after the Eagles’ Super Bowl LII win. It would be disingenuous for anyone who previously talked about how great Stout was to now act like it’s no big deal that he’s gone. The Eagles likely downgraded at offensive line coach this offseason. That said, the early returns on his replacement — Chris Kuper — seem to be positive. We saw the Eagles’ run game have success in training camp settings, for whatever that’s worth. The Eagles’ young backup offensive lineman seem to be developing nicely. Multiple Eagles offensive linemen have expressed excitement about the new offense as it relates to making their jobs easier. Lane Johnson has talked about how he’ll have more help now as opposed to almost always being on an island at right tackle. Johnson and Jordan Mailata have also discussed how the new scheme is going to make their offense less predictable. Of course, it’s easy for players and fans to look on the bright side before the games actually start. I do think the Eagles’ offensive line will be better than it was last year because they should be healthier. The entire group isn’t coming off the massive 2024 rushing workload that clearly took a toll on them. Cam Jurgens in particular seems to be removed from the back injury that tanked his 2025 season. I do have some concerns about Landon Dickerson, who doesn’t look back to his Pro Bowl form based on what I saw in training camp, but there are worse starting guards in the league. To be determined if schematic tweaks help or hurt the o-line, if they even make a big difference at all. 2) What will the Eagles offense look like being run by Sean Mannion? How big of a change is that from last year? Great question! It’s not easy to know exactly what to expect, both in terms of aesthetic and the extent to which it is effective. We did see enough in training camp to lead one to believe there will be meaningful differences from the past. There was much more under center play-action usage. There was a good deal of pre-snap motion. Jalen Hurts seemed to throw over the middle of the field more frequently than he has in the past. Do these tweaks guarantee that the offense will be a lot better than it was in 2026? I don’t think they do. But they could certainly help. I mean, it’s hard to get worse than last year’s offense that led the league in three-and-out percentage. But there are still a lot of questions here. Mannion isn’t only a first-time play-caller, he’s entering the third year of his entire coaching career. He’s inexperienced. I already touched on Stoutland above. A.J. Brown is gone, that’s a pretty big loss. It’s also not like the Eagles are the only team trying to reinvent their offense to some degree. Offensive coordinator change has become the norm in the NFL; the longest tenured play-calling OC is from 2025! Most seem to be chasing the Sean McVay/Kyle Shanahan systems, which is where Mannion draws experience from. But while teams understandably covet those influences, it remains to be seen which (if any) disciples can effectively enact their visions. And if these teams might be too late to a trend. The thinking here is that the Eagles’ offense could have some success early on since they begin the season with games against the Commanders and Titans. But things might get bumpy after that and I tend to think that progress might not be linear for this offense. There could be some ups and downs before they hit their stride, if they ever do. 3) What are your thoughts about the Eagles’ trade of AJ Brown and how it will affect the team? I think it’s a bummer because Brown is an awesome player (not was, still is) and Eagles fans should ultimately remember the Super Bowl LIX champion as a big contributor to the most successful sustained stretch in franchise history. But it’s not quite that simple because Brown clearly didn’t put his best foot forward for the Eagles in 2025. Keeping him moving forward clearly wasn’t an option; the Eagles were never going to get the motivated version of Brown in 2026 that the Patriots will be getting. And that’s a shame, for a lot of reasons. I do think the Eagles did reasonably well to get a 2028 first-round pick and a 2027 fifth-round pick for him. But I also think they’re going to miss Brown. Similar to what I said about Stoutland earlier in this correspondence, I think it’s silly for people to espouse Brown’s greatness during his time in Philly only to then act like replacing him is no big deal. I’m not concerned about DeVonta Smith at all; I think he’s going to have a great season as the Eagles’ undisputed top target. But I do have questions about the other Eagles receivers. Dontayvion Wicks had an encouraging summer and he’s poised to…

title: Commanders punter Tress Way ‘pretty sure’ he’ll retire after 2026 NFL season
summary: Tress Way has been an institution in Washington for more than a decade. The Commanders claimed him off waivers back in 2014 and he has been their punter ever since, with a sterling track record that included three Pro Bowl selections and a second-team All-Pro nod.   That time playing for the Burgundy and Gold, […]
full_text: Tress Way has been an institution in Washington for more than a decade. The Commanders claimed him off waivers back in 2014 and he has been their punter ever since, with a sterling track record that included three Pro Bowl selections and a second-team All-Pro nod. That time playing for the Burgundy and Gold, or for anyone else, may be coming to an end. The 36-year-old told on-site reporters on Thursday afternoon that 2026 may be his final season. While he’s old by NFL player standards, Way remains at the top of his game and one of the best punters in the league. Way also said that he informed Commanders general manager Adam Peters and head coach Dan Quinn that he’s strongly considering retirement. He was clearly in a reflective mood during his Thursday meeting with media discussing the prospect of hangin’ em up. “The Pro Bowls are sweet. That’ll be — having that the rest of my life – the few jersey hanging up will be really special for me,” Way said to reporters, with video from NBC4’s JP Finlay . “This year, too, is special because I’m pretty sure this is my last season.” “I talked with AP and DQ and gave them a head’s up. I didn’t want to spring that on them. It’s one of those – I’m just taking it all in. I feel like someone’s cutting onions all the time around here.” Tress Way says he thinks this will be his last season pic.twitter.com/l4nLJA1CMF — JP Finlay (@JPFinlayNBCS) September 10, 2026 Way is a fan favorite for his special team ability and for his welcoming personality to the fan base, so even the thought of having to replace him will hit hard. He’s also popular in the locker room and he was just voted a team captain for the fifth time. 5-time captain 🥹 pic.twitter.com/ZkM0FyZT2d — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) September 9, 2026 It’s going to hit hard in the locker room to possibly lose the team’s longest-tenured player, as you can see here: Jeremy Reaves teared up when talking about Tress Way and his likely retirement. pic.twitter.com/raY48MADwH — Nicki Jhabvala (@NickiJhabvala) September 10, 2026 Way also told reporters how much he appreciated the Commanders fans for all of their support, especially a statistical anomaly that makes the rival Cowboys look bad. Way said he has felt wanted every year he’s been here and didn’t want to play anywhere else. He thanked the fans for how they’ve supported him and for reminding him that he has more passing yards in a conference championship than Dak Prescott — Zach Selby (@ZachSelbyWC) September 10, 2026 What are your thoughts on Tress Way most likely retiring at season’s end? title: Stefon Diggs ready to be part of Commanders offensive ‘engine’ right now
summary: The Commanders went through an arduous training camp with weeks of practice designed to push conditioning levels and work under near-constant stress tests.   Stefon Diggs didn’t experience every day of it, but Washington’s new receiver has been through enough to fully prepare for the regular season and put his stamp on this offense.   […]
full_text: The Commanders went through an arduous training camp with weeks of practice designed to push conditioning levels and work under near-constant stress tests. Stefon Diggs didn’t experience every day of it, but Washington’s new receiver has been through enough to fully prepare for the regular season and put his stamp on this offense. His Aug. 7 signing lifted the entire team, adding a needed offensive weapon and leadership element to this group. It has been easy to extoll his virtues and see how he has been a tone setter thus far. “Football IQ, very savvy, great vet, great locker room guy,” quarterback Jayden Daniels said in a Wednesday press conference . “Super competitive and he’s a dog, man. He wants the best, not for just himself, but everybody around him too.” Now we’re on the cusp of his Commanders debut, formally kicking off Sunday afternoon in Philadelphia. Diggs has produced everywhere he has gone, save a 2024 campaign in Houston cut short by a torn ACL. He has worked to build chemistry with Daniels and make the instant impact expected of someone with his resume. “It’s kind of being the engine of an offense,” Diggs told on-site reporters on Wednesday, via video from the Commanders . “You want to be one of the pieces of the engine at least and see that things go well.” Building chemistry with Daniels has gone well to this point. The quarterback and receiver have worked together a relatively limited time but are off to a solid start. Diggs considers it a “work in progress,” with he and Daniels “reaching for perfection.” David Blough is at the podium. Said he’s excited for Stefon Diggs and Jayden Daniels to show the chemistry they’ve worked on this weekend — Zach Selby (@ZachSelbyWC) September 10, 2026 Diggs has been around the block enough to understand what a young quarterback needs from a receiver. In a word: reliability. Diggs is good at providing that. He has had 1,000-plus yards in seven of the last eight seasons and a 70% reception rate when targeted, a number that peaked at 83% last year in New England. “I would say to have a knack for catching the ball, for being open — the space, timing, being where you’re supposed to be consistently and running good routes,” Diggs said. “When you have a knack for being in the right spot, it’s a little easier.” The veteran receiver once again called Daniels a “superstar,” then lauded his decisiveness and arm talent. Terry McLaurin also plays on the opposite side, which should even out coverage for both guys. "We want to be the engines of the offense" I asked Stefon Diggs how he and Terry McLaurin will compliment each other pic.twitter.com/hDNnoyrOri — Mitchell Tischler (@Mitch_Tischler) September 10, 2026 That’ll help increase his stat line, which has nothing to do with his goals for the season. “Just winning,” Diggs said. “That’s all I want to do.” What do you think Stefon Diggs provide against the Eagles, and what stat line will he produce in his first Commanders season? summary: The Daily Slop – 10 September 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Daily Slop – 10 September 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links all white for week one pic.twitter.com/LXBXzJNz7E — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) September 9, 2026 Articles The Athletic (paywall) The Commanders bet on David Blough’s ability to remake their offense — and teach it To be sure, professional football is primarily about physical strength and playing to the edge of mayhem — but with purpose and precision. As Washington guard Sam Cosmi puts it, “It’s really hard to mimic (the physicality required for) O-Line. If I did that in public, I’d be behind bars.” But it’s also about processing data, at an incredibly advanced rate, found within complex ideas. That requires someone who can teach those ideas and terminologies to players who learn in different ways and at different speeds. For the first time in his meteoric rise through the NFL’s coaching ranks, Blough is the primary instructor. Of all the bets the Commanders are making in this third season under general manager Adam Peters and head coach Dan Quinn, among the biggest is that their two new, first-time coordinators — Blough on offense and Daronte Jones on defense — can teach their systems, rapidly and completely and effectively, to their respective sides of the football, starting Sunday against the Philadelphia Eagles. Nothing much is riding on this, other than the success or failure of a multibillion-dollar franchise, centered around a once-in-a-generation quarterback in Jayden Daniels, and/or the head coach’s job security. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE The Athletic (paywall) NFC East roundtable: Eagles, Cowboys, Commanders enter critical seasons; Giants seek new culture Who’s the player not enough people are talking about who’s going to make a big impact for the team you cover? Jhabvala : Brandon Coleman. He’s received more attention lately, and that will only continue. Coleman replaced Tunsil at left tackle, a spot he played as a rookie in 2024. The Commanders shifted him inside to left guard last season — he was benched two games in — but moved him back to tackle when Tunsil got hurt. Coleman spent the offseason training with Tunsil and admitted he needed the experience to learn how to better take care of his body to try to avoid preventable nagging injuries. It’s impossible to truly replace Tunsil, but Coleman handled the transition well in training camp and is best-suited for the role among Washington’s linemen. If Coleman performs well, it could ultimately put him on track for a longer-term future in Washington. If he struggles, it could affect the entire offense, particularly Daniels. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Sports Illustrated Jayden Daniels Wants to Play Point Guard in Washington’s New Offense On Wednesday, Daniels was asked about the weapons around him: “I trust those guys to go out there and make plays. I love basketball,” Daniels said. “Just being a point guard, getting the ball to playmakers, the ball in space, and let them do their thing. When it’s time for me … to go get a bucket, I’ve got to go do that sometimes.” Clearly, Daniels’ killer mindset hasn’t changed while trying to focus on the new system over the last few months. The point-guard role Daniels mentions is a good comparison, since his job will be to create an explosive play without actually being the explosive play. Giving him Stefon Diggs and Chig Okonkwo alone on top of Terry McLaurin made his life 80% easier, as better surrounding talent will give Daniels more chances to turn ordinary completions into productive plays. The overall idea is for the offense to grow more from what happens after Daniels puts the ball in the right place, not from him creating everything himself. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders Roundtable Commanders vs Eagles: Three key matchups to watch SAF Nick Cross & LB Sonny Styles vs. RB Saquon Barkley & TE Dallas Goedert This is the matchup that will define Washington’s defense on Sunday. Saquon Barkley torched the Commanders for 132 rushing yards in their last meeting — gaining nearly 100 yards before contact in that game alone. Washington allowed the most yards before contact per run attempt of any defense in the league last season – a number Daronte Jones has made a specific emphasis to fix in his first year as defensive coordinator. That’s where Nick Cross comes in. The former Colts safety arrived this offseason ranked fifth among all defensive backs in the league with 46 stops resulting in negative EPA plays in 2025. His job on Sunday is to be the physical presence in the box that forces Barkley into the second level where linebackers can finish. If Cross plays assignment-sound football and Styles can process quickly enough to get off blocks, Washington can hold Barkley under 100. If either one freelances, Philadelphia may have their way in the running game. Goedert is the other half of this problem. The Eagles’ tight end set a career high with 11 receiving touchdowns last season — 10 of them in the red zone — on 60 catches for 591 yards. He caught a touchdown against Washington in their late-season meeting in 2025. Washington allowed the fourth-most fantasy points to tight ends of any defense last season, a damning statistic that this new defensive scheme under Jones was specifically designed to address. Sonny Styles’ coverage ability is the most important rookie trait on this entire defense — and his first real NFL test is matching up with one of the best red-zone tight ends in football. Styles has the athleticism to make this work. Whether a first-year linebacker executes it consistently against a veteran with a decade of NFL experience is the central question of Washington’s entire defensive game plan. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Riggo’s Rag 5 Commanders poised to catch the entire NFL off guard in 2026 Ben Sinnott – Commanders TE The Commanders are giving Ben Sinnott a chance to secure a bigger role under new offensive coordinator David Blough. Things have not gone according to plan for the 2024 second-round pick over the first two years of his time in Washington, but it’s also clear there was some friction between the tight end and previous play-caller Kliff Kingsbury. Sinnott’s taken some shots at Kingsbury’s offense throughout the summer. He didn’t feel like he got a fair shot, and Blough’s offense is bringing much more out of the Kansas State product. While the third-year pro is still behind Chig Okonkwo and blocking specialist John Bates, seeing the field more is more than feasible. Blough is expected to make more of the tight ends within his system. The more security blankets quarterback Jayden Daniels has, the quicker he’ll be able to get the football out. And even though Sinnott was used sparingly under Kingsbury, the stats show his reliability as a pass-catcher whenever targets come his way. It’s now or never for Sinnott. That’s not up for discussion. title: How will Commanders’ David Blough, Daronte Jones impact Eagles clash?
summary: The season’s just starting and the Washington Commanders have a massive NFC East clash right out of the gate. There’s no easing into a crucial 2026 campaign, with a road game in Philadelphia to start us off.   This longstanding rivalry is a passionate one, with little love for those on the other side. This Week […]
full_text: The season’s just starting and the Washington Commanders have a massive NFC East clash right out of the gate . There’s no easing into a crucial 2026 campaign, with a road game in Philadelphia to start us off. This longstanding rivalry is a passionate one, with little love for those on the other side. This Week 1 matchup is intriguing for all the mystery surrounding two teams that know each other well. Three of the four play callers are brand new, without a history in the job to draw from. Commanders offensive coordinator David Blough was promoted from within. Washington defensive coordinator Daronte Jones was hired away from Minnesota. Philadelphia brought new offensive coordinator Sean Mannion in from Green Bay. Incumbent Eagles DC Vic Fangio is about as creative as they come. So it’s fair to expect plenty of unscouted looks and surprise decisions as the three new guys start showing us what they’re all about. That brings us to the first question in a new Hogs Haven feature. It’s a reverse Q & A, if you will, where I bring up the topics and you address them in the comments. This story series will publish on a Thursday morning and I’ll update it that same evening by featuring some of the answers from the comments in the original story. We’ve added some of your answers to the story! Thanks to everyone for chiming in. Lots of great stuff in the comments: Question 1: Which new coordinator will have the biggest impact on this game? There are some good options, especially on the Commanders side. B&G Beatdown: Daronte Jones – Not only do I have high hopes for his system, but AP made a concerted effort to improve the talent on that side of the ball. Jones has the ingredients he needs to cook, and I think that’s what he’ll do. Hurts will be doing his best Drake Maye impression. Cheddar0806: Hard choice. The defense was disastrous last season, so I am going to go with Daronte Jones. If we can create some turnovers, then we have a chance to win this game. If not, it will be a tough start to win on the road. Question 2: What kind of impact do you expect Commanders rookie linebacker Sonny Styles to have on this game? What role will he have in his first (real) NFL game? Cheddar0806: I think he’s going to primarily be a middle-of-the-field eraser. We’ve had a liability in the middle for a while now (every opposing TE says thanks), but I think that ends with Styles. He has coverage ability and range we’ve been lacking for a while. Also I seem to recall reading that Mannion wanted to utilize the middle of the field more in his system, so heads up Sonny. Cheddar0806: I expect Styles to be solid in coverage. He has been very good in that category so far. His athletic traits allow for that to come pretty naturally. But the Eagles will test him early. They like to run the ball and Styles has struggled defending the run in the preseason. Question 3: Which Washington position group (no quarterbacks, please) will have the biggest impact on Sunday, and why? Eidolons: From my perspective, controlling the ball will be the deal make or break for the Skins in this game. I expect the passing game to function reasonably well. It comes down to the running game to control tempo of the game, create run/pass options and reduce risk if pass blocking isn’t there yet to support a deep passing threat (JD’s strength). That depends upon the o-line and the RB room working together. We have no idea how this will play out at this point – nothing in preseason. So, in my book, the pressure is really on Blough to make it happen. E Double: It’s a toss up between the front 7 and the C-LG combo. Can the front 7 commit to keeping Jalen Hurts in the pocket and staying disciplined in the run game, and can Allegretti and Paul open run lanes and keep Jayden clean? Question 4: We’ve heard nothing but good things about Jayden Daniels coming out of camp. What are your expectations for Washington’s quarterback heading into Week 1? SkinsaneAsylum: I expect Jayden Daniels to instantly remind people he is HIM. Full demon mode. The National Media stoking/provoking his elite competitive fire after the game was taken away from him last season…holy smokes get your popcorn ready. Abu Coletrane: IF the IOL holds up, I expect that he will have a big game, with a few explosive plays. I would expect that they offense may struggle to get things going initially, but hopefully knock some rust off and shock gthe Philthy fans. Question 5: Which Philadelphia Eagles player or matchup poses the biggest threat to a Commanders victory? SkinsaneAsylum: Jalen Carter/Jordan Davis pose the biggest threat on Sunday MarkTyler: Carter and Davis against Allegretti and Paul. This keeps me up at night! E Double: Saquon Barkley. Keep him reigned in and making Jalen Hurts beat you from the pocket is the way to beat this team. If Saquon has one of his typical big days against the Commies, it’s gonna get ugly.

title: Six NFL records that could be broken during the 2026 season
summary: Can a team break the NFL's rushing record? Will we see a new long in field goal kicking? Could there be a new single-season tight end receiving yardage mark?
full_text:
The 2026 NFL season is already here. Unfortunately, through two games, no NFL record has been broken. Boring!

 Last time we saw regular-season football, Myles Garrett was setting a single-season sack record (23) and Trey McBride was catching more passes (126) than any tight end in NFL history. With a 17-game season and rules skewed to favor offenses, it feels like more and more records are within reach every year.

 I wanted to find more NFL records that could be broken in 2026, so I went through a long list of candidates. Among them were:

 
 Highest average punt distance for a single season (the Cardinals' Blake Gillikin and Packers' Daniel Whelan both hit 51.7 yards per punt last season, tied for third all time). 
 Most receiving touchdowns in a game (Jerry Rice had five -- if it were four, I would have included it). 
 Most penalized team in NFL history (somehow the 17-game season isn't really affecting total penalty numbers). 
 
 After I ruled those out, I landed on a final six that could reasonably fall this season. There's some statistical reasoning for a few, some schematic considerations considered and some straight vibes rolled in. I want to see a 70-yard field goal. I want to root for a 70-yard field goal. Give me a 70-yard field goal!

 

 But let's start with a new receiving record for tight ends.

 Jump to a record: 
 Most TE receiving yards in a season  
 Most fourth-down conversions in a game 
 Most team rushing yards in a season 
 Longest field goal in NFL history 
 Highest completion percentage in a season 
 Most fumbles forced by a player in a season 

 

 Single-season receiving yards by a tight end 
 Current record holder:  Chiefs tight end  Travis Kelce (1,416 in 2020)

 We have entered a new era of high-volume receiving from tight ends.

 Last season, McBride was the Cardinals' only bright spot when he set a new single-season NFL record for tight end receptions with 126. He broke Zach Ertz 's record of 116 receptions, which Ertz accomplished in a 16-game season (7.25 receptions per game) as a member of the Eagles in 2018. McBride's 126 in a 17-game season was even enough to beat Ertz out on a per-game basis (7.41).

 Tight ends have cracked 100 receptions 13 times, and eight of them have come in the past six years. In 2024, the Raiders' Brock Bowers broke the record for all rookie receptions (not just tight ends) with his 112-catch season. As tight ends become better receivers and coordinators become more clever in featuring them, the inherent reliability of a tight end target lends itself to high reception totals. Just last season, TE targets had a 72% completion rate, while WR targets had a 62% completion rate.

 

 So why bet on the tight end receiving yardage total to be broken? While it is generally the case that tight ends are targeted closer to the line of scrimmage and can't create explosives downfield ... there are a few exceptions to the rule.

 Bears tight end Colston Loveland averaged 12.3 yards per reception over the course of the 2025 season in Ben Johnson's explosive-oriented offense -- that was third among all high-volume tight ends, and it doesn't even include his wild-card round explosion (eight catches, 137 yards) against the Packers. Because Loveland started the season slowly as a rookie coming off injury, he wasn't heavily targeted, accounting for 15.0% of the Bears' team targets relative to McBride's 27.4% with the Cardinals.

 I thought Bowers would be a second excellent candidate to set the arc here, but a late meniscus surgery has him out for at least the next couple of weeks. The good news is that Bowers is far from the only young, exciting tight end looking for a spike in receiving.

 Colts tight end Tyler Warren was on pace for over 1,000 yards last season before Daniel Jones fractured his fibula ahead of Week 12 and the offense suffered . With target sponge Michael Pittman Jr . off the Colts roster, Warren could more than pick up where he left off. Jaguars tight end Brenton Strange has always had the explosiveness (12.3 yards per reception) but never the volume (10.9% of the team's target share) -- but the Jaguars want  more multi-TE sets this year, which should open him up as he takes on fewer blocking assignments. Lions tight end Sam LaPorta now has offensive coordinator Drew Petzing, who was McBride's playcaller when he broke out as a high-volume pass catcher over the past two seasons. And the Cardinals have a new coaching staff as well -- maybe they'll think about McBride's role a little more vertically.

 I'm certain we'll see some candidates challenge the receptions record -- it's just too good of a time to be a pass-catching tight end in the NFL. But ... Kelce's 1,416 yards is a bit trickier to reach. Set in 2020 in the throes of Chiefs hype, Kelce benefitted from the ceiling-lifting speed of Tyreek Hill and the pass-happiness of head coach Andy Reid (and some of the greatest quarterback play in the history of the universe from Patrick Mahomes , of course). Even with an additional game, McBride was almost 200 yards off Kelce's total in 2025 -- he had more targets but he couldn't match Kelce for explosiveness.

 

 Every candidate we've discussed above has a weakness in his profile.

 Loveland should have explosiveness and volume within the Bears' passing game ... but Chicago runs it way more than those 2020 Chiefs did (they had the fifth-highest pass rate over expectation in the past 10 seasons, per NFL Next Gen Stats). LaPorta has the ceiling-lifting speedsters in receiver Jameson Williams and the right scheme for big explosives ... but will he get enough targets sharing time with Williams, receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown  and running back Jahmyr Gibbs ? Bowers should have the scheme, the volume and the big plays ... but will his quarterbacking quality be enough?

 

 If it were easy to break a record, it would happen every year. Of all the receiving records (yards, receptions and touchdowns) across all the positions (running back, receivers and tight ends) I know I want to be betting on tight end records to fall. Bowers broke one in 2024. McBride broke one in 2025. Kelce's total yardage may be the toughest nut to crack at the position, but this new wave of big-play tight ends has the constitution for it.

 
 Single-game fourth-down conversions 
 Current record holder: Los Angeles Chargers (six, 2021) and Dallas Cowboys (six, 2025)

 That's right: Two teams in NFL history have successfully converted on six fourth-down tries in a single game, and one was last season .

 You're forgiven for forgetting the finer details of the Cowboys' 30-23 Christmas Day win over the 4-11 Commanders, who were starting backup quarterback Josh Johnson . You were drowsy on eggnog anyway. But Dallas attempted and converted six fourth downs on the day, tying the 2021 Chargers (coached by Brandon Staley, the straw man of much fourth-down debate over the past several seasons) for the most in NFL history.

 Most of the Cowboys' fourth-down attempts were unspectacular. There was a fourth-and-1 from their own 44-yard-line on the first drive. On their second drive, another fourth-and-1 -- this one at midfield -- was quickly joined by a fourth-and-2 from the Commanders' 23 and a fourth-and-1 from the Commanders' 10. According to ESPN Research, that sequence is just the third drive in the past 45 years to start in the first quarter and have three fourth-down conversions. Two of the three were last season. We live in a different world.

 The Cowboys had another no-man's land conversion (fourth-and-2 from their own 45) late in the fourth quarter, then ended the game on a fourth-and-1 sneak to snag their sixth conversion.

 It took a unique day of near-conversions on third downs for the Cowboys, who never had to attempt a fourth down longer than 2 yards out. These auto-go situations on fourth-and-1s are why the single-game record is easily within reach. Even as teams attempt more fourth downs than ever before (3.3 per game in…

full_text:

We have Josh Allen vs. C.J. Stroud . We have Derrick Henry vs. Jonathan Taylor . And we have Packers vs. Vikings and Cowboys vs. Giants.

 We're here to get you ready for the action. First, our NFL Nation reporters take you inside the locker room with the best thing they heard this week, and ESPN Research provides a key stat to know. We also have Football Power Index (FPI) game projections, and Maldonado, Moody and Walder all give us final score picks for every game.

 Viewers rating (out of 10): 8.8.
