title: What is the oldest NFL stadium?
summary: Many different characteristics make NFL stadiums unique. Age is a hot topic among fans. Here's how stadiums stack up from oldest to newest.
full_text:
Originally opening in 1924, Soldier Field has served as the Chicago Bears ' stadium since 1971.

 Soldier is the NFL's oldest stadium by a large margin. But how much longer will the Bears call it home? Both Bears chairman George H. McCaskey and team president and CEO Kevin Warren have affirmed the organization's commitment to building a new fixed-roof stadium in Hammond, Indiana.

 Take a look at each NFL stadium, from oldest to newest, below: 

  

 Soldier Field, Chicago Bears , 1924 

 Since Soldier Field opened, it has been renovated a number of times -- most recently in 2003, which caused it to be delisted as a National Historic Landmark. The Bears played charity games there dating back to 1926, but the Chicago Cardinals were the first team to call Soldier Field their full-time home (in 1959). The Bears didn't move into Soldier Field full time until 1971.

 Lambeau Field, Green Bay Packers , 1957 

 Lambeau Field opened in 1957, and it's the oldest stadium that was built specifically to host an NFL team. It was originally called City Stadium, but renamed Lambeau Field in 1965 to honor Packers' founder, player and head coach Earl "Curly" Lambeau, who had just died. Lambeau led the Packers to six NFL championships. With 81,441 seats, it has the second-largest capacity among NFL stadiums.

 GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium, Kansas City Chiefs , 1972 

 GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium opened Aug. 12, 1972. It has been updated a number of times, including a $375 million renovation in 2010. With a seating capacity of 76,416, it's the fourth-largest stadium in the NFL. It was selected as one of several venues that hosted matches during the 2026 FIFA World Cup.

 Caesars Superdome, New Orleans Saints , 1975 

 The Caesars Superdome opened in 1975, initially under the name Louisiana Superdome. In addition to being the home of the New Orleans Saints, the Superdome has hosted countless big events, including eight Super Bowls (most recently in 2025), five NCAA men's basketball championships and the annual Sugar Bowl. 

 Hard Rock Stadium, Miami Dolphins , 1987 

 Hard Rock Stadium opened in 1987, and it's the home of the Miami Dolphins and Miami Hurricanes. It has hosted six Super Bowls, two World Series, four BCS National Championship Games, a College Football Playoff National Championship Game, the annual Orange Bowl and more. The stadium has had many names over the years, including Joe Robbie Stadium, Pro Player Park, Pro Player Stadium, Dolphins Stadium, Dolphin Stadium, Land Shark Stadium and Sun Life Stadium. The naming rights deal with Hard Rock Cafe extends through 2034.

 EverBank Stadium, Jacksonville Jaguars , 1995 

 EverBank Stadium is the seventh-oldest NFL stadium, yet it's not even 30. It opened in 1995, and has had quite a few names over the years, including Jacksonville Municipal Stadium, Alltel Stadium, EverBank Field and TIAA Bank Field. It hosted the Super Bowl in 2005. It's also the home of the annual Florida-Georgia rivalry game and the Gator Bowl.

 Bank of America Stadium, Carolina Panthers , 1996 

 Bank of America Stadium was built in Charlotte, North Carolina, in 1996, and it was renovated in 2007, 2014, 2019 and 2020. It is the home of the Carolina Panthers and Charlotte FC as well as the Duke's Mayo Bowl. It was originally known as Carolinas Stadium and then was called Ericsson Stadium from 1996 through 2004.

 Northwest Stadium, Washington Commanders , 1997 

 Originally known as Jack Kent Cooke Stadium, this stadium opened in 1997 and has been the home of the Washington team ever since. In the 2000s, the stadium had the largest seating capacity in the NFL (91,000). However, after the seating capacity was reduced in 2021, it now has the lowest in the league (58,000).

 M&T Bank Stadium, Baltimore Ravens , 1998 

 M&T Bank Stadium is the home of the Baltimore Ravens, but the stadium has also hosted the Army-Navy game, the Crab Bowl Classic (between Maryland and Navy) and more. The attendance record was set in 2012, when 71,547 people packed into the stadium to watch the Ravens defeat the Houston Texans in a divisional playoff game.

 Raymond James Stadium, Tampa Bay Buccaneers , 1998 

 From 1976 through 1997, the Tampa Bay Buccaneers played their home games at Tampa Stadium (aka The Big Sombrero). However, it became clear that the Bucs needed an upgrade, and Raymond James Stadium opened in 1998. The USF Bulls also play their home games at Ray J, and the stadium has been the site of three Super Bowls (including Super Bowl LV, which the Buccaneers won, becoming the first team to win the Lombardi Trophy in their own stadium). Perhaps the most famous aspect of this stadium is the replica pirate ship in the north end zone.

 Huntington Bank Field, Cleveland Browns , 1999 

 Huntington Bank Field opened in 1999 as "Cleveland Browns Stadium" and was known as "FirstEnergy Stadium" from 2013-2023. Huntington Bank Field and Allegiant Stadium (which opened in 2020) are the only venues that have never hosted a playoff game.

 Nissan Stadium, Tennessee Titans , 1999 

 Nissan Stadium opened in 1999, and it's the home of the Tennessee Titans and Tennessee State Tigers as well as the TransPerfect Music City Bowl. It was previously known as Adelphia Coliseum, the Coliseum and LP Field. The Titans' new enclosed 60,000-seat Nissan Stadium is on track to be completed around February 2027, with the team expected to move in for the 2027 season.

 Paycor Stadium, Cincinnati Bengals , 2000 

 Previously known as Paul Brown Stadium, Paycor Stadium opened in 2000 and has been the home of the Cincinnati Bengals ever since. In addition to hosting the Bengals' home games, Paycor Stadium also houses the team's practice and training facilities and administrative offices. The seating capacity is 65,515, and fans often refer to it as "The Jungle."

 Acrisure Stadium, Pittsburgh Steelers , 2001 

 Acrisure Stadium, previously known as Heinz Field, is the home of the Pittsburgh Steelers and Pittsburgh Panthers. The stadium opened in 2001, replacing Three Rivers Stadium. Acrisure Stadium has also hosted the NHL Winter Classic and NHL Stadium Series among other events.

 Empower Field at Mile High, Denver Broncos , 2001 

 Empower Field at Mile High opened in 2001, replacing Mile High Stadium. Mile High refers to the fact that Denver is 1 mile above sea level, which gives the Broncos a significant home-field advantage. Previously, this stadium went by many names, including Broncos Stadium at Mile High, Invesco Field at Mile High and Sports Authority Field at Mile High.

 Ford Field, Detroit Lions , 2002 

 In 2002, Ford Field opened and replaced the Pontiac Silverdome as the Detroit Lions' stadium. In addition to hosting the Lions, Ford Field is home of the USFL's Michigan Panthers, the Quick Lane Bowl, the Mid-American Conference championship game, the MHSAA state wrestling championships and the MCBA marching band state finals.

 Gillette Stadium, New England Patriots , 2002 

 Gillette Stadium opened in Foxborough, Massachusetts, on May 11, 2002. It was originally known as CMGI Field, but that lasted less than three months and then Gillette stepped in. In addition to the New England Patriots, Gillette Stadium is home of the New England Revolution of the MLS. It has hosted many notable playoff games thanks to the Patriots' Super Bowl runs, and it hosted several matches during the 2026 FIFA World Cup.

 Lumen Field, Seattle Seahawks , 2002 

 Lumen Field opened in July 2002 and in addition to being the home of the Seattle Seahawks, it's also where the Seattle Sounders (MLS), Seattle Sea Dragons (XFL) and OL Reign (NWSL) play their home games. It was previously named Seahawks Stadium, Qwest Field and CenturyLink Field before being renamed in 2020.

 NRG Stadium, Houston Texans , 2002 

 In addition to being the home of the Houston Texans, the Texas Bowl and the Houston Livestock Show, NRG Stadium was also the site of this year's CFP National Championship game.…

title: Springboks captaincy aside, RGR series proves Siya Kolisi is an all-time flanker great
summary: Siya Kolisi has not unanimously been recognised as a top-tier loose forward in the history of the game. If there was any doubt remaining, this series should have put that to bed.
full_text:
Siya Kolisi broke the record for Test wins as South Africa captain in Saturday's 29-24 win over New Zealand, but the Rugby's Greatest Rivalry (RGR) series has proven he is not only one of the greatest captains ever, but also one of the top flankers.

 Kolisi's 55th Test win as captain saw him officially surpass John Smit's 54 for the Springboks, but realistically, he cemented his legacy as the greatest Bok captain to date when he became the first to lift a second successive Rugby World Cup in 2023.

 Still, he has not unanimously been recognised as a top-tier loose forward in the history of the game. If there was any doubt remaining, this series should have put that to bed, and will be cemented in Baltimore on Saturday.

 

 Leadership aside, the difference between a Springbok side with and without Kolisi has been absolutely visible in pure rugby terms.

 In the first Test, the Boks started with a loose trio of Paul de Villiers, Pieter-Steph du Toit, and Jasper Wiese.

 They fared well in the first half, but Wiese aside, lost control in the second. Marco van Staden - who came on for de Villiers after the hour-mark - was yellow-carded late on, doing little to help the cause.

 Kolisi returned to the fold from injury for the second Test in Cape Town, scoring a crucial try and drawing a roar from the crowd with a huge hit on Ardie Savea as the latter received the ball at the back of a lineout.

 He made a huge contribution in the third Test, too - particularly on defence when the Boks were under the cosh during periods of the first half.

 

 On For the Love of Rugby , injury-embattled veteran Springbok prop Trevor Nyakane said: "If you sleep at a breakdown and Siya is around it, you best know he is going to put you on your back.

 "If you really understand the game that we play, things like that - donkey work - it's invaluable.

 "Most people don't see. You always see the guys that are scoring the tries, but you don't ask yourself: 'How did that space open up?'

 "It comes from guys like Siya who will be selfless in the team, in the structure - understanding that it's not him. We all drink from the same cup. When we win, it's not one person that won; it's South Africa that won."

 

 It is true that much of what Kolisi does goes unseen. However, the stats alone are increasingly beginning to favour the argument for the 35-year-old going down as one of the game's all-time greats in his position.

 Only seven players playing predominantly as flankers have ever reached 110 Test caps: Richie McCaw, Pablo Matera, Michael Hooper, Alessandro Zanni, Peter O'Mahony, Ardie Savea, and George Smith.

 Kolisi (currently on 106) is on course to become the eighth by the end of this year if he stays fit. McCaw is the only one among the seven flankers with 110 caps to have ever won a World Cup - captaining the All Blacks to victory in 2011 and 2015.

 For a flanker to have the consistency of Kolisi in an elite team puts him in almost unparallelled territory. Being drafted into a series against the All Blacks after missing the first Test through injury and having such a clear impact aged 35 should see him honoured as world class in pure rugby terms alone.

 He may have avoided placing himself among the game's all-time greats when he discussed the topic in his 2021 autobiography "Rise". However, much has changed since then.

 Kolisi won a second World Cup. Then, he endured a difficult 2023-24 season with Racing 92 and announced later in 2024 that he would be getting divorced - but still won Rugby Championship titles in 2024 and 2025 even amid the personal turmoil.

 In November 2025, he made it to 100 Springbok caps, and in 2026, he has played an instrumental role in salvaging the RGR series - which will either end in a draw or a Springbok win.

 Kolisi will undoubtedly be honoured alongside McCaw as one of the game's greatest ever captains. When its greatest ever flankers are listed, both belong at the top.

full_text:
Deep sighs. Long pauses. Cracked voices.

 Twenty-five years later, it's still hard for some in the NFL community to talk about the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks -- any community, for that matter. The pain and trauma from the tragedies in New York; Washington, D.C.; and Shanksville, Pennsylvania, will be felt for generations.

 Like the rest of the country, the NFL was reeling in the aftermath. Players, coaches and officials were gripped by grief, fear and confusion -- raw emotions that gradually shifted over the course of 12 tumultuous days.

 

 By the time they resumed games on Sept. 23 -- a hiatus that included intense, behind-the-scenes meetings on when it was appropriate to play football again -- the league had experienced a look-in-the-mirror moment that many believe set up a return that was galvanizing for the nation.

 To commemorate the anniversary, ESPN is sharing the 9/11 experiences of more than a dozen people: Players, coaches, team officials, a league official and a fan who believes his love for the New York Giants saved his life.

 Their memories are vivid. They remember the sense of pride born from the restorative healing process, and they remember the profound sadness.

 Chris Mara, now a top Giants executive and a member of the Mara family that founded the franchise, began his interview with an apology.

 "Please bear with me, this isn't going to be easy. I lost four close friends that day," he said, clearing his throat. "But we'll get through it."

 A quarter-century later, the effects are still felt, but we examine how they got through the trying times -- along with the lasting impact.

 Jump to a section: 
 'All hell broke loose' 
 'Some things I wish I had never seen' 
 'We're not going to play' 
 'There wasn't a dry eye' 
 'The best in people' 

 

 

 

 'All hell broke loose' 
 The NFL was waking up on a Tuesday (the day off for players) when, in the span of 51 minutes on a brilliantly sunny day, three hijacked planes struck the north and south towers of the World Trade Center and the Pentagon. At 10:03 a.m., four minutes after the first of the two towers collapsed, United Flight 93 from Newark, New Jersey, crashed in a field near Shanksville as passengers fought a valiant battle against the hijackers. 

 The New York Jets , based on Long Island at the time, were only 20 miles from the Towers. The Giants, who lost the night before in Denver, arrived at Newark on a red-eye shortly before Flight 93 took off and about 90 minutes before the first tower was hit. Some in their traveling party exited the airport via the United terminal. 

 What follows is an oral history, with accounts from people who were there (titles from 2001). 

 Ernie Accorsi, Giants general manager: We didn't find out until later that the gate next to ours was the terrorist plane, the one that crashed in Pennsylvania. [Giants personnel] walked right by that plane boarding.

 Michael Strahan, Giants player: It kind of messes with your mind because you realize at the time that we were leaving the airport, walking through the terminal, people were going to get on these flights that we all know did not end well.

 Tiki Barber, Giants player: I lived on the Upper East Side of Manhattan when I was playing. I remember getting home, my wife was at work, I was home by myself. You started to hear rumblings from people texting you or calling you. I didn't answer my phone because I wanted to go to sleep. I kept getting these phone calls, phone calls, phone calls, text messages.

 Eventually I answered one and they said, "Turn on your TV, this is crazy. Are you OK?"

 Herm Edwards, Jets coach: I can remember sitting in my office. It was a beautiful day. From my office, you could always see planes going to LaGuardia.

 Around when 9/11 happened, I didn't see any planes. I was like, "That's strange. Why are there no planes in the air?" Usually, you see them. It didn't sound right. It didn't look right. I turned the television on, and when I turned the television on, I saw it. I'm like, "Are you kidding me?"

 Vinny Testaverde, Jets player: A bunch of us were watching it unfold on TV in the trainers' room, and you could see guys getting nervous and talking about what the possibilities were.

 Shortly after that, everyone took off and went home. I remember calling my wife on the way home, telling her to get the kids out of school. We were all nervous, on edge.

 Strahan: I was at home, Montclair, New Jersey, sleeping. Phone rings, pick up the phone and someone says, "Look out the window." And from where I lived, I had a view of the entire Manhattan skyline. I looked out the window, and I saw smoke coming from the first tower.

 Jason Garrett, Giants player: We lived on 79th Street and West End Avenue. ... I think I fell asleep and then I just started hearing these fire trucks going by our window. And it's like sirens and trucks and sirens and trucks. And I'm thinking to myself, "What the hell is going on?"

 Joe Andruzzi, New England Patriots player: I was sitting in a dentist's chair and heard on the radio that a plane hit the towers. So not thinking anything of it, I got back in my car. By then, the second plane had hit and it was all commotion on the radio.

 When I finally realized what the hell was really going on, my heart was in my throat. I just had a gut feeling that one, if not two or three of my brothers [members of the FDNY] were all a part of it.

 Damien Woody, Patriots player: I was in shock at what I was watching, unfolding on television -- an attack on our country, on American soil. That's something I had never seen before. It was surreal, watching everything unfold in real time.

 Accorsi: All hell broke loose. From our practice field [in East Rutherford, New Jersey], you could see the towers smoking.

 Dave Szott, Washington player: I was home in Morristown [New Jersey]. Marty Schottenheimer was the coach and he let me have Monday and Tuesday off with my family. From the hill in my neighborhood, you could see the towers burning. We couldn't get a hold of my brother, Kevin, who was working in Building 5 [at the World Trade Center]. To complicate matters, my brother is visually impaired. He's legally blind. ... So now I have a visually impaired brother we can't get a hold of, possibly involved directly.

 Mara: My daughter, Kate [an actress] was headed to L.A. from New York on an American Airlines flight that left basically when all the other planes that crashed took off. We went through many hours of trying to figure out where she was and was she being affected by this? Were there going to be any more planes that it was going to happen to? We had no idea. It was pretty hairy.

 Barber: I didn't know what to do. I always kind of know what to do. I'm aware, I feel like I can see things, I understand things. I had no idea what to do and I felt lost.

 Kevin Mawae, Jets player: There are people who can tell you exactly where they were when JFK was shot. I know exactly where I was when the Challenger blew up in '86. There are defining moments in people's lives that change the entire world. You remember those things with clarity that's [unbelievable]; 9/11 is the same way.

 Garrett: The world was about to change.

 

 

 

 'Some things I wish I had never seen' 

 More than 3,000 people were killed in the attacks. NFL teams returned to work the following day for practice even though there was uncertainty on whether the Week 2 games would be played. It was a time for reflection. 

 In the ensuing days, the Jets and Giants boarded buses and visited Ground Zero to deliver supplies and boost the morale of rescue workers. The Washington players went to Arlington National Cemetery for a memorial service. Players visited fire departments, police stations and hospitals. 

 Some waited anxiously to hear from loved ones. Everywhere there were chilling reminders of what had occurred.

title: Commanders' crab stuffed pretzel headlines new NFL 2026 foods
summary: The latest NFL season has no shortage of unique concession items that will debut across stadiums.
full_text:
When it comes to the NFL, the league seems to level up each season. The same applies to foods debuting at league stadiums.

 

 Arguably the best from any team is a crab stuffed pretzel sold at Northwest Stadium, home of the Washington Commanders . The crab-shaped pretzel is filled with lemon tarragon crab dip topped with garlic butter and grated parmesan cheese created by Levy Restaurants.

 

 Here's a look at some of the top new foods at NFL stadiums this season.

 

 Pittsburgh Steelers : Black N' Gold Chicken and Waffle 

 The iconic colors of the Steelers are represented in a classic Southern meal that includes fried chicken, coleslaw, bacon jam, sweet potato fries and hot honey.

 

 

 Philadelphia Eagles : Tush Push Taters 

 Philadelphia fans have seen their share of success with the tush push in recent years. Now, the play has a meal named after it. The item consists of a deep-fried potato with a fried chicken cutlet, mac and cheese, bacon hot honey jam, scallions and 215 sauce.

 

 

 Eagles: Broad Street Beast 

 Now available at Lincoln Financial Field is an 18-inch chalupa shell that includes wagyu beef shank, fried jalapeno poppers, tomatillo avocado salsa, Oaxaca queso, shallots and cilantro.

 

 

 Cincinnati Bengals : Who Dey Sausage 

 The Bengals' "Who Dey" chant is the namesake for a 24-inch BBQ cheddar pork sausage served on a bun with pickled red onions, jalapeno and BBQ sauce.

 

 

 Carolina Panthers : The Big 'Dilla 

 The two-foot smoked adobo chicken quesadilla includes a cheddar and jack cheese seared tortilla plus cilantro, pico de gallo and chipotle crema.

 

 

 Denver Broncos : Beast in a Blanket 

 Denver's take on a two-foot item is a hot dog with brisket burnt ends, cheddar and goat cheese wrapped in a puff pastry. It's topped with secret sauce, avocado cream, pickled onions and jalapeno.

 

 

 Houston Texans : Battle Red Berry Bird 

 Houston rocks battle red uniforms, therefore, it's only right that a concession item named after the threads is created. Fried chicken breast is tossed in a strawberry buffalo sauce and topped with coleslaw, pickles and Cajun cheese curds on a challah bun.

title: NFL Week 1 latest intel, buzz questions, news, fantasy tips
summary: What should we expect from Patrick Mahomes? How will the Raiders handle their QB situation? Which receivers could break out? Our insiders have Week 1 intel.
full_text:
As we hit Week 1 of the  2026 NFL season , league insiders Jeremy Fowler and Dan Graziano have been making calls to sources around the league for the latest news and notable buzz.

 What should we expect from Patrick Mahomes and other players returning from significant injuries in the early parts of the season? Which teams might be flying under the radar and could surprise? Where are the most interesting and uncertain quarterback situations around the NFL? And for all those fantasy football managers out there, which players might come out of nowhere in Week 1?

 It's all here, as Jeremy and Dan answer big questions and empty their reporting notebooks with everything they are hearing heading into the 2026 campaign.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Injury comebacks | Playoff sleepers 
 QB situations to watch | Breakouts 
 More notes, intel entering Week 1 

 
 

 Which player returning from a significant injury is best set up for a strong comeback? 
 Graziano: Let's start with the biggest name: Mahomes. He tore the ACL  in his left knee late enough last season that many wondered if he'd play at all in the early part of the 2026 season. But it was clear early in camp that he attacked his rehab and would be ready to go in Week 1. We should see him Monday night against the Broncos, and though the injury to left tackle Josh Simmons does give me a little pause, I think there's reason to believe the Chiefs' offense will be better around Mahomes.

 

 Kansas City replaced Matt Nagy with Eric Bieniemy at offensive coordinator, which doesn't seem like a big change given Bieniemy's history there, but the Chiefs also changed out several other offensive assistants. And they are counting on a fully healthy Xavier Worthy , a ( hopefully ) fully healthy and engaged Rashee Rice and newly signed running back Kenneth Walker III to make them more explosive. I have the Chiefs bouncing back and reclaiming the AFC West title.

 Fowler: What helps Mahomes is a supporting cast that seems improved, especially if rookies Emmett Johnson and Cyrus Allen ascend, although Simmons' injury also gives me pause. But Mahomes is well-positioned to win Comeback Player of the Year. He hears the noise, the hint of doubt about his place in the QB pantheon for the first time in his career. I expect him to respond accordingly -- with a big season.

 But he isn't the only QB on the comeback trail. Jayden Daniels can reclaim his place as a premier quarterback, and there's considerable hype in league circles that Daniels will get back on track and be a problem for the rest of the NFC East. Kyler Murray has everything he needs in Minnesota to succeed if he can maximize Kevin O'Connell's offense.

 Graziano: I believe Daniels is a fantastic player and will play well as long as he's healthy. I have significant concerns about the group around him, particularly his offensive line, capping his (and the team's) performance ceiling this season. Hopefully for their sake I'm wrong.

 Some guys who I think are good enough to win Comeback Player of the Year if they come back healthy and play are:

 
 Giants wide receiver  Malik Nabers  if he helps to elevate Jaxson Dart and the Giants to playoff contender status 
 Packers edge rusher Micah Parsons if Green Bay makes a second-half defensive turnaround and a playoff run once he returns 
 Jaguars receiver/cornerback  Travis Hunter  if he plays like a lockdown corner and catches, say, three touchdown passes on offense. The Jags playing well again also would help. 
 
 Fowler: Parsons could provide a timely October lift for the Packers to contend. And the way Jacksonville plans to use Hunter -- as a primary zone corner and a "package" receiver -- will showcase his splash-play ability.

 And let's not forget about 35-year-old Aaron Donald . No, he's not returning from an injury, but he is unretiring -- and he will be a major force if he can get to 80% of his previous play. Interior rushers have proved they can play well into their mid-30s (see  Cameron Heyward  and Calais Campbell ). The sheer talent around Donald should free up rushing lanes and one-on-one opportunities. Still, the ramp-up will take some time. The Rams are sitting him this week , and returning after two-plus years out of football is no small feat. Part of the Rams' plan will be to keep Donald fresh for December and January snaps. That's the right strategy -- even if that sacrifices early-season sack numbers.

 

 

 
 Based on your preseason conversations, which team could be a real playoff sleeper? 
 Fowler: Sleepers are harder to find because of the league's deep parity, but let's go with the Giants, who won only four games last season. An NFL truism remains that you win with line play, and the Giants have that. They finally found an offensive line combination that works, resulting in a top-five rushing offense last season. The defensive line is well-stocked, even without defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence II . Dart is widely viewed as a quarterback with an upward trajectory. Add the John Harbaugh confidence boost and Nabers' imminent return , and New York might have something. So, give me the Giants as a sneaky NFC playoff team.

 Graziano: The people I talk to seem to agree with you somewhat on the Giants. Those who buy into Dart as a real NFL starting QB point out how good they look up front on defense and that the offense has plenty to work with if Nabers is truly healthy. Those who doubt Dart are obviously more hesitant to back the Giants as sleepers.

 But, in general, I agree with you in that it's tough to find many true "sleepers" -- as in, teams most people don't think will be good but could end up being good. I keep talking myself into the Jets having a passable offense and maybe even a good one, but I don't expect them to contend with Buffalo and New England in the AFC East. I do think we will be talking about them as a potentially good spot for a rookie QB to land next spring.

 I'm going to stretch the definition a bit: I think people are sleeping on just how good the Jaguars can be. Jacksonville was 13-4 last season, won nine of its final 10 regular-season games and ended up winning the AFC South. It seems as if a lot of people have already conceded that division to the Texans, but it wouldn't surprise me to see Jacksonville build on last season's progress under Liam Coen, repeat as division champs and make a playoff run.

 Fowler: The Jaguars are deep and will be able to move the ball. Their three-man receiving corps is among the league's best. The offensive line faces questions -- it's lacking ideal size and has had some injuries. But Coen made it work with that group last season and should again.

 

 Your point on the Jets is a fair one -- I was there for camp and the roster is better. But the Jets haven't won eight or more games since 2015, so it's tough to bank on them until they show it. But here's a snoozefest of a sleeper, if we're going that deep: the Browns.

 I'm not declaring that Cleveland will make the playoffs just yet, but there's legitimate talent on both sides of the ball. The defense has a chance to be stout. Resources were spent to replenish the line. The offense is well-stocked with intriguing young talent. If Deshaun Watson 's play graduates from poor to passable, Cleveland might be in decent shape in Todd Monken's first season .

 Graziano: If Watson had played passably in 2022, 2023 or 2024, Monken probably wouldn't be there, because Kevin Stefanski probably would have kept his job. We haven't seen Watson play well since 2020, so I'm going to have to see a lot of success from Watson/Cleveland before I believe it.

 I also need to point out that while many seem to see the NFC West as a two-team race (or even a one-team race!), the 49ers should be a threat to win that division if they can keep everyone healthy ( I know, I know ). They were still in the hunt for the division title and the NFC's No. 1 seed in Week 18 last season despite their injury issues. If San Francisco…

title: Why Cowboys see DC Christian Parker's youth as an X factor
summary: Parker is the youngest DC in Cowboys history and is tasked with turning around the NFL's worst defense from last season.
full_text:
FRISCO, Texas -- When Christian Parker was gripped tight by the profession of coaching, he wrote down his goals on a piece of paper.

 He started coaching at Virginia State -- a historically Black Division II university in Petersburg -- when he was 21, younger than some of the players, but he had it all mapped out, hoping to manifest what would be a lifelong path in football.

 "It was like, 'I want to be this by 25. This by 30,'" Parker said. "I didn't think I was maybe going to get into the league until I was 35 years old because there's one of only 32 teams. It's hard to get the internships, and how are you going to make those connections?

 "And then you start getting going and you realize that those timelines don't matter. It's bigger than that. And it's just about putting the work in and trusting God and obviously taking advantage of opportunities when they're presented to you."

 Thirteen years later, one year before he thought he would get into the NFL, Parker, 34, is the youngest defensive coordinator in the history of the Dallas Cowboys .

 The success of the Cowboys' 2026 season, which starts Sunday against the New York Giants  ( 8:20 p.m. ET, NBC ), could largely hinge on what Parker does for a defense that was staggeringly poor last season -- allowing the most points in the NFL and finishing 30th in yards allowed.

 The changes have been enormous. The Cowboys switched to a 3-4 front, could have as many as 14 new key contributors compared to Week 1 last year, and there is only one coach remaining from the 2025 defensive staff (J.J. Clark). 

 Despite Parker's age and relative inexperience -- his first NFL job was as the Green Bay Packers ' defensive quality control coach in 2019 -- Dallas believes its new coordinator is ready to turn the defense around.

 "When I handicap age, I can certainly value the experience, but I can also value the youthful qualities that you have of never having done it before and want to show them," owner and general manager Jerry Jones said. "And I think that's a comparable edge."

 

 

 PARKER'S HIRING ALMOST did not happen. He was the ninth of Dallas' nine Zoom interviews.

 The Cowboys were down the road with a couple of candidates, including Daronte Jones, then the Minnesota Vikings ' defensive passing game coordinator, who was viewed by a few in Dallas' organization as the front-runner to replace Matt Eberflus, who was fired in January. (Jones is now the Washington Commanders ' DC.)

 "Actually, I really didn't want to do it," coach Brian Schottenheimer said. "I felt really good about the candidates, but a few people, [game management coordinator] Ryan Feder being one of them, said, 'Hey, you need to do this,' because Christian had been on my radar for a while.

 "First interview was great, but it wasn't until probably that we got him in the building and saw him in front of the room."

 Parker stood in a meeting room at The Star, the Cowboys' headquarters, and went through a defensive install as if he was talking to players. They wanted Parker to coach them like he would the players.

 

 Schottenheimer and eight to 12 others in the room, including vice president of player personnel Will McClay, were transfixed. A coach with only four years of experience coaching defensive backs owned the moment as if he had been called to do it.

 "It became very apparent that he would be a great hire," Schottenheimer said.

 Parker's age came up during interview processes over the years, but he felt it was more about how he would deal with coaching players who were older than him, not his expertise. He would win that argument with his detail, his memory, his confidence.

 "I don't know anything else because I've always been young," Parker said. "So maybe I'll be able to answer that in 20 years or so. But, yeah, sometimes it comes up and I think that at the end of the day, players want you to be able to help them get better. And they want to know that you care about their development, you care about winning. I think that no matter what your age is, that's all that matters."

 Derrick Ansley, the Cowboys' defensive passing game coordinator, first met Parker at the scouting combine in 2021 in Indianapolis at an annual dinner among the league's defensive backs coaches. Parker was going into his first year as the Denver Broncos ' defensive backs coach. Ansley was coaching the Los Angeles Chargers secondary at the time.

 "He was a stud back then. He's a bigger stud now," Ansley said. "Very well spoken. He's a connector. He's done a really good job of leading the staff and defining our roles, and that's gone down to the players. He can relate to those guys."

 

 

 IN 2022, MARCUS Dixon was in his first year as the Broncos' defensive line coach and he immediately gravitated to Parker. They discussed then that whenever Parker became a coordinator, Dixon would join his staff.

 "He's always been ready for the moment," said Dixon, who is now Dallas' defensive line coach.

 Dixon said Parker's superpower is his memory.

 "His recall is crazy. Plays, players, situations that might've happened years before, things he might've saw on tape, it's pretty incredible," Dixon said. "And then it's this way of communicating with the staff and with the players of what he wants it to look like, and he's also being collaborative. He's the ultimate team guy, but he's very clear and precise on what he wants."

 

 Parker was a two-time All-District cornerback at Battlefield High School in Haymarket, Virginia. He also played basketball. He went to Richmond to play cornerback, but by his sophomore year, he was moved to wide receiver because of injuries on that side of the ball. He became something of a coach to the receivers, giving them tips on what a defender would do.

 That, along with his work in summer football camps at Richmond, solidified the thought of coaching being his life's work.

 When asked about his influences over the years, Parker did not mention any coaches first. He talked about his parents, Cleveland and Donna. His dad worked in construction sales in Richmond and Manassas, Virginia. His mother was a personal trainer and aerobics instructor.

 Parker mentioned Ernest McGowen, his campaigns and elections professor in his junior year at Richmond.

 "The way he compartmentalized information and taught me was real important," Parker said.

 Then Parker listed off 10 coaches from college to the NFL, including Eagles defensive coordinator Vic Fangio, having spent the past two seasons as Philadelphia's defensive passing game coordinator and defensive backs coach.

 "I'm missing a lot of them, but there's been a lot of high-level teachers I've been around," Parker said.

 Part of teaching is knowing the student. How do they learn best? Some might need to see it on film. Others might need to write it down. Others might need to go through a walk-through. For others it comes through studying on their own.

 He uses Kahoot, a tool that elementary and middle school teachers use to create quizzes, for the players. On the field, he will have one-on-one sessions with players, going through intricacies of body lean from a receiver and how a defensive back should respond to hand placement when attacking a blocker.

 "You want to try to be as diverse with the teaching style as possible, so it's hitting the brains of each student in the room," Parker said.

 

 

 SCHOTTENHEIMER KNOWS WHAT Parker is about to go through. He was 32 when he became the coordinator for the New York Jets in 2006.

 In recent years, the league has trended toward using younger offensive minds as head coaches and coordinators. Kellen Moore became the Cowboys' offensive coordinator in 2019 when he was 32. Dak Prescott had a then-career-high 30 touchdown passes in their first year together. There are eight offensive coordinators younger than Parker, but only two defensive coordinators: Sean Duggan, 33, with the Miami Dolphins and Nick Rallis, 33, with the Arizona…

title: Can Goff, new-look Lions offense set aside disappointing 2025?
summary: After tumbling from playoff contention last season, Detroit promises a team focused on the prize in 2026.
full_text:
DETROIT -- For months, Jared Goff has fielded non-stop questions concerning the  Detroit Lions ' disappointing 2025 season.

 The veteran quarterback and his teammates will finally have a chance to put the past to rest, which Goff feels is fueling them collectively as they enter Week 1.

 "Yeah, I think so. I think it adds a little bit of a chip on your shoulder, but I think we're pretty internally motivated and want to win a championship and want to be the last team standing," Goff said. "And I think last year is a bad taste, but we've got however many chances in front of us now to go make a right."

 

 Goff and the Lions will open the 2026 season with a home contest against the New Orleans Saints on Sunday. Both teams missed the playoffs last season, have a lot to prove, and have plenty of new faces on their rosters, which adds another level of uncertainty to this early matchup.

 In a symbolic gesture, Lions wide receiver Jameson Williams  chopped his dreadlocks off on Wednesday night in anticipation of the new season, ringing in the new campaign with a new hairstyle.

 "I think it's been behind us since last season. We talked about it and we've been off of it since last year. We've been on to bigger and better things," said Williams, who is coming off back-to-back 1,000-yard seasons. "Focusing more on this year and what we've got coming up this week. New Orleans is coming in and we're just trying to get a win."

 Detroit is entering this year with a 40% chance to win the NFC North, according to ESPN Analytics, which is the highest of any team in the division. The Saints finished just 6-11 in 2025.

 Still, Lions running back  Jahmyr Gibbs isn't allowing himself to buy into those early narratives.

 "It's going to be a good game. Every team can win any given Sunday. You know that so we're not going to take anybody lightly," Gibbs said. "No matter what record they had. I mean, we didn't make the playoffs either, so I mean, they probably look at it the same way. It's going to be fun. It's going to be tough fight, but we look to win every time."

 The Lions used the offseason to sharpen their weaknesses.

 Goff, for instance, worked to develop a bond with first-year offensive coordinator Drew Petzing, which gives the QB confidence the team will be better this year than last season. For his part, Petzing said he isn't afraid to hold Goff accountable either -- or vice versa.

 

 "He's doing the same to me, asking questions, making, 'Hey, we thought about this? Do we have an answer to that? Can we do this?' I think that back and forth has been fun," Petzing said of Goff. "It's part of the job that I love, but it also makes us better."

 After failing to reach the postseason for the first time since 2022, Detroit could benefit from the league's second-easiest schedule in 2026.

 After entering their Week 8 bye with a 5-2 record last season, the Lions went 4-6 over the final 10 games. From Week 6 onward, Detroit did not win consecutive games the rest of the way.

 Lions edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson  said nothing about last year will be carried into the upcoming season.

 "I've never been like a big chip guy. I'm more just, man, like, I don't dwell on the past too much," Hutchinson said. "I see the potential that we have, and we've had that for a few years now. So, whatever's happened in the past is forgotten and we're just going to focus everything we have on this year."

title: Career reboots: Vikings' Murray faces Packers' Gannon
summary: Jonathan Gannon coached Kyler Murray with the Cardinals, and now they seek second chances with new teams.
full_text:
The beauty of the NFL's opening weekend is the unknown. 

 With no tape to study of previous games, the Green Bay Packers will have to guess how the Minnesota Vikings might deploy new quarterback Kyler Murray on Sunday at U.S. Bank Stadium ( 4:25 p.m. ET, CBS ). The Vikings, in turn, can only project how new Packers defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon will scheme to stop them. 

 That Murray played for Gannon from 2023 to 2025, when Gannon was head coach of the  Arizona Cardinals , is mere coincidence in what might be the determinative schematic battle of the game. 

 "I'd say he knows exactly, probably, what [Murray] likes and doesn't like," Packers coach Matt LaFleur said of Gannon. "But it's a different scheme, a different system. There's 10 other guys out there, and I think that's a pretty good supporting cast he's got around him. There's a lot of playmakers out there. I think their O-line is one of the better O-lines in the league, so they've got a lot of talent around him." 

 Sunday's game represents a fresh start for both parties. 

 

 They were a coach-QB pairing for three years, which ended after last season. Murray did not play after Week 5 because of a foot injury, and Gannon was fired after going 15-36 in his first NFL head coaching job.

 Gannon landed in Green Bay to replace defensive coordinator Jeff Hafley, who became the Miami Dolphins ' head coach. Murray signed with the Vikings after the Cardinals released him in March and won a training camp competition with J.J. McCarthy for the starting job. 

 Thursday, Murray called Gannon "one of my favorite coaches. ... Transparent. Believed in his players no matter the circumstances."

 Not long after the preseason ended and attention turned fully to the opener, LaFleur was asked how much he will rely on Gannon to prepare for Murray and the Vikings. 

 "I think J.G. is leaning on J.G. to prepare for that," LaFleur said. 

 Murray displayed his live arm and elite open-field ability during Minnesota's training camp this summer, but his most notable struggles came when facing heavy pressure. By coincidence -- or perhaps not -- those present for Packers training camp were struck by how regularly Gannon's defenders were working on their blitz packages.

 

 Gannon could have taken a year off after he was let go by the Cardinals. He had two years left on his contract and would have been paid handsomely to do nothing. Another year in Arizona and it would match the longest he's lived in one place since his first NFL coaching job with the Falcons in 2007. 

 Instead, he waited exactly 20 days to take another job. 

 "Very grateful for the opportunity," Gannon said this week. "Put all our energy and effort into maximizing it, I know that."

 Some vagabond coaches prefer to set up a home base in one place and let their family have some sense of stability in an unstable business. Not Gannon. His wife, Gina, and their three children, Rocco, Lola and Angelo, moved with him in an indication that his stay in Green Bay might be more than a one-year stint. 

 "My eighth NFL city," Gannon said as a matter of fact.

 "They're here, they're loving life," Gannon said of his family. "They're loving life. ... School's been awesome. It's been good."

 

 LaFleur loved the idea of having another head coach on his staff, something he previously had with special teams coordinator Rich Bisaccia, even if Bisaccia was only interim head coach of the Raiders for part of a season.

 LaFleur did not set out to hire Hafley 2.0 despite the success Hafley, the former Boston College head coach, had in his two seasons with the Packers before he was hired by the Dolphins. 

 "I had a pretty good idea of the man we were getting when we got him," LaFleur said of Gannon. "He understands football. He understands offensive football, which I think is imperative when you're in one of those roles -- you'd better know the other side of the ball. And he understands the importance of trying to give similar looks and have different things off of that.

 "So I think he does a great job. He's a great communicator. He holds these guys to a high standard now."

 From the players' perspective, the transition from Hafley to Gannon has been smooth. As well-liked as Hafley was, players have taken to Gannon just as quickly. Player after player has raved about Gannon's energy, innovation and scheme. 

 No one seems to care about the lack of success by Gannon in Arizona. 

 "I see why they [brought] him in here," Packers cornerback Keisean Nixon said. 

 If one thing has stood about Gannon so far, it's his willingness to adjust. 

 

 His defenses in Arizona, run by coordinator Nick Rallis, did not feature much blitzing. In fact, the Cardinals had the lowest blitz rate in the league among the 32 teams during Gannon's first season (2023) and then ranked 17th and 19th in blitz rate the following two seasons. When Gannon was the coordinator with the Philadelphia Eagles , his defenses ranked 30th and 22nd in blitz rate. 

 Yet the most noticeable thing about Gannon's defense this summer in training camp was how often -- and with so many different players -- that he blitzed. Gannon blitzed linebackers Edgerrin Cooper and Zaire Franklin up the middle, brought cornerbacks off the edge and safeties from the slot.

 Murray's struggles against the Vikings' blitz packages in camp are relevant and reflect his performance against it in recent seasons. Looking at a recent sample size, beginning with the 2024 season, Murray's QBR against the blitz (65) is slightly below the NFL average (69). 

 

 In Minnesota this summer, public attention focused more on McCarthy's fate and future than it did on Murray, the 2019 No. 1 draft pick, who is seeking a career restart at age 29. As the page turns to the regular season, with McCarthy now positioned as the No. 3 quarterback, Murray will take center stage.

 He begins with a clean slate after seven years of mixed reviews with the Cardinals, as the Vikings' veteran roster absorbed him in ways that a less-established group might not have. Known in Arizona as an introvert, Murray has found ways to connect -- and direct -- players from receiver Justin Jefferson to running back Aaron Jones Sr .

 "He has a different way of leading," Jones said. "He'll come and wrap his arms around you on the side. Give you some words, get on the same page, different things like that. It might not be to everybody [at once], but he's making sure he's getting his words in to each and everybody, one by one. You get a little more of a personal relationship like that."

 Murray told ESPN earlier this month that he hoped to make 2026 his " best season ever " and could not stop smiling this week when asked about Sunday's matchup.

 "I don't know how many years I played football," he said Thursday, "[but] this has got to be right up there for most anticipated. I can't tell you how excited and ready I am just to be on the field again."

 Gannon kept his comments vanilla when asked about Murray early in the week.

 "Really good player," Gannon said of his former quarterback. "He's in a really good offense with some elite players. Obviously I've got nothing but love and respect for K1. He's competitive, he's smart, can make all the throws, and beat you with his legs. So big time challenge."

 As this week went on and the final touches were being placed on the game plan, Packers players could tell this was a different kind of week because of their coordinator's connection to the opposing quarterback. They left little doubt that Gannon has given them some extra notes on Murray.

 "He gives a lot of respect to that quarterback, I'll say that much, as he should," Packers safety Evan Williams said. "He's done some great things in this league. He does a lot with his feet, is able to extend plays, is able to make plays on the run.

 "A guy like that isn't a first overall pick for nothing. So a lot of respect for him, but JG got answers. He's always got…

title: Betting buzz: Rams suffer worst opening loss by preseason Super Bowl favorite in 50 years
summary: The Los Angeles Rams' defeat in Week 1 in Melbourne, Australia was a historic low for a preseason Super Bowl champion.
full_text:
Everything that happens in sports has additional context when viewed from a sports betting perspective. From season-changing injuries to record-setting moments and so much more, the sports news cycle will constantly and significantly affect the sports betting industry. 

 Our NFL betting buzz file, with contributions from David Purdum, Doug Greenberg and others, aims to provide fans a look at the sports betting stories that are driving the conversation throughout each week of the season.  

 Key links: NFL futures | Awards odds |  Sports betting home  |  DraftKings   

 

 Sept 11: Rams suffer worst opening loss by preseason Super Bowl favorite in 50 years 

 by David Purdum 

 Preseason Super Bowl favorites have lost before, just not as badly as the Los Angeles Rams did Thursday in Melbourne, Australia.

 The Rams lost 27-7 to the San Francisco 49ers , becoming the first preseason Super Bowl favorite to lose its opener by 20 or more in the past 50 seasons, according to SportsOddHistory.com. The 1993 Dallas Cowboys lost by 19, and the 2017 New England Patriots and 1987 New York Giants each lost by 15 in their season openers. Both the Cowboys and Patriots would play in the Super Bowl in those seasons, with the Cowboys winning and the Patriots losing, but the Giants failed to make the playoffs.

 Los Angeles closed as a 3.5-point favorite over the 49ers and attracted the bulk of the bets and money from bettors. BetMGM reported that 60% of the money bet on the point spread was on the Rams.

 The Rams have attracted more than twice as many bets to win the Super Bowl as any other team at DraftKings Sportsbook. They remain the favorites to win the Super Bowl, NFC and NFC West, but their odds dipped from 5-1 to 6-1 after Thursday's loss, and their odds to win the NFC West shifted from -105 to +164.

 The 49ers, in turn, improved from +300 to +180 to win the division. The defending-champion Seattle Seahawks moved from +215 to +184 in the tightly contested NFC West. San Francisco improved from 19-1 to 14-1 to win the Super Bowl at DraftKings.

title: Expectations for Saints' Tyler Shough in Year 2? 'Doesn't faze me'
summary: Named a captain this season, the 26-year-old QB is out to prove he can lead New Orleans to the postseason.
full_text:
ON THE FINAL Monday before the Saints' 2026 season opener against the Detroit Lions , the entire team gathered at a local Italian restaurant in Metairie, Louisiana.

 The "Captains' dinner" is an annual tradition for the Saints, a chance to mingle, laugh, and look ahead to the season. It's where the Saints announce their team captains -- in this case, all nine of them.

 "It's kind of that official start of the regular season, Monday night, just having a dinner together," Saints coach Kellen Moore said. "And then we announce the captains, and they have an opportunity to share a message with the rest of the team."

 Zach Wood , Justin Reid , Cameron Jordan and Erik McCoy had all been captains before. Others, such as Chris Rumph II , David Edwards , Kaden Elliss and Chase Young are new.

 Quarterback Tyler Shough , 26, was perhaps the most significant addition. Saints captains are determined by a player vote, and only one year before, the team's 53 players declined to name a quarterback to the captain's group.

 

 Shough, who took over for Spencer Rattler as the starter midway through the 2025 season, has spent this offseason proving he has earned a permanent role. He has immersed himself into the culture of New Orleans, aligned with Saints legends such as Pro Football Hall of Famer Drew Brees and worked to get to know his teammates on-and-off the field. Shough has shown he can be the face of the franchise, and the players' vote of confidence backs up that statement.

 "Everybody in the room knew from OTAs on who the leader of the team was and he's done a really great job," Elliss said. 

 Shough later called being named a captain one of the biggest things he has accomplished in his career so far.

 "The NFL is such a hard business because there's so much fluidity," Shough said. "... I felt like with this business and the guys that come in and out, you have to be really intentional about getting to know all of your teammates ... and it means a lot. But I also know that there's more work to be done."

 As the Saints prepare to face the Lions Sunday ( 1 p.m. ET, Fox ) in their first of two road games to start the season, the true test of his leadership and his abilities start now. For Shough and the rest of the team, the bar has been raised from last season. Can Shough prove he's capable of translating all the momentum from the end of the 2025 season into 2026 and lead the team back to the playoffs for the first time since Brees retired five years ago?

 He's certainly going to try.

 "He's mature beyond his years, especially beyond his years in the league being a quarterback," Elliss said of Shough. "He speaks much more like a Year 6-7 type of guy and he's going to have a great year."

 
 THE LEADUP TO the captains' vote didn't happen overnight.

 Over the past eight months Shough has juggled all the things that come with being a starting quarterback. Once a backup whose sole job was to run the scout team, now Shough is being pulled in different directions. He and his wife Jordan had their first child , son Grayson, in February. More is asked of him off the field from family obligations, to media and appearance requests, and from his coaches and teammates, who look to him to set the tone for the team.

 His time is carefully structured to make sure nothing slips through the cracks.

 "It's very routine based. I've built out a system ... that I try and stick to and have a lot of time, maybe on an off-day to go do charity stuff or maybe a shoot or some family time. But throughout the week it's very much detailed as far as built-in media time, built-in meetings, and obviously have my own time. A lot of time I just get in early to do a lot of prep work and then stay late to do it," Shough said.

 Shough has operated with intentionality and looked for ways to coordinate responsibilities while also connecting with teammates.

 In early February, he rode on a Mardi Gras float with teammates like McCoy. With McCoy's second child being born around the same time as Shough's a weeks later, parenting topics became a common thread between them and Edwards, whose fourth child was also born this past winter.

 

 "Just knowing that we're all kind of in the same season, like, 'Oh, how'd your kids sleep last night? Oh, mine was up at 1, 3, 5, and 7 [a.m.].' It's fun to talk about, and I feel like that gives you a way to bond even just outside of ball," McCoy said during camp.

 Shough didn't take much of a step back once he became a dad. On the contrary, he appeared to be everywhere in the spring. Brees and Shough made a guest appearance during the Savannah Bananas stop in New Orleans . In April, Shough went to the Hondo Rodeo Fest in New Orleans and golfed in the Zurich Classic Celebrity Shootout.

 And during all the engagements, Shough has been a cheerleader for each new Saints player, taking free agents such as Travis Etienne Jr . to dinner and posting on social media his excitement with each new draft pick New Orleans selected.

 "He was the first guy on the team to text me after I signed," Elliss said.

 But the biggest effort -- and the one that further shows the leadership gains the young QB has made -- was when Shough organized a week-long trip to California, offering to pay for his teammates' accommodations to entice them to participate. Some of the attendees included Etienne, running back Audric Estime , tight end Noah Fant , wide receivers Chris Olave and Devaughn Vele . Rookie wideouts Barion Brown and Bryce Lance went as well.

 Shough and tight end Juwan Johnson stayed in the same house that week with their families. The two men have known each other since they played at Oregon and have reconnected since Shough was drafted No. 40 overall by the Saints last year. But the California adventure was another way to strengthen their bond.

 "It was a full house, three kids, two dogs. Oh man, it was a lot, but it was extremely fun," Johnson said. "When you have that camaraderie and you're able to be around people, even staying in the same house, I feel like you learn a lot about people. And that translates on the field, believe it or not."

 Johnson said riding roller coasters or eating breakfast together might not seem like big moments, but it builds friendships that make teammates want to fight for each other.

 "I'm going to do whatever I can to make plays because we took that trip to San Diego or we started throwing routes in February or we went and did some things together. ... You spend time together, you find ways to dig a little deeper because you know that person on a more intimate and deeper level," Johnson said.

 

 
 SHOUGH WOULD BE one of the first people to admit he is still a work in progress. He has described himself as "light years ahead" of where he was at this time last year in training camp, when he was not quite ready to be the starter yet.

 A year ago Shough didn't truly push Rattler in camp until the Saints held scrimmages with "call-it" periods from both coordinators. When the scripted part of practice was taken away to raise the competitive stakes, Shough rose to the challenge.

 In November, with the Saints struggling to a 1-7 start, the coaches felt confident enough in Shough to start him over Rattler based on the progress they'd seen in practice.

 "You always worry about that transition from scout team to playing in games," Saints offensive coordinator Doug Nussmeier said. "But we'd already seen that. We knew his eyes were in the right place. He was seeing things. It just wasn't happening fast enough. But I think probably Week 4 or 5 you really started to see like, OK, he's starting to get it."

 A similar step forward happened this offseason. The Saints' offense didn't automatically gel in the first few weeks of camp. The Saints ran an unscripted red zone session on Aug. 11 in which the defense clearly won, with Shough throwing two interceptions and almost going for a third. Multiple false starts were also an issue for the…

title: Can Saquon Barkley recapture his 2024 dominance?
summary: Philadelphia's heavy under-center, wide zone scheme is largely new to the veteran running back.
full_text:
PHILADELPHIA -- There were moments this summer when running back Saquon Barkley stirred the echoes, flashing a quick burst or a sudden jump cut or a moment of competitive overdrive that brought to the surface what he's done and what he's capable of.

 Day 8 of training camp might have been the highlight. It started when he barreled into the end zone on a deep red zone run and finished the play with a well-spirited shove of cornerback Quinyon Mitchell , helping awake a sagging offense.

 Moments later, with the unit backed up, Barkley hit Jordan Davis with a hop step move that left the defensive tackle chasing wind as Barkley sped through the crease and raced to daylight.

 The days the attack looked best this offseason were the ones when Barkley was featured. This should come as no surprise to anyone who watched their Super Bowl run in 2024, when Barkley set the NFL record for most single-season rushing yards, including playoffs, or saw how the operation fell off last year as the ground game labored to find its footing behind an ailing offensive line.

 But it was a reminder that for all the discussion about quarterback Jalen Hurts and his fit in the new system , so much of the Eagles' fate is actually tied to whether Barkley, in Year 9 and five months away from his 30th birthday, can recapture his NFL Offensive Player of the Year form while acclimating to a new scheme.

 

 "The more productive we are in the run game and stuff feeds off that, we'll see the Saquon of two years ago," Eagles right tackle Lane Johnson  said. "We'll see the big plays, we'll see him flexed out wide at receiver, see him in the screen game."

 Barkley acknowledged he's "going back to like I'm a little kid again" in some respects, working on his steps and techniques to match the new Kyle Shanahan/Sean McVay-like system implemented by offensive coordinator Sean Mannion. This heavy under-center, wide zone scheme is largely new to him.

 "Guys who do really well in outside zone scheme stuff are more like one-cut backs," he said. "I naturally, especially after my ACL [tear in 2020], like to cut off of two, so just prepping myself."

 Barkley is known to study his contemporaries -- players such as  Christian McCaffrey , Bijan Robinson , Jonathan Taylor , Derrick Henry and Jahmyr Gibbs -- as well as the "OGs" to see how he can improve his game. This offseason, he reached out specifically to Todd Gurley , the former Ram great, for advice on how to thrive in this type of system.

 The main difference between inside zone -- which he has majored in since coming to Philly -- and outside zone is that inside zone requires a healthy amount of patience and a strong jump cut, Barkley said, whereas outside zone necessitates a mindset of "attacking it more, stretching them, getting the defense to expand, and when you get the opportunity to put your foot in the ground, do it fast, violent and physical."

 With the offensive line creating wide angles by getting out in space, Johnson likened it to "riding that wave," where if the back can't get to the perimeter, he'll read the backside blocks and choose the gap to shoot through.

 "I feel like it creates a lot more running lanes instead of, we were in more of a narrow style angle last year so it's more sideline to sideline and his ability to cut back," Johnson said.

 As training camp showed, the big-play potential is there.

 That was the bread and butter for the 2024 Eagles offense, as Barkley led all backs with 46 rushes of 10-plus yards. A lot of the credit goes to the offensive front, with Barkley also leading running backs in average yards before contact (4.17). Last season, the yards before contact plummeted to 2.31 yards on average (25th) and he dropped to eighth in runs of 10-plus yards (28). Overall, he ran for 1,140 yards (4.1 YPC) last season compared to 2,005 (5.8 YPC) the season prior.

 The offensive line enters the season largely healthy, offering promise that Barkley will have some big holes to fly through once again.

 

 "I think he's been very excited about being able to run in a new scheme and maybe have some more consistent action to some degree," Hurts said. "I know he's worked his tail off and I have a lot of confidence and excitement for him and his ability and what he's going to do."

 Not only is the offensive line in a better place but Barkley is as well. He shot past his career high in carries (345) during the regular season in 2024 and added 91 more rushes in the postseason. That number fell to 280 last season. And while the wild-card playoff exit against the San Francisco 49ers was disappointing for the Eagles, it gave everyone more of a physical and mental break this offseason, including the 29-year-old Barkley.

 "Huge," said running backs coach Jemal Singleton, on the benefits of the longer layoff. "He could take the time from the offseason and get his rest but then come back and start working. So I feel like he's in a really, really good place now. ... It's going to be exciting to kind of see him go."

 Singleton can see it most in the conditioning part of it where Barkley, who shares a backfield this season with a pair of capable backs in Tank Bigsby and Will Shipley , has stayed on the field for more plays during long drives while looking "explosive."

 Put the fresh legs with a revitalized offensive front in this run scheme, and there is optimism Barkley can ascend to the top of the running back class once again.

 "Being a better playmaker," Barkley said on what he wants to improve from last season. "That's why I was brought here, that's what I feel I'm one of the best in the league [at] and just bringing that back."
